It forms over land, not sea, because the sea does not cool appreciably overnight, and it typically burns off with morning insolation.
ADy5UIIovmj3Z9B0XlKh: At a warm front the advancing warm air is less dense, so it cannot displace the cold air and instead rides up over it on a shallow slope of roughly 1:150. That gentle, widespread ascent gives the extensive layer cloud, continuous precipitation and slow clearance typical of a warm front. At a cold front the denser cold air undercuts the warm air on a much steeper slope.
aJ6vjCPagoqym0KuGuFQ: Virga, or fallstreaks, are trails of precipitation leaving a cloud base and evaporating or subliming before reaching the surface, seen as wispy streaks hanging beneath the cloud. They indicate a dry layer below the cloud, and the evaporative cooling can drive strong downdraughts and microbursts, so virga beneath a convective cloud is an operational warning sign.
aJkzFkFHzOzkoWvoeKxH: The WMO standard exposure for an anemometer is 10 m above the ground over open, unobstructed terrain, so that the measurement is representative of the free airstream and not distorted by buildings, trees or surface roughness. Placing it lower, or on a roof, would give readings biased by local friction and eddies and would not be comparable between stations.
AnpS8cstNYuZp0vtY5bP: The ICAO Standard Atmosphere has a sea-level temperature of 15 C and pressure of 1013.25 hPa, with temperature falling at 6.5 C per 1000 m (1.98 C per 1000 ft) up to the tropopause at 11 km, where it reaches -56.5 C and then remains constant to 20 km. The 3 C per 1000 m distractor is the dry adiabatic rate, which applies to a moving parcel, not to the standard environment.
apGm7TUkD68sDCtNGC0f: Airmass (or heat) thunderstorms develop within a single warm, moist, unstable air mass when strong afternoon surface heating over land triggers convection. They peak in the mid to late afternoon, are usually isolated and short-lived, and dissipate after sunset as the heating source is removed. Frontal thunderstorms, by contrast, are triggered by mechanical lifting and can occur at any hour.
ApY3nRDifBqzIAVnIHCl: Showers (SH) come from convective, cumuliform cloud, where strong updraughts allow droplets to grow large by collision and coalescence and where the cloud has limited horizontal extent. The result is precipitation that starts and stops abruptly, varies rapidly in intensity, and covers a small area. Stratiform cloud in stable air produces continuous, widespread, steadier precipitation instead.
As1qE2aiFmVMSmITCoCp: The tropopause is highest where the troposphere is deepest and warmest, so over the equator it lies at about 16-18 km (roughly FL550), against about 11 km in mid-latitudes and 8 km over the poles. This is why tropical cumulonimbus can reach far higher tops than mid-latitude storms - there is no stable lid until much greater heights.
AtYrrTLbypaw2AQN9ZUb: The wet south-west monsoon withdraws from India through September, October and November as the land cools and the thermal low over the subcontinent fills, and it is replaced by the dry north-east monsoon blowing off the Asian landmass. The reverse transition, north-east to south-west, occurs in April and May.
aUOiMw2GhLGuSKlD8gkH: A frontal depression is steered by the flow in its own warm sector, so the centre moves roughly parallel to the warm sector isobars, with the low pressure on the left in the northern hemisphere. The speed of movement is broadly proportional to the warm sector geostrophic wind. This is the basic rule of thumb for forecasting where the low will be next.
auYYVXKPeXawWW9ndNRm: Serious icing requires abundant supercooled liquid water, which means a thick cloud with a high water content, sub-zero temperatures and continuous droplet supply. Nimbostratus is deep, water-rich and extensive, so an aircraft stays in it long enough to accumulate moderate to severe ice. Not every cloud gives severe icing - thin cirrus is all ice crystals - and clear air, above or below the freezing level, has no liquid water to freeze.
b1W9z7VK0zW9NP2SpT7O: Ahead of an approaching warm front the pressure falls steadily as the depression approaches. QFE (pressure at aerodrome level) and QNH (that pressure reduced to sea level) are two expressions of the same atmospheric pressure separated only by the fixed aerodrome elevation, so they always move together. Both therefore decrease. Any answer showing them moving in opposite directions is physically impossible.
B3cpgdwwTbifz39qQztO: This is a wind shear performance problem, not a limits problem. Using runway 27 you start with a 5 kt headwind and, on climbing through the inversion, meet a 30 kt tailwind - a 35 kt loss of airspeed at 300 ft, which is a classic shear accident. Using runway 09 you accept a 5 kt tailwind on the roll and then gain a 30 kt headwind through the shear layer, an increasing-performance shear. Departing into the shear with the light tailwind is the safe choice.
b4jpse5H7JlUAq5bdRSC: The 0 C to -10 C band holds the greatest concentration of large supercooled water droplets, which freeze on impact and produce the heaviest, most tenacious clear ice. Between -10 C and -20 C the cloud is increasingly mixed and rime becomes typical, and below about -20 C to -40 C most cloud is glaciated into ice crystals, which bounce off rather than adhere.
B5yQv2TxSNll3yLY80AW: Cirrocumulus (CC) is a high cloud, so in temperate latitudes its base lies roughly 16,500-45,000 ft above sea level. With the ground itself only 1600 ft up, the base is on the order of 15,000-35,000 ft above the terrain. Remember that cloud classification is by base height above the surface: low 0-6500 ft, medium 6500-23,000 ft, high above that, and all three bands vary with latitude.
bAaBdZUq2XXqzwk59BLj: QFE is the pressure at aerodrome level, QNH is that value reduced to sea level using ISA, and QFF is the same value reduced to sea level using the ACTUAL temperature profile. The temperature only matters over the height being reduced through. With the aerodrome exactly at sea level there is nothing to reduce, so QFE, QNH and QFF are all the same 1022 hPa and the missing temperature is irrelevant.
bDE93pqh9UVaaUABBSej: Below the jet core the cold air lies on the polar side, so a rising outside temperature means you are tracking toward the equator, i.e. southward in the northern hemisphere. The jet itself blows from west to east, so on a southerly heading that westerly flow arrives on the aircraft's right-hand side. The reverse holds above the core, where the temperature gradient is inverted.
bfqlB3Hbg4zuBz1Zh6dl: With 1013 set the altimeter reads 1310 ft on a runway that is 1715 ft high, so it is under-reading by 405 ft. At about 27 ft per hPa, that is 405 / 27 = 15 hPa. The subscale must be increased by 15 hPa to make the altimeter read the true elevation, so QNH = 1013 + 15 = 1028 hPa. A reading below true elevation always means QNH is above 1013.
BhjDxdiu7nfXFdhRSKbX: Turning right to allow for drift means the drift is to the left, so the wind is coming from the aircraft's right. Buys Ballot's law for the southern hemisphere: stand with your back to the wind and low pressure is on your RIGHT. With the wind on the aircraft's right beam, backing into the wind puts the low ahead of the aircraft. (In the northern hemisphere the low would be behind.)
bJ6Dh0sE5zm9aJPN8wPs: The polar front jet is the jet directly associated with a surface front, because it exists as the thermal-wind consequence of the sharp temperature contrast across the polar front, and it lies above and slightly on the cold side of the surface front. The subtropical jet sits at the poleward limit of the Hadley cell with no surface front beneath it, and the arctic and equatorial easterly jets are seasonal features unconnected to a frontal system.
bMVz9IaGOV7Uv8uM8xTr: Report C shows Q1009 (low and, by inference, falling), a south-westerly 15 kt, a lowering multi-layer cloud sheet at 3000 and 7000 ft, a temperature-dewpoint spread of only 3 C, and BECMG 4000 forecasting deteriorating visibility. That is the signature of an approaching warm front. The others show high pressure with NOSIG, or fog under a high, none of which imply frontal rain.
BO3mjRJSuYMSm0KQ4S57: A microburst is an intense, small-scale downdraught from a convective cloud. The descending air is cooled by evaporating precipitation, so it is denser and colder than its surroundings, which is what drives it down and makes it spread violently outward on striking the ground. On approach it produces a headwind gain, then a severe downdraught, then a sudden headwind loss - the most dangerous low-level wind shear there is.
boi8dEePtRr9rnjO1ALt: By definition a downburst is classed as a microburst when its damaging outflow spans 4 km or less; anything larger is a macroburst. The intense phase is very short, typically 1-5 minutes, which is exactly what makes it so dangerous: it can develop and strike the approach path between one aircraft and the next with no useful warning.
boqhM3L2InXlYhYC2Bk2: A jet stream is a very flat feature: typically a few thousand feet deep (about 2 km) but 100-300 km wide, so the depth-to-width ratio is on the order of 1:100. That is why a climb or descent of a few thousand feet can take you out of the core, while a lateral escape requires a large track change - the standard advice for escaping jet-stream CAT is to change level.
bXQr64IMwX521TNOe7CL: The classic passage sequence is: several hours of continuous rain or snow from nimbostratus ahead of the warm front; a break in the warm sector, where precipitation largely stops and low stratus, drizzle and mild, murky conditions prevail; then a short, sharp burst of showers or thunderstorms as the cold front goes through, followed by clearing skies, good visibility and cumulus in the cold air behind. Precipitation increasing in the warm sector would be the wrong way round.
Cedq9X7YBx7kJpK0jhiy: One knot is one nautical mile per hour, and one nautical mile is 1.852 km, so 25 kt is 25 x 1.852 = 46 km/h, roughly 45. The quick mental conversion is to double the knots and subtract about 10 percent: 25 becomes 50, less 5, giving 45.
ceq23cLkrofhxV00D6Wg: The geostrophic wind is the speed at which the Coriolis force exactly balances a given pressure gradient force. Coriolis force is proportional to the sine of the latitude, so it is weaker nearer the equator and a higher wind speed is needed to achieve the balance. For the same isobar spacing, the geostrophic wind therefore increases as latitude decreases and is greatest at 40 N.
cFJDRvdFnnv7MSwUPTTV: Drizzle (DZ) consists of very small droplets, under 0.5 mm, with almost no fall speed, so it can only come from a cloud with a very low base, no significant updraught and plenty of small droplets: stratus, or stratocumulus. Altostratus is a medium-level cloud and produces light continuous rain or snow, not drizzle, and much of it evaporates before reaching the ground.
cjFhWNHK7qwyp96Thx25: Typical polar front jet core speeds are 60-100 kt in summer and 150-200 kt in winter, with 250 kt considered exceptional. Speeds around 350 kt have been recorded, mainly over Japan in winter where the polar and subtropical jets merge, but they are genuinely rare worldwide. So 350 kt is possible but very unusual - not impossible, and certainly not routine.
cL4oE1Ai7nkF4j9VaRG7: An unsaturated (dry) parcel cools at the dry adiabatic lapse rate, which is fixed at 1 C per 100 m, equivalently 3 C per 1000 ft. Once the parcel saturates, latent heat release slows the cooling to the saturated adiabatic rate, which is variable and lower. The 0.65 C per 100 m figure is the ISA environmental rate and applies to the surrounding atmosphere, not to a rising parcel.
CLPjFgjJHg3Ng2QVfkSs: A cold air pool (cut-off low) is a mass of cold air aloft, often with little or no signature on the surface chart. Cold air is dense, so the pressure surfaces above it are depressed and it appears as a closed low centre of contour heights on an upper chart such as the 500 hPa. Because it is cold aloft over relatively warmer air below, the lapse rate is steep and it brings instability, showers and thunderstorms.
CM580hrgxblueyRM8GjC: QFE is the pressure at aerodrome level, so it is QNH reduced by the pressure equivalent of the aerodrome elevation. At about 27 ft per hPa, 1411 ft is 1411 / 27 = 52 hPa. QFE = 994 - 52 = 942 hPa. QFE is always lower than QNH for an aerodrome above sea level, and the two are equal only at sea level.
cpwjUuYV65FJkVKXikLl: With QFE set, the altimeter datum is the official aerodrome elevation, so it reads zero on the ground and shows height above that reference - but only in ISA conditions, since the instrument is calibrated to the standard atmosphere and non-standard temperature introduces an error. It cannot be the height of the wheels, because the reference is the aerodrome datum point rather than the particular part of the runway being crossed.
CRrMt88yKbfB7raTpJHb: The tropopause marks the top of the troposphere, where the steady decrease of temperature with height comes to an end and gives way to isothermal conditions and then, higher in the stratosphere, a temperature increase. Pressure continues to fall with height right through it. Because the tropopause is stable it acts as a lid on convection and on the vertical transport of water vapour.
cS2ECgbKOwNjN8BzJDfe: The dry adiabatic lapse rate is 1 C per 100 m, equal to 3 C per 1000 ft, and it is a constant set by thermodynamics rather than by the state of the atmosphere. The 0.65 C per 100 m alternative is the ISA environmental lapse rate, which describes the surrounding air rather than a moving parcel, and 2 C per 1000 ft is roughly the ISA rate expressed in feet.
cT01ZBCgxr1XDWwg5GE4: Isobars join points of equal pressure, and their spacing is a direct measure of the pressure gradient. Close spacing means a steep gradient, a large pressure gradient force and therefore a strong wind; widely spaced isobars mean light winds. Lines of equal temperature are isotherms, and surface winds cross isobars at a shallow angle of about 10-30 degrees, never perpendicular.
CTh4IneM9OJ7298pLWqN: The ICAO Standard Atmosphere is defined at mean sea level by a pressure of 1013.25 hPa (29.92 inHg), a temperature of 15 C and a density of 1.225 kg/m3, with temperature falling at 1.98 C per 1000 ft to the tropopause at 36,090 ft. It is the reference against which all altimeters, flight levels and aircraft performance data are calibrated.
cvbfTgPBJdUGins2gp6g: High cloud - cirrus, cirrocumulus and cirrostratus - forms above about 16,500 ft where temperatures are typically -40 C or colder, so it is composed almost entirely of ice crystals. That is why high cloud gives optical effects such as haloes and sun dogs, and why it presents very little icing risk: ice crystals bounce off the airframe rather than adhering.
CXN3A9THCzEsaFDUFwaO: The cumulus, or building, stage is defined by updraughts throughout the cell, drawing in warm moist air and lifting the growing cloud, with no precipitation yet reaching the ground. Downdraughts, surface rain and frequent lightning all mark the mature stage, which begins when precipitation starts falling out of the cloud base.
CxY97s7Vq2ag4mOXPRWD: Hail requires updraughts strong enough to keep a growing stone suspended above the freezing level while it accretes successive layers of ice, and only cumulonimbus produces that. Nimbostratus is deep but has only gentle ascent, giving continuous rain or snow, while altocumulus and cirrostratus have neither the depth nor the vertical motion.
dAHHyBT9Ok3vZvsSk5Ip: Fair weather cumulus (cumulus humilis) is the visible top of convective thermals, so its presence means the air below and within cloud level is convectively active and therefore turbulent - a familiar bumpy ride for light aircraft on a sunny afternoon. The same convection mixes the lower atmosphere thoroughly, which normally gives GOOD surface visibility, and the shallow, capped nature of these clouds is precisely what distinguishes them from thunderstorm precursors.
dCIoJH2ZRi2sfOy1dLfc: Heavy freezing rain (+FZRA) is the most severe airframe icing condition there is: large supercooled drops strike the airframe, run back and freeze as dense clear ice well aft of the protected leading edges, at accretion rates that overwhelm de-icing systems. Hail and ice pellets are already frozen and bounce off, and snow showers are made of ice crystals that generally do not adhere to a cold airframe.
dcKZDJpJN5pH0QhE3qIc: In the southern hemisphere air circulates CLOCKWISE around a low, and friction below 2000 ft adds an inward component toward the centre. Flying directly away from the low, the circulation therefore arrives from the aircraft's left, and the inflow component - which is directed back toward the low, i.e. behind the aircraft - shows up as a slight headwind. So the wind is from the left and slightly on the nose.
DhxiWN9lKAYyUWjnQz2V: Strong vertical development means a parcel lifted from the surface stays warmer and less dense than its surroundings through a deep layer, which is the definition of an unstable atmosphere. An inversion or warm air aloft would cap the convection and produce flattened, spreading cloud instead, and the vigorous mixing that builds large cumulus usually improves rather than degrades surface visibility.
dlYRjUKQ44lXxFFj64rI: Setting 1013 when the actual QNH is 1023 means the subscale is 10 hPa too LOW, so the altimeter under-reads by 10 x 27 = 270 ft. On the ground at an elevation of 290 ft it will therefore show 290 - 270 = 20 ft. The general rule: a subscale setting below the actual QNH makes the altimeter read low, and one above it makes the altimeter read high.
dMo2V1HzZ4b3CcsFcA0m: Precipitation is water, liquid or solid, actually falling out of a cloud and reaching the ground. Drizzle (DZ) qualifies. TS is a thunderstorm, which is a descriptor of a convective situation rather than the precipitation itself; SQ is a squall, a sudden increase in wind; and SA is sand, a lithometeor. Only DZ is coded in the precipitation group.
dp9RxBJKIIshD8GSl7o3: The ice type is decided by how fast a droplet freezes on impact, and that is governed by the temperature and by droplet size. Large drops near 0 C release enough latent heat to freeze slowly, so water runs back and forms dense clear ice; small drops well below freezing freeze instantly, trapping air and giving opaque rime. Airspeed and aerofoil shape affect catch rate and where the ice sits, but not which type forms.
Dtv79JvXRHWEboEnGQHE: The Chinook is the Foehn wind of the eastern slopes of the Rockies. Air forced up the windward side cools at the saturated rate and loses its moisture as precipitation, then descends the lee side warming at the faster dry adiabatic rate, so it arrives markedly warmer and much drier than the air at the same level upwind. Temperature rises of 20 C in a few hours are common, which is why it is called the snow-eater.
DuY56mDj45VKkVeQzYbJ: A summer warm sector in tropical maritime air is warm, very moist and stable, having been cooled from below on its long sea track. That stability traps moisture and pollution in the lower layers, giving haze, mist and low stratus, so surface visibility is typically only moderate - a few kilometres - rather than good. It is the classic murky, mild, grey warm-sector weather.
Dw4UMdI1YhRcOxcvwCK0: In the ICAO Standard Atmosphere the temperature falls at 0.65 C per 100 m (6.5 C per km, or 1.98 C per 1000 ft) from 15 C at sea level up to the tropopause at 11 km, where it reaches -56.5 C and then stays constant. This is a defined reference profile, not a measurement; the real atmosphere's environmental lapse rate varies continuously.
DWxEHDDRyPflOOikKsSq: Freezing rain gives the fastest accretion of all because the droplets are very large, the liquid water content of the air is high and the drops arrive already supercooled, so they run back and freeze as dense clear ice over a large area of the airframe. Stratus has small droplets and low water content, cirrus is glaciated, and snow consists of ice crystals that do not adhere to a cold surface.
DYuafVj0duq0o8MjZc7u: Cirrus lies above about 20,000 ft where temperatures are typically -40 C or lower, so it is made of ice crystals with essentially no supercooled liquid water. With no liquid water there is nothing to freeze onto the airframe, so icing is nil. Cirrus is also thin and tenuous, so in-cloud horizontal visibility remains good, generally well over 1000 m.
E0IqiqTzwY4xZH5CpagH: The ICAO standard lapse rate is 1.98 C per 1000 ft, taken as 2 C per 1000 ft for mental arithmetic. Descending from FL140 to FL110 is 3000 ft, so the temperature rises by about 6 C: -12 + 6 = -6 C. Watch the direction of the sum - going down means warming.
eC7EcJlARNi2lkStFbWR: The description - a grey layer with a uniform base and appearance, sometimes giving drizzle or snow grains, through which the sun's outline stays clearly discernible, and which can appear as ragged patches (stratus fractus) - is the WMO definition of stratus. The visible solar disc is the giveaway: altostratus renders the sun as a diffuse bright patch as if seen through ground glass, and nimbostratus obscures it entirely.
ED82kMGKyXATBjRB9TxJ: QNH and QFF are both the station pressure reduced to sea level, but QNH uses the ISA temperature profile while QFF uses the ACTUAL temperature. Air 10 C warmer than ISA is less dense, so the real column between the airfield and sea level weighs less and QFF gains less pressure in the reduction. QNH, computed on the denser standard column, gains more, so QNH is greater than QFF: more than 1016 hPa.
eg1zMokhv868fmuKHcTT: Nocturnal radiation cools the ground, and with a moderate rather than light wind the mechanical turbulence mixes that cooling upward through a layer instead of confining it to the surface. The whole layer reaches saturation aloft rather than at the ground, so the result is a low stratus sheet instead of fog. Convection and instability give cumuliform cloud, and latent heat release opposes cooling.
egJc7Xxke38YelELNJNT: Friction slows the air near the surface. The Coriolis force is proportional to wind speed, so it weakens too, while the pressure gradient force - set by the isobar spacing - is unchanged. The balance is therefore broken in favour of the pressure gradient force, and the resultant wind is turned toward low pressure, crossing the isobars by about 10 degrees over the sea and 30 degrees over land.
EjSOzQqVOItiDKdZAj2H: Hail can be encountered anywhere in and beneath a cumulonimbus, from the surface right up to the cloud top, and in temperate latitudes vigorous CB tops can reach FL450. It can also be thrown out of the anvil and met in apparently clear air several miles from the cell, which is why the standard advice is to avoid a CB by at least 10 NM rather than to rely on any altitude band being safe.
EM3qoIRUld3GzLYF7lrX: In August the north Indian Ocean is under the summer monsoon regime, and the tropical easterly jet dominates the upper troposphere over southern Asia at around 10-15 N. The upper-level flow at FL370 is therefore easterly. A Bombay to Bangkok routing is eastbound, straight into that flow, so headwinds must be planned for.
EMqwIIWzy8mSpT9aFQg1: With a high pressure area and a slack gradient, the synoptic wind is too weak to mask local effects, so the diurnal circulation takes over. On a sunny afternoon the land heats far faster than the sea, forming a shallow thermal low over the land, and the surface wind blows from sea to land as a sea breeze. The reverse land breeze, land to sea, develops overnight and is normally weaker.
EOQBeOuusfzVfOC7sMHb: Relative humidity is the amount of water vapour present expressed as a percentage of the maximum the air could hold at that temperature. It therefore depends on two things: the actual moisture content, and the temperature, which sets the saturation capacity. This is why simply warming air lowers its relative humidity without removing any moisture at all.
eRKgLRkq5TX6TObE8SeO: The polar front jet core sits at the tropopause break, on the warm-air side of the polar front and just beneath the higher, warm-air tropopause - in other words within the warm air mass, immediately above the sloping frontal surface. This is why the strongest CAT is usually found on the cold (polar) side and just below the core, where the vertical and horizontal shear is greatest.
EuIjKJQzgSGfPqrVPEfK: Burning kerosene produces carbon dioxide and a large quantity of water vapour. At cruise levels the surrounding air is extremely cold, so that added vapour immediately saturates the exhaust plume and condenses, then freezes onto soot particles as ice crystals, forming a visible trail. Whether the trail persists or evaporates depends on the humidity of the ambient air, which is why contrails are a useful indicator of upper-level moisture.
EWxOeTZMcqVmLuXL1ah0: At -12 C a cloud contains both supercooled droplets and ice crystals, so the accretion is mixed ice rather than pure clear or pure rime. Orographic lifting on the windward side of mountains forces continuous ascent, which sustains a much higher liquid water content than a flat-terrain cloud of the same type, so the severity climbs to moderate or severe. Nimbostratus is deep and extensive, which prolongs exposure.
Ex85wOt5hIjKi9vcpNnQ: Stability describes the atmosphere's response to a displaced parcel. In a stable layer a rising parcel cools faster than its surroundings, becomes colder and denser than the ambient air, so its upward motion is damped and it returns to its original level. A rapid decrease of temperature with height (a steep environmental lapse rate) is the signature of instability, not stability.
eXUMw1eobBpUDS4JmcwW: The standard upper-air charts and their approximate ISA heights are 850 hPa near FL50, 700 hPa near FL100, 500 hPa near FL180, 300 hPa near FL300 and 200 hPa near FL390. A pressure level of 30,065 ft therefore corresponds to the 300 hPa chart, which is the usual chart for locating the polar front jet.
exWtfwAIQYo4Em3G30zm: QFF reduces the station pressure to sea level using the ACTUAL temperature, while QNH uses the ISA profile. Air 10 C colder than ISA is denser, so the real column between the airfield and sea level weighs more and QFF gains more pressure in the reduction than QNH does. QNH is therefore lower than QFF: less than 1016 hPa. (Cold air, QFF above QNH; warm air, the reverse.)
ezRHIpAfZpIUyrBjVjrM: MIFG is shallow fog: a layer less than 2 m deep over land, so it lies below the observer's eye level. Horizontal visibility is measured at eye level, above the fog layer, so a reported visibility of 5000 m is entirely consistent with shallow fog beneath. The temperature and dewpoint both being 2 C confirms saturation at the surface, exactly as expected. The report is valid.
F1U0tYbKPCd5SLLcD5vN: The summer (south-west) monsoon draws deep, very moist maritime air off the Indian Ocean over a strongly heated landmass. The result is marked instability with towering cumulonimbus, frequent thunderstorms and torrential rain showers, often organised into monsoon depressions. Sandstorms and fog belong to the dry north-east monsoon in the winter half of the year.
f4U5pA2vpxXxAJptkQ58: On a sunny afternoon the sea breeze blows from sea to land, and since the runway lies parallel to the coast that flow is essentially perpendicular to the runway - a pure crosswind. Fix the geometry from the downwind leg: downwind is over the sea with the airfield on the RIGHT, so the sea is on the aircraft's left. Final is flown in the opposite direction, so the sea is now on the right, and the crosswind comes from the right.
fbw0B0LsQphfJszUDeIE: CAVOK requires all three of: visibility 10 km or more; no cloud below 5000 ft or below the highest minimum sector altitude, whichever is greater, and no CB or TCU at any level whatever; and no significant weather. Low drifting snow (DRSN) counts as significant weather, so its absence is guaranteed. Cloud above 5000 ft may still be present, and CAVOK says nothing about wind shear.
fFCKgtN39suiRavbi9lU: ICAO grades icing as light, moderate or severe. Severe means the accretion rate is such that de-icing and anti-icing equipment cannot control it and the ice is degrading performance to a dangerous degree, so an immediate change of heading and/or level is required. Moderate makes a diversion desirable, and light needs action only if the encounter is prolonged beyond about an hour.
fg2PZ9tKKUs4jD4mPomw: Stability is determined by comparing the environmental lapse rate - the actual temperature profile of the surrounding air - with the adiabatic rate at which a displaced parcel would change temperature. The ELR is the variable in that comparison and is what a radiosonde ascent measures. The adiabatic rates are fixed constants, and surface temperature or pressure alone say nothing about the profile aloft.
fi32GkoIgzAHCtgtjbgN: Rime ice forms from small supercooled droplets, typically at temperatures below about -10 C. Each tiny drop freezes almost instantly on impact, trapping air between the frozen droplets, so the deposit is white, opaque, brittle and relatively light. It builds forward from the leading edge and, being brittle, is readily shed by de-icing boots - unlike clear ice, which comes from large drops that run back before freezing.
FimeVD7ZkducdBnCYGET: QNH reduces the station pressure to sea level using the ISA temperature profile; QFF does the same using the ACTUAL temperature. Air 10 C colder than ISA is denser, so the real 200 m column weighs more than the standard one and QFF gains more pressure in the reduction. QFF is therefore greater than QNH: more than 1009 hPa. Cold air gives QFF above QNH; warm air gives QFF below QNH.
FJkV0NsFJ0TpdUVTAOFl: In the ICAO Standard Atmosphere the temperature falls uniformly at 1.98 C per 1000 ft (0.65 C per 100 m) from 15 C at sea level to -56.5 C at the tropopause, 36,090 ft. Above the tropopause it remains constant to 20 km. The real atmosphere frequently departs from this, most obviously through inversions, but the standard profile is the reference for altimetry and performance.
FNzxJZ6u2wqyuS2zf2hn: Radiation fog needs the ground to radiate its heat away freely overnight, which requires little or no cloud - a cloud sheet would radiate heat back down and prevent the surface cooling. The other requirements are moist air (a small temperature-dewpoint spread), a light wind of a few knots to mix the cooling through a shallow layer, and a long night. Dry air, strong winds and a cloudy sky all prevent it.
fr42DJfqdbxY8Gou4O1X: The altimeter is already set to the correct QNH, so there is no pressure error to allow for - only a temperature error. Air 15 C warmer than ISA is less dense and expands, so the aircraft is physically HIGHER than the altimeter indicates. To be truly at 15,000 ft you therefore read less: correction = 4 ft per 1000 ft per degree = 4 x 15 x 15 = 900 ft, giving an indication of 15,000 - 900 = 14,100 ft. Warm air is the safe case; cold air is the one that kills.
frgErpXYV3WcV5HgUw6S: Convective turbulence follows surface heating with a lag. The ground goes on gaining more heat than it loses until mid-afternoon, so thermals are strongest and the convective boundary layer deepest in the early afternoon, typically 1400-1600 local. Before sunrise the surface is at its coldest and the air is stable and smooth, and after sunset the thermals collapse.
fSxT7WkyDaZJ6M0Hhe7L: In the northern hemisphere air circulates ANTICLOCKWISE around a low, and below the friction layer it also spirals inward. Flying directly toward the centre, the circulation therefore comes at you from the left, and the inflow component - directed toward the centre, i.e. the way you are already going - shows up as a slight tailwind. Hence from the left and behind. Buys Ballot: back to the wind in the NH puts low pressure on your left.
Ftb0ObfXmAI9Bh6TSqZe: The ICAO Standard Atmosphere is defined at mean sea level by 15 C, 1013.25 hPa and a density of 1.225 kg/m3, with temperature decreasing at 0.65 C per 100 m (1.98 C per 1000 ft) to the tropopause at 11 km. The 1 C per 100 m figure in the other options is the dry adiabatic lapse rate, which describes a rising parcel, not the standard environment.
FXo8zj2f8Fs1J8RmUV8x: Between about 10 N and 30 N the flow on the equatorward side of the Azores high is the north-east trade wind, a remarkably steady year-round feature over the open Atlantic. The south-east trades are its southern-hemisphere counterpart, and monsoonal reversals occur over land-dominated regions such as India and West Africa, not over the central Atlantic.
g2jED2eDfGIb6RBqVfua: A parcel rising in an unstable layer keeps ascending only while it remains warmer than its surroundings. It stops where the layer becomes stable again - at an inversion, a subsidence lid or the tropopause. The depth of the unstable layer therefore sets the vertical extent of the cloud, which is why a shallow unstable layer capped by an inversion gives fair weather cumulus while a deep one gives cumulonimbus.
G2T5ZIZqnuGsw1gWbN7u: The halo round the moon is caused by ice crystals in cirrostratus - the first cloud of an approaching warm front, arriving many hours ahead of it. The sequence then runs to altostratus and nimbostratus, giving the continuous rain and the low, uniform grey ceiling described. The rise in temperature confirms warm air is replacing cold. A cold front would bring showers, a sharp clearance and a temperature FALL.
G3GKGYKOZdox8cCUy9uo: Clear ice needs large supercooled drops that freeze slowly enough to run back across the surface, and the greatest concentration of large liquid drops in a cumulonimbus is close to the freezing level, where powerful updraughts are still carrying abundant liquid water and glaciation has not yet occurred. Further up the cloud progressively turns to ice crystals, which do not adhere, so accretion falls off sharply.
g3hwhGzR8LOwdpMj5894: A descending parcel is compressed and warms, which lowers its relative humidity, so any cloud droplets it carries evaporate. Evaporation ABSORBS latent heat, and that heat comes from the parcel itself, partially offsetting the compressional warming. The parcel therefore warms at the saturated adiabatic rate, which is lower than the dry rate, for exactly as long as liquid water remains. (Condensation and its heat release belong to the ascending case.)
g3NW4xT540CTGEdC5iob: Around a low the air follows a curved path, and in the rotating frame the centrifugal force acts outward, directly opposing the inward pressure gradient force. Less of the pressure gradient force is therefore left to be balanced by Coriolis, so a lower wind speed achieves balance: the gradient wind around a low is SUB-geostrophic. Around a high the centrifugal force acts with the pressure gradient force and the gradient wind is super-geostrophic.
g9rhYwBU87dQ6KL3zfC3: In winter the two dominant surface anticyclones affecting this region are the Azores high, over the eastern subtropical Atlantic, and the very intense, cold Siberian high over the Asian landmass, which is a winter-only feature driven by radiational cooling of a continental interior. Iceland and north-east Canada are the seats of winter LOW pressure, not high.
gar9yU7j0RKwrPhqDDAK: A summer cold front over Central Europe undercuts warm, moist, unstable air steeply, triggering cumulonimbus with tops far above FL100. Inside a CB the updraughts and downdraughts can exceed 3000 ft/min side by side, giving severe turbulence. FL100 is right in the most active part of the cell. Stratus and nimbostratus belong to a warm front and give far less turbulence.
GBlzjjWl1UrpDIuTZlJ0: The standard upper-air charts and their approximate ISA heights are 850 hPa near FL50, 700 hPa near FL100, 500 hPa near FL180, 300 hPa near FL300 and 200 hPa near FL390. A pressure level of 38,662 ft therefore corresponds to the 200 hPa chart, which is the usual chart for long-haul cruise levels and for locating the subtropical jet.
gBxRhttO92y2Vl8N7nEJ: A TREND is a short landing forecast appended to a METAR or SPECI, valid for the two hours following the observation and expressed with BECMG, TEMPO or NOSIG. It covers only wind, visibility, weather and cloud. It is not a stand-alone product: the routine aerodrome forecast is the TAF, and the warning of hazardous en-route conditions is the SIGMET.
GGyDhwctjt6yawXVFoMT: Cirrus (CI) forms above about 20,000 ft at temperatures typically below -40 C, so it is composed entirely of ice crystals with essentially no supercooled liquid water. Crystals bounce off the airframe rather than adhering, so icing can be ruled out. Stratocumulus, nimbostratus and cumulus all contain supercooled liquid water at sub-zero temperatures and can all ice an aircraft.
giVpO0QUjK46WUJsnIUa: Convective (cumuliform) cloud forms wherever a parcel lifted from below stays warmer and less dense than its surroundings and keeps rising - that is, in an unstable atmosphere. The trigger can be surface heating, orographic lifting, frontal lifting or convergence, so it is not confined to summer, to daytime, or to any latitude band. Stable air gives layer cloud instead.
gLdGmpyiH647v62CKN6E: An occlusion is classed by comparing the two cold air masses. In a cold occlusion the air arriving behind the cold front is colder than the air that was ahead of the warm front, so it undercuts BOTH and the coldest air ends up behind the front. In a warm occlusion the rear air is the less cold of the two and rides up over the air ahead, so the coldest air lies ahead of the front.
GLgKPBKU9gF9masWbXOI: QFE is QNH reduced by the pressure equivalent of the aerodrome elevation. 200 m is about 656 ft, and at roughly 27 ft per hPa that is 656 / 27 = 24 hPa. QFE = 1025 - 24 = 1001, approximately 1000 hPa. QFE is always below QNH for an aerodrome above sea level, and the two coincide only at sea level.
guY3hmbogUNiLry96Ffx: A thunderstorm needs three ingredients together: an adequate supply of moisture to sustain condensation and release latent heat, conditional instability so the saturated parcel keeps accelerating upward through a deep layer, and a trigger to lift the air to its condensation level - surface heating, a front, orography or convergence. Remove any one and the storm cannot develop. An inversion actively suppresses it.
GVasfXQiwu5WCmmQOWWR: Air flows from the subtropical high-pressure belt toward the equatorial trough, and Coriolis deflects it to the LEFT in the southern hemisphere, turning a southerly flow into a south-easterly. So the southern-hemisphere trades are the south-east trades, the mirror image of the north-east trades of the northern hemisphere. The two meet at the ITCZ.
gxOPOUPsOxvdL5U01OZx: By WMO definition a jet stream is a narrow band of strong winds in the upper troposphere or lower stratosphere with a core speed of at least 60 kt, along with marked vertical and lateral shear. The 60 kt threshold is the definition; typical polar front jet cores run 100-150 kt and can exceed 200 kt in winter.
gZ4yDOs17XFEyas30r39: Mountain waves require a wind of at least 20 kt at ridge level blowing within about 30 degrees of perpendicular to the ridge, wind speed increasing with height, and a STABLE layer at and just above ridge height. Stability is essential: it makes the displaced air oscillate about its equilibrium level, setting up the standing wave train downwind. Unstable air would simply carry on rising as convection and no wave would form.
H6FFxpi8hkFGsc0l4F5j: The phrase 'in still air' means this is a measurement of the surrounding atmosphere rather than of a moving parcel, so it is by definition the environmental lapse rate - the actual observed temperature profile, which varies with time and place and can take any value. The adiabatic rates are fixed parcel-process constants: the dry rate is exactly 1 C per 100 m and the saturated rate is always less than that, so neither can be 1.2 C per 100 m.
H7Ffg0XquaYFpZ1t87xz: The 250 hPa surface lies near 34,000 ft in the standard atmosphere, between the 300 hPa chart at about FL300 and the 200 hPa chart at about FL390. It is a commonly used chart for jet cruise levels. In practice the actual height varies with the mean temperature of the layer below: higher over warm air, lower over cold air.
H7JMGdFn6yA4yvbMUVr1: The ITCZ is the belt where the two trade wind systems converge, forcing deep ascent in warm, extremely moist air, so cumulonimbus with very high tops occur frequently and are its defining hazard. It is an area of low pressure but of HIGH relative humidity, and it migrates seasonally with the sun, though it never shifts entirely into one hemisphere - over the oceans it stays close to the equator all year.
h99WX7ztdxIQMi4MZcnd: The geostrophic wind is the balance between the pressure gradient force and the Coriolis force, so it depends on the pressure gradient itself and on the factors that set the Coriolis force and the mass being accelerated: air DENSITY, the earth's rate of rotation, and the geographic latitude (Coriolis varies with the sine of the latitude). Centripetal force plays no part - that enters only in the gradient wind, where the isobars are curved.
H9QPIhxzhsQnxOGbApLu: Around a high the air curves anticyclonically, so in the rotating frame the centrifugal force acts outward - the same direction as the pressure gradient force, which also points outward from the high. A larger total outward force needs a larger inward Coriolis force to balance it, and Coriolis is proportional to speed, so the gradient wind is SUPER-geostrophic. Around a low the centrifugal force opposes the pressure gradient force and the gradient wind is sub-geostrophic.
hcGjZyoxpKgiWJKYJCPV: Nimbostratus, altostratus and stratus are all layer clouds, and layer cloud forms when a wide expanse of stable air is lifted gently and uniformly - by a frontal surface, by orography or by large-scale convergence. Because the air is stable it spreads horizontally instead of building vertically, giving the extensive uniform sheets. Sinking air dissolves cloud, and convection would give cumuliform cloud instead.
HeFdi2MwIY6ibwgN6zjR: The cumulus, or building, stage is defined by updraughts throughout the cell, drawing in warm moist air while the cloud grows vertically, with all precipitation still held aloft. Rain or hail at the surface marks the start of the MATURE stage, and frequent lightning and roll cloud also belong to the mature stage, once downdraughts have developed alongside the updraughts.
hikdf70QIqTZTsKTYNE7: ICAO Annex 3 requires RVR to be reported throughout any period in which either the meteorological visibility or the RVR itself falls below 1500 m. That 1500 m threshold is the trigger, not 800 m - though 800 m is a familiar figure elsewhere, as the usual visibility below which low-visibility procedures are considered. RVR appears only in METAR and SPECI.
HkM70wWrp5e3EizznikA: An aneroid altimeter simply displays static pressure on an altitude scale. With a uniform pressure pattern and no convective activity, the pressure at a fixed point changes by only a fraction of a hectopascal over ten minutes, which is a handful of feet - too small to be visible on the instrument. Rapid or fluctuating indications on the ground would signal a passing front, a thunderstorm gust front, or an instrument fault.
hKTKL1bsFkDjzS5No8nI: Flying at a constant flight level means following a constant-pressure surface, and if the true altitude is also constant then that pressure surface is neither rising nor falling along the track - the aircraft is flying along a contour (isohypse). The geostrophic wind blows parallel to the contours, so it is parallel to the track: there is no crosswind and therefore no drift. This is the basis of the pressure-pattern flying technique.
HllM85Y3WWaOz2DKfvpq: The jet core sits at the level where the horizontal temperature gradient changes sign - below the core the cold air is on the polar side, above it the gradient reverses - so at core level there is effectively no horizontal temperature gradient. Wind speed is proportional to the slope of the pressure surfaces, so the maximum wind occurs exactly where that slope is greatest, which is at the core.
HLvDtNUWH5kGBSiKotdR: The tropopause is the boundary between the troposphere, in which temperature falls with height and virtually all weather occurs, and the stratosphere above, in which the temperature is first isothermal and then increases. Its height varies from about 8 km over the poles to 16-18 km over the equator, and it acts as a stable lid on convection.
HLWBQWQbw6jbBrmrarsq: An adiabatic process involves no exchange of heat with the surroundings, and while the parcel stays unsaturated it is fully reversible. It cools at 1 C per 100 m on the way up and warms at exactly the same rate on the way back down, so it returns to its starting temperature. Had it been taken ABOVE the condensation level, latent heat release would have made the process irreversible and it would have returned warmer - the Foehn effect.
HOMbpNuzCI4siTfP0msT: Both hemispheres have jet streams, and both have westerly and easterly ones. The polar front and subtropical jets are westerly and occur in each hemisphere. The tropical easterly jet is a summer feature over southern Asia and Africa, which places it in the northern hemisphere, so the northern hemisphere carries both westerly and easterly jets.
hoZu8yoPtGmVXHIT8KWM: Unstable air is well mixed by convection, so haze, smoke and moisture are dispersed vertically instead of accumulating near the surface, and visibility between clouds is normally very good. What ruins it, briefly and locally, is the heavy shower precipitation the convective cloud produces. Drizzle, haze and low stratus are all products of STABLE air, where the lack of mixing traps everything in the lower layers.
HqBJ3KsWujx4uBSxcHuF: METARs at major European aerodromes are issued half-hourly, normally at H+20 and H+50. Elsewhere hourly issue is common. A SPECI is issued in between whenever a significant change occurs - for example visibility, RVR, wind or cloud crossing an operationally important threshold, or the onset of thunderstorms or freezing precipitation.
hr5xhNatqTcZp8Jcqwci: Report B says it explicitly: SCT040CB reports cumulonimbus already present at 4000 ft, the temperature-dewpoint spread of 26/18 shows a warm, moist and unstable airmass, and the TEMPO group forecasts 24018G30 with TS - gusts to 30 kt and thunderstorms. The other reports show layered stratiform cloud, low cloud with improving visibility, or snow, all with NOSIG or a benign trend.
HTJHQcQkhht3VXZXbXv5: The dewpoint is the temperature to which air must be cooled to saturate it, so the temperature-dewpoint spread is a direct measure of how far the air is from saturation. Dry air has to be cooled a long way, giving a large spread; moist air is already close to saturation, giving a small one. The absolute temperature is irrelevant - very cold air can be saturated and very warm air can be bone dry.
HvMQ5HebLgPAxBRJ2by3: Under clear anticyclonic skies the surface wind has a marked diurnal cycle. Daytime heating drives convection, which mixes faster-moving air down from above the friction layer, so the surface wind is strongest in the early afternoon and veers toward the gradient direction (in the northern hemisphere), reducing the cross-isobar angle. At night the surface layer decouples under the radiation inversion, and the wind falls light and backs.
HVuwXZk9FAhVsIGf5dBr: Warm sector air is tropical maritime: warm, very moist and stable, which over the sea or in winter gives stratus, drizzle and poor visibility. Over a strongly heated summer continent, however, surface heating destabilises the lowest layers, breaks up the stratus and converts it into fair weather cumulus with good visibility. The season and the land surface are what change the answer here.
i6zX1Vd790HCAqfWCYMM: Radiation fog is caused by the ground losing heat by long-wave radiation on a clear night, cooling the moist air in contact with it below its dewpoint. It requires a clear sky, light wind, high humidity and a long night, and forms over land. Cold air moving over warm ground is unstable and gives convection or steaming fog, and frontal passage gives frontal fog - a different mechanism entirely.
ieHU1CNvhGnmOeZ6Hz6j: With curved isobars the centrifugal force enters the balance. Around a HIGH it acts outward, in the same sense as the pressure gradient force, so a larger Coriolis force - and hence a higher wind speed - is needed to balance it: the anticyclonic gradient wind is super-geostrophic. Around a LOW it opposes the pressure gradient force and the wind is sub-geostrophic. Same isobar spacing, different speeds.
IFDoZZSRvgch6b89DNAE: The atmosphere is nearly transparent to incoming solar radiation, so it is warmed from below rather than directly by the sun. Convection carries sensible heat upward from the heated surface, and condensation releases the latent heat that was absorbed when the water evaporated, depositing it aloft where the cloud forms. Evaporation and vaporisation do the opposite - they absorb heat and cool their surroundings.
iiMYZysNo91sXjYLeOhf: At night the land cools by radiation faster than the sea, so the pressure gradient reverses and air drains from land to sea: the land breeze. It is weaker than the daytime sea breeze because the night-time land-sea temperature difference is much smaller than the daytime one, and because the stable nocturnal inversion suppresses the circulation. The sea breeze can reach 15-20 kt; the land breeze rarely exceeds a few knots.
ing4CGjupK6cjdLMmBws: Tropospheric depth follows the mean temperature of the air column, so it is deepest where the surface is warmest: about 16-18 km over the equator, 11 km in mid-latitudes and only about 8 km over the poles. This is why tropical cumulonimbus can reach much higher tops than mid-latitude storms, and why the tropopause has a 'break' at the polar front where the two depths meet.
ioykIRHHAJoBRUxEVXx6: An isohypse, or contour, joins points of equal height of a given constant-pressure surface on an upper-air chart - for example the height of the 500 hPa surface. It is the upper-air equivalent of an isobar, and the geostrophic wind blows parallel to it with low heights on the left in the northern hemisphere. Close contour spacing therefore means strong upper winds.
ISZg1DLjETMT4iH9dDTF: A microburst is intense but very short-lived: the damaging phase lasts typically 1-5 minutes, within an outflow less than 4 km across. That brevity is what makes it so hazardous - it can form and strike the approach path between one aircraft and the next, so a preceding aircraft's smooth approach is no guarantee. Longer-lived, larger downbursts are classed as macrobursts.
iT67oGlcHOZLXwzva1Qy: A squall line is a line of vigorous thunderstorms typically 50-300 NM AHEAD of a fast-moving active cold front and roughly parallel to it, formed where the cold downdraught outflow undercuts the warm sector well in advance of the surface front. It is often more severe than the front itself and cannot be circumnavigated easily because of its length, which is why it is a mandatory SIGMET item.
Itn2nP5v9hAU87wAkJ07: The roll cloud sits on the leading edge of the gust front, where the cold downdraught outflow spreads out at the surface and undercuts the inflowing warm air, setting up a horizontal rotor. Downdraughts only exist once precipitation begins, which by definition is the MATURE stage. The cumulus stage has updraughts only, and by the dissipating stage the cell is decaying.
IxvUwSMofzewgY8udLfO: Latent heat is released whenever a substance moves to a more ordered state: gas to liquid (condensation), liquid to solid (freezing) and gas to solid (deposition, or sublimation in the meteorological sense). It is absorbed in the reverse directions - evaporation, melting and sublimation. The latent heat released by condensation in a rising parcel is what powers thunderstorms and tropical revolving storms.
iylGG492q2iz5gftGOxY: Air masses take their properties from their source region. The Azores is a warm ocean, so it produces tropical maritime air: warm and very moist. Northern Russia in a continental interior at high latitude produces polar or arctic continental air: cold and very dry, because cold air holds little water vapour and there is no moisture source. So the Azores air is both warmer and more humid.
jA5ZflOrfLVjHEzX1gfI: Wind speed near the ground is set by the pressure gradient, so the strongest winds are found where the isobars are most tightly packed. That happens in the transition zone between two air masses - along a front - where the pressure gradient is sharply concentrated, giving the strong, gusty, veering winds of a frontal passage. The centres of highs and lows, and any area of little pressure variation, all have slack gradients and light winds.
jCYn46jcb7JZuuuRgdP9: Changing the subscale changes the reading by about 27 ft per hPa. Going from 1013 down to 991 is a decrease of 22 hPa, so the indication falls by 22 x 27 = 594 ft: 3600 - 594 = 3006 ft. The rule to remember is that winding the subscale DOWN winds the indicated altitude down with it, and vice versa.
jipXa5ajr3zO3JlZQVBm: A trough is an elongated extension of low pressure, so air spirals in toward it and converges along the trough line. Converging air cannot enter the ground, so it must rise, and the widespread ascent cools it adiabatically to saturation, giving cloud and precipitation. A ridge is the opposite - divergence with subsidence and generally fine weather.
jl219ukxLDIr7fey0Tfc: A tropical revolving storm needs a sea surface temperature of at least about 26.5 C through a deep layer, and the oceans reach that only after a full season of solar heating. The northern hemisphere season therefore runs roughly June to November, peaking in late summer and early autumn - the sea, not the air, is the limiting factor, which is why the peak lags the solstice by two months.
JmgaW36MGCh60aI3TL1p: The subtropical high-pressure belt lies at about 25-35 degrees in each hemisphere, where the poleward-moving upper branch of the Hadley cell descends. That subsidence gives the belt its clear skies, light variable winds (the horse latitudes) and the world's great deserts. The trade winds flow out of it toward the equator and the westerlies toward the poles.
jNQlj6UL4hnGyfTz186a: The TAF is valid 1500-2400. The main body forecasts 9999, meaning 10 km or more. The TEMPO group covers 1600-2000, which includes an ETA of 1800, and forecasts 8000 - 8 km - with heavy showers and CB. The lowest quoted visibility at ETA is therefore 8 km. Note that TAF and METAR visibilities are always in metres, never nautical miles.
jnyB9qXPJKIioWlHPzXy: Pressure falls roughly exponentially with height, so the atmosphere's mass is heavily concentrated near the surface: half of it lies below about 5.5 km, which is close to the 500 hPa level (roughly FL180). Around three quarters lies within the troposphere's lowest 11 km, and about 99% below 30 km.
Jot7ZSs0Lys0x4IOUEyV: Clear ice comes from LARGE supercooled drops, typically at temperatures between 0 C and about -10 C. A large drop releases enough latent heat as it starts to freeze that only part of it solidifies on impact; the rest runs back over the surface and freezes progressively, producing a dense, transparent, tenacious sheet that spreads well aft of the leading edge. Small drops freeze instantly and give opaque rime instead.
Jpgq5NDZgrGJJxt4i8p8: In a southerly Foehn the air has dropped its moisture as precipitation on the Italian side, then descends the northern slopes warming at the dry adiabatic rate. It arrives warm, very dry and cloud-free, so visibility on the north side becomes exceptional. The strong downslope flow over rough terrain, with its rotors and mountain waves, makes turbulence the main hazard - not icing or precipitation, both of which are on the southern side.
JPjmLqP0c6dxCvi2XCa8: Nimbostratus is a deep, dense, extensive layer cloud whose base is low and whose top can reach medium levels, so it holds a large amount of water and gives continuous, often heavy, rain or snow over a wide area. Stratus and stratocumulus are shallow and give at most drizzle or light precipitation, and cirrostratus is thin high ice cloud giving none at all.
jQWIeP2FFHpofWLLMInD: Freezing precipitation is liquid precipitation that is supercooled when it strikes a surface, so it can only be freezing rain (FZRA) or freezing drizzle (FZDZ). Hail and snow are already solid and cannot 'freeze' on contact. It occurs where a warm layer aloft lies over a sub-zero layer beneath - typically ahead of a winter warm front, but also possible at a slow-moving cold front.
JREm3foVmB3IFnmxdO2A: Radiation fog needs four things together: a clear sky, so the ground can radiate its heat away; a light wind of a few knots, to mix the cooling through a shallow layer without dispersing it; moist air, so only a little cooling is needed to reach the dewpoint; and a long night. Cloud cover blocks the radiational cooling, strong wind lifts the layer into stratus, and dry air never reaches saturation.
jtz3PL4Et6nU0FHVTvLw: The standard upper-air charts sit at roughly 850 hPa near FL50, 700 hPa near FL100, 500 hPa near FL180, 300 hPa near FL300 and 200 hPa near FL390. FL60 is therefore closest to the 850 hPa chart. The actual height of any of these surfaces varies with the mean temperature of the air beneath: higher over warm air, lower over cold air.
jwjUDUUm0sEU3lE5DV3R: The pressure gradient is the rate at which pressure changes with horizontal distance, so a steep gradient shows on the chart as closely spaced isobars and produces a large pressure gradient force - and therefore a strong wind. Isobar spacing is a direct visual measure of wind strength. Temperature is a separate variable and is shown by isotherms, not by isobar spacing.
JXwHWywe5pyun1G2uMlK: Airmass thunderstorms in Central Europe are triggered by surface heating, and the surface goes on gaining more heat than it loses until mid-afternoon. Convection therefore peaks around 1400-1600 local, with the cells decaying in the evening once the heating source is removed. Frontal thunderstorms, driven by mechanical lifting rather than heating, have no such diurnal preference.
JzXOwIilIA75yshJQtdj: Cumulonimbus is the only cloud that routinely occupies all three levels at once: its base is typically low, at 1000-5000 ft, and its top can reach FL450 or higher, spreading into the characteristic anvil of ice crystals. That is why CB is treated separately in reports and why CAVOK is prohibited when any CB is present, at any level.
k5by8TGFwvH97xMSNOdJ: A summer mid-latitude cumulonimbus spans temperatures from well above freezing at its base to below -40 C at its top, so it contains all three phases: ordinary water droplets in the warm lower part, supercooled water droplets in the 0 to -20 C zone, and ice crystals in the glaciated upper part and anvil. The coexistence of ice and supercooled water in the mid-levels is what drives both hail growth and electrical charge separation.
k83e8zBIdo9dhjUqAHpb: Conditional instability means the environmental lapse rate lies BETWEEN the saturated and dry adiabatic rates: SALR < ELR < DALR. Since the DALR is exactly 1 C per 100 m, the ELR must be less than 1 C per 100 m. The layer is therefore stable for unsaturated air and unstable only once the air is saturated - hence 'conditional'. The SALR is variable, not fixed at 0.65, which is the ISA environmental value.
KaBrIVhjPnMv9otQJLbd: Hailstone size depends on updraught strength, because the stone must be held aloft above the freezing level long enough to accrete successive layers of ice. Only a severe thunderstorm has updraughts strong enough to produce large stones. Hail occurs in airmass as well as frontal storms and at all latitudes where deep convection occurs, and large stones are typically layered, alternating clear and opaque ice.
KaehvX1B2EoZ3WdBB2Te: An isothermal layer has an environmental lapse rate of zero, which is far less than either adiabatic rate. A parcel displaced upward cools at its adiabatic rate while the surroundings do not cool at all, so the parcel immediately becomes colder and denser than its environment and sinks back: absolutely stable. Inversions, where temperature actually increases with height, are more stable still.
KbqS4g0zJ2rVYR7sm8tl: Arctic air is the coldest classification of all, originating over the permanently ice-covered polar regions north of about 70 degrees, where the surface radiates heat away all winter and the source air can reach -40 C or below. Polar air, whether maritime or continental, comes from lower latitudes and is less extreme, and tropical continental air is hot and dry.
kDwmbKDCsAUhkcnPVs5F: Convection over mountains is driven by surface heating, so on an unstable summer day the cumulus builds through the late morning, the cells mature into thunderstorms in the afternoon, and turbulence, downdraughts and reduced visibility peak with them. The morning, before the heating has taken effect, gives the smoothest air, the best visibility and the highest cloud bases - which is why mountain flying is traditionally done early.
ke61Y9rGRqfqjZn55nLE: With a southerly Foehn the air ascends the Italian side, where it cools, condenses and drops its precipitation, then descends the northern slopes warming at the dry adiabatic rate. Warming lowers the relative humidity, so the cloud evaporates and the north side stays dry and clear. Fronts and occlusions are lifting mechanisms and give precipitation, and a northerly Foehn would put the dry descent on the SOUTHERN side.
kFO7h1gNarxKspG8rPwn: The arctic jet is the lowest of the jets, with its core around 20,000 ft (FL200), because the tropopause above the very cold arctic air is itself low. The polar front jet core sits near 30,000 ft and the subtropical jet near 39,000 ft. Jet height mirrors tropopause height, which is lowest over the poles and highest over the equator.
kGN5YtjW6GV1hVVq7ziO: Darwin lies on Australia's tropical north coast and is well within the southern-hemisphere cyclone belt. The southern season runs roughly November to April, when the sea north of Australia is at its warmest and the ITCZ has migrated south - the mirror image of the northern hemisphere's June-November season. December to April is the period of greatest risk.
kgphsA7BeenETZfPj1aa: The 300 hPa surface lies at roughly 30,000 ft (FL300) in temperate latitudes, which makes it the standard chart for locating the polar front jet. Its exact height varies with the mean temperature of the layer below it: it is higher over warm air and lower over cold air, which is why the contour pattern on the chart mirrors the thermal structure beneath.
klJ3vQIVIQJPJRCwDhdw: In northern summer the Azores (Bermuda) high is at its strongest and expands, extending its ridge west over the south-eastern United States and north-east over south-west Europe, which is what gives both regions their settled summer weather. The winter cold highs over Greenland and northern Canada weaken or disappear as those surfaces warm, and Iceland remains a seat of low pressure.
kNHeybXpz1Fnq5RTYG46: Tornadoes need strong low-level moisture, steep instability and marked vertical wind shear together. Over North America that combination peaks in spring and early summer, when warm moist Gulf air surges north beneath cold dry air from Canada while the jet stream is still strong overhead. The classic Tornado Alley peak is April to June.
knnshASvnjgJtA88mb6H: Use the standard lapse rate of about 2 C per 1000 ft. To fall 6 C below zero requires a climb of 6 / 2 = 3000 ft above the 0 C level. With the freezing level at FL50, the -6 C level is at FL80. This is the everyday calculation for finding the icing layer from a forecast freezing level.
kNZZfh34qrjuKFEo67NH: ICAO grades icing as light, moderate or severe. MODERATE means that even a short encounter is potentially hazardous and that use of de-icing or anti-icing equipment, and a diversion, is desirable. Light icing needs action only if prolonged beyond about an hour; severe icing means the equipment cannot cope and an immediate change is required.
kPD5iI4ZFtkp2jSmSA2w: As air descends, the ambient pressure rises and compresses it, and that compression does work on the parcel and warms it at the dry adiabatic rate. Its moisture content is unchanged, but warmer air can hold far more vapour, so the relative humidity falls and any cloud droplets evaporate. Note the direction: expansion cools, compression warms - and the parcel warms by compression rather than by reaching warmer surroundings.
KpG7uGUcpnDGtlHkvjW1: Stability is defined by how the atmosphere responds to a displaced parcel. In a stable air mass a rising parcel cools faster than its surroundings, becomes colder and denser than them, and so decelerates and sinks back - the vertical motion weakens and dies. A lapse rate of exactly 1 C per 100 m is the dry adiabatic rate, which gives NEUTRAL stability, and a rapid decrease of temperature with height indicates instability.
KqMUZdH8kjE4VqK7GPA0: Both low pressure and low temperature make the aircraft lower than the altimeter indicates. A QNH below 1013 puts the 1013 datum below sea level, so a flight level sits lower than its nominal altitude, and colder-than-ISA air contracts, lowering it further. A cold low combines both errors in the dangerous direction. The mnemonic is 'from high to low, or hot to cold, look out below'.
Ks9pUcqRKyVBGByvtI2R: A gust front is the leading edge of the cold downdraught outflow spreading away from a thunderstorm at the surface. It can run 15-20 NM ahead of the cell, so it is met in apparently clear air well before the storm itself, and it produces a sudden wind shift, a sharp increase in speed, a temperature drop and severe low-level shear - often marked by a roll cloud along its leading edge.
ktnQX1VeSdBBp0i77mGB: The 850 hPa surface lies at roughly 5000 ft (FL50) in temperate latitudes, which makes it the usual chart for low-level winds and for identifying air masses. The standard set runs 850 hPa near FL50, 700 hPa near FL100, 500 hPa near FL180, 300 hPa near FL300 and 200 hPa near FL390.
ktRq35IcMcphCVAlDcxB: An unsaturated parcel cools at the dry adiabatic rate of 1 C per 100 m. Once saturated, condensation releases latent heat which partially offsets the expansional cooling, so a saturated parcel cools more slowly, at the variable saturated adiabatic rate. Unsaturated therefore cools MORE rapidly. The 0.65 C per 100 m figure belongs to the ISA environment, not to a parcel.
KvqxpnsUeZmq3Aoy2Zc2: Pressure at any level is simply the weight of the air above it, so it must always decrease with height. The rate is not constant, however: it is about 1 hPa per 27 ft near sea level but around 1 hPa per 50 ft at 18,000 ft, because the air aloft is less dense. Diurnal and seasonal pressure variations exist but are small and not universal.
kwnXT4AhToCD5WgYE5WU: Nimbostratus is a deep, water-rich stratiform cloud formed by gentle widespread ascent in stable air, so it gives continuous precipitation - rain, sleet or snow depending on the temperature profile - and its depth and high liquid water content make icing probable, ranging from light to severe. Because the ascent is gentle rather than convective, turbulence is rarely worse than moderate. Severe turbulence with hail is the cumulonimbus signature.
kxD3VrH8hjUhkRxVcTq0: NOSIG is a trend group meaning no significant change is expected in the two hours following the observation - specifically, no change to wind, visibility, weather or cloud that would cross an operationally significant threshold. It replaces BECMG or TEMPO in the TREND section of a METAR or SPECI.
KXMQEV4d95D0KKSpQKKw: Freezing rain requires a warm layer aloft above a sub-freezing layer at low level. Precipitation leaves the cloud as liquid rain in the warm layer, then descends into air below 0 C where it becomes supercooled but stays liquid, and freezes instantly on striking the airframe or the ground. That structure is typical ahead of a winter warm front, and it produces the most severe icing conditions there are.
Ky7bKeNdpD7VVzN7uIXy: Pressure falls steadily as an active cold front approaches, then rises sharply once it has passed. An altimeter reads height above the pressure datum set on its subscale, so falling ambient pressure makes it read HIGHER even though the aircraft has not moved. This is also why an altimeter left set to an old QNH becomes progressively more wrong as a front goes through.
KYJpdp17r2DDpcYqzJXQ: The sea breeze is a shallow daytime circulation driven by the land heating faster than the sea, typically confined to the lowest 1000-3000 ft and extending 10-20 NM inland, with a compensating return flow above it. It occurs at any latitude where a sufficient land-sea temperature difference develops - it is common in the tropics - and it dies away at night, when the weaker land breeze replaces it.
KZXAZYQdVNpWmtgUEtNp: The difference between a flight level and true altitude has two independent causes: the pressure error, which depends on how far QNH differs from 1013, and the temperature error, which depends on the deviation from ISA. With QNH unknown you cannot separate the two, so a 100 ft discrepancy could arise from either or from both cancelling partially. No conclusion about the temperature is possible.
kZZobm5tr265UyDHZd1k: A contour, or isohypse, joins points where a given pressure surface lies at the same height - for example all points at which the 500 hPa surface is 5520 m above sea level. It is the upper-air equivalent of an isobar: the geostrophic wind blows along the contours with low heights on the left in the northern hemisphere, and close spacing means strong winds.
l0TcTiVIrE2W1dU8Iwdv: A supercooled droplet is liquid water existing at a temperature below 0 C. Pure water in small droplets needs a freezing nucleus to solidify, and in the absence of one it can remain liquid down to about -40 C, below which it freezes spontaneously. Supercooled droplets are the entire basis of airframe icing: they freeze on contact with the aircraft, which acts as the trigger.
L1hEu64xVgNYLQmOXOw9: 2000 ft AGL is above the friction layer, so the wind there is the gradient wind. Reversing the standard over-land friction rule - surface wind backed 30 degrees and roughly half the speed - means going up you VEER about 30 degrees and DOUBLE the speed. 190 becomes about 220 and 15 kt becomes about 30 kt, giving 22030KT. Over the sea the correction would be only about 10 degrees and a smaller speed change.
lB2OnRz7T6wgOXpeZAki: Read the temperature and the pressure trace. Early morning: heavy rain with an overcast at 3000 ft, then the rain stops, the cloud lifts, the wind veers 230 to 250 and the temperature JUMPS from 13 to 18 C - a warm front passing. Late afternoon: a forecast of gusts and thunderstorms, then +TSRA with CB and 35 kt gusts, after which the temperature FALLS from 24 to 13 C, the pressure begins rising and the sky clears - a cold front. Warm front first, cold front later.
LBNi2phWNnwwwbCXBmK6: Altocumulus lenticularis is the classic standing lenticular cloud that forms at the crest of a mountain wave, where air rising in the wave cools to saturation. The cloud appears stationary while the air flows through it. Its presence means a stable layer, a strong cross-ridge wind and a standing wave train downwind, with the associated severe turbulence in the rotor zone beneath.
LBUY9E74p2Gs7kkml6m3: ISA temperature falls at 1.98 C per 1000 ft, so at FL100 it is 15 - 19.8 = about -5 C. Air 10 C warmer than standard therefore reads -5 + 10 = +5 C. This ISA-deviation calculation is the basis for both altimeter temperature corrections and true airspeed computations.
lDHP1gOmh5mla5OmLfUD: Warm advection into the TOP of a layer raises the temperature aloft while the bottom is unchanged, which reduces the temperature difference across the layer and so flattens the environmental lapse rate. A smaller lapse rate means a displaced parcel more readily becomes colder than its surroundings, so stability increases. Warm advection at the BOTTOM, or cold advection at the top, would do the opposite.
LHPRjiGkaIxJ7uUoExxH: Advection fog forms when relatively warm, moist air is carried horizontally over a colder surface and is cooled from below to its dewpoint. Here the air at 15/12 crosses a sea at 5 C, well below its dewpoint, so it saturates. Unlike radiation fog it needs a wind - 10 kt is ideal, since some turbulence is required to deepen the fog - it forms over the sea, and it persists day and night.
llN53YPZf4StiMKT5b2E: With a temperature-dewpoint spread of only 1 C just before dawn, the air is on the point of saturation and only the wind decides the outcome. Radiation fog needs a light wind: enough gentle turbulence to mix the surface cooling through a shallow layer, which is what a light, variable wind provides. In dead calm the cooling stays right at the surface and gives dew or frost rather than fog, while a steady stronger wind mixes the layer too deeply and produces low stratus.
lN6fGzUzFIEhLpvQ7tPF: 5000 ft AGL is above the friction layer, so the wind there is the gradient wind blowing parallel to the isobars. At the surface, friction slows the air, which weakens the Coriolis force and lets the pressure gradient force turn the flow toward low pressure - backing it by about 30 degrees over land. A south-westerly aloft therefore appears as a southerly at the surface. Coriolis is weaker at the surface, not stronger, precisely because the wind is slower.
LONyz7DiJttQligTAhMH: CAT is generated by wind shear, and shear is greatest where the jet is sharply curved - around a deep trough - because the flow must change speed and direction rapidly. The worst CAT is typically found on the cold (polar) side and just below the core, and downwind of the trough axis. A straight jet at low latitude in summer is weaker and gives much less shear.
LOrKxQuyOVY9PrVt6jPn: By definition a downburst counts as a microburst when its damaging outflow spans no more than 4 km; anything larger is a macroburst. Despite the small footprint it is the most dangerous form of low-level wind shear, because within it an aircraft meets a headwind gain, then a powerful downdraught, then a sudden headwind loss - all within a minute or two.
lpxoNguUXHIuUnaXbKkX: Radiation fog is caused by the ground radiating heat away on a clear night and cooling the moist air in contact with it below its dewpoint; it needs a light wind, forms over land, and burns off with daytime heating. Advection fog is caused by warm, moist air being carried horizontally over a colder surface; it needs a moderate wind of around 10-15 kt, forms over sea or cold land, and can persist day and night.
LsUJWBn4F0HjT7qr9Hw4: The QNH is identical at both ends, so there is no pressure change to explain the drift. A constant flight level follows a constant-pressure surface, and that surface rises over warmer air because warm air is less dense and expands. A steadily increasing true altitude at a fixed flight level therefore means the air is progressively warmer along the route. Nothing is wrong and no action is needed.
LsUOXiQKS7etHlDAaKwp: A cold pool, or cut-off low, is a detached mass of cold air in the middle and upper troposphere. Being cold and dense it depresses the pressure surfaces above it, so it shows clearly as a closed low centre on an upper chart such as the 500 hPa, while at the surface the pressure pattern may be almost featureless. Cold aloft over warmer air below means a steep lapse rate, hence instability, showers and thunderstorms.
LXUm7Em29OwvlTXIRIq8: Contour heights on upper-air charts are given in DECAMETRES (tens of metres), so 552 means the 500 hPa surface lies 5520 m above mean sea level at every point on that line. Higher values indicate a warmer, deeper air column beneath; lower values indicate colder air. The label is a height, not a pressure - the pressure is 500 hPa everywhere on the chart.
lY4524aGu4XnrQKwQe93: Freezing rain needs liquid rain falling into air below 0 C. In the cold wedge beneath the frontal surface, temperatures are sub-zero above 2000 ft, so anywhere from about 2000 ft up to the frontal surface the rain arrives supercooled - 3000, 5000 and 9000 ft are all exposed. At 12,000 ft, however, you are in the warm air ABOVE its own 10,000 ft freezing level, so the precipitation there is still snow or ice crystals and has not yet melted. That is where freezing rain is least likely.
LZ7skFpNhiDsmjWZhwR0: Tropopause height follows the depth and warmth of the troposphere beneath it, so travelling from the equator to the pole the tropopause DESCENDS, from about 16-18 km to about 8 km. Its temperature runs the opposite way: about -75 C over the equator, -56.5 C in mid-latitudes and only about -45 C over the pole. Higher tropopause, colder tropopause.
M0595gXZP7nKaPq0dAD3: Vertical wind shear is the change of the HORIZONTAL wind - in speed, direction or both - with height. It is what produces clear air turbulence at jet stream level and the low-level shear encountered on approach beneath an inversion or a thunderstorm outflow. A change of the horizontal wind with horizontal distance is horizontal shear, a different quantity.
M0KkxDqUaojV5PLHUHYz: With the centre passing to the SOUTH, the observer is on the northern side of an anticlockwise circulation throughout. Take the three stages: with the low approaching to the south-west the wind is south-easterly; as the centre passes due south it becomes easterly; and as the low departs to the south-east it becomes north-easterly. SE to E to NE is an anticlockwise change of direction, i.e. continuously backing. Had the centre passed to the north, the wind would have veered.
M1IvVD6sCQ4Y0u5KmpCD: Use the standard lapse rate of about 2 C per 1000 ft. The air is 2 C below zero, so the 0 C level lies 2 / 2 = 1000 ft BELOW the aircraft: FL120 - 1000 ft = FL110. Watch the direction - descending warms the air, so the freezing level is always below you when the OAT is negative.
m2pmCj7eMPdd7RDygnQ1: The equatorial (tropical) easterly jet is a seasonal feature, appearing only in the northern-hemisphere summer over southern Asia and Africa, where the monsoon circulation reverses the upper-level flow. Its core sits very high, around 100-150 hPa or roughly 45,000 ft, and unlike every other jet it blows from the EAST. The polar front and subtropical jets, by contrast, are westerly and present all year.
M347FIncjvxSNs6En5vA: A thick, blunt aerofoil deflects the airflow well ahead of itself, and small droplets have little inertia so they follow the streamlines around it. A thin, sharp profile disturbs the flow much less, so the droplets carry straight on and strike the surface: its catch efficiency is higher. This is why thin high-speed wings, tailplanes and antennae ice up faster than a thick wing in the same cloud.
m4IyquGNuB6aliMDt4S8: A jet stream is only a few thousand feet deep but 100-300 km wide, so the fastest escape from its shear zone is vertical. A change of flight level of 2000-4000 ft, preferably away from the core, usually clears the turbulence, whereas a heading change would have to be very large and held for a long time. Reducing to turbulence penetration speed protects the airframe but does not escape the CAT.
m5v7WIgDUEoqWLR1hgIj: Clear ice comes from LARGE supercooled droplets, typically between 0 C and -10 C.
