Such a drop releases enough latent heat as it begins to freeze that only part of it solidifies on impact; the remainder spreads back over the surface and freezes progressively, producing a dense, transparent, tenacious sheet well aft of the leading edge. Water vapour freezing directly onto a cold airframe is hoar frost, a different phenomenon.
M6xtr2Pzz2iheBTAF0TE: In the northern hemisphere Coriolis deflects moving air to the right, which makes the circulation around a low anticlockwise; friction in the boundary layer then turns the surface wind across the isobars toward the centre. So surface air spirals anticlockwise INTO a low, and clockwise OUT of a high. The inflow into the low is what forces the ascent that gives its cloud and rain.
MaO1eqYpJL4g35fvDnTm: A small droplet contains little latent heat, so on striking a cold surface it freezes essentially instantaneously where it lands, trapping air between the frozen droplets. The result is rime: white, opaque, brittle and comparatively light, building forward from the leading edge. Only large droplets carry enough latent heat to stay partly liquid, run back, and build clear ice.
mcTbNbZYOi3stztsxsoD: A marked surface-based inversion decouples the air above it from the surface, so the layer below stays light and often calm while the air just above retains the full gradient wind - a difference that can exceed 30 kt across a few hundred feet. Crossing that boundary on approach or departure produces the sharpest low-level shear, which is why a reported nocturnal inversion with a strong wind above it is an operational warning.
mDdSihE6TZ3CKkmH4yiY: The ITCZ is the belt where the north-east trades of the northern hemisphere converge with the south-east trades of the southern hemisphere. That convergence forces deep ascent in warm, very moist air, producing the near-permanent line of cumulonimbus and heavy showers that marks it. It migrates seasonally with the overhead sun, moving furthest over the continents.
mETLs9zcdpeyMwFWaSoY: A cloud containing only water, with no ice phase, cannot use the Bergeron process, so its droplets can only grow by collision and coalescence. In the shallow, gently ascending low cloud typical of mid-latitude warm-water cloud, the droplets never grow large, so the precipitation is drizzle. Heavy rain and hail in mid-latitudes almost always involve ice crystals higher in the cloud.
miKazcihIiAlYWkIvJgK: Virtually all atmospheric water vapour - around 99% - is in the troposphere, and most of that in its lowest few kilometres, because the source is evaporation from the surface and because the temperature falls rapidly with height, so the air's capacity to hold vapour drops away. The tropopause acts as a lid on vertical moisture transport, which is why the stratosphere is extremely dry.
MJe4eUaEaGuAzeqSqe8m: The Q-group in a METAR gives QNH in whole hectopascals, rounded DOWN to the next lower whole hPa. Rounding down is deliberate: a slightly low subscale setting makes the altimeter read slightly low, which places the aircraft slightly higher than indicated - the safe direction of error. QFE is never given in the METAR pressure group.
MkI7kHvybSBkJjIKwjym: Showers, of rain or snow, come from convective cloud - cumulus and cumulonimbus - because the strong updraughts allow particles to grow large and the cloud has limited horizontal extent, so the precipitation starts and stops abruptly. Snow showers are typical of cold unstable air behind a cold front. Stratiform cloud such as nimbostratus or altostratus gives continuous, widespread snow instead.
Mkpd7SIgsBMp2etC2z9e: The standard upper-air charts sit at approximately 850 hPa near FL50, 700 hPa near FL100, 500 hPa near FL180, 300 hPa near FL300 and 200 hPa near FL390. FL170 is therefore closest to the 500 hPa chart, which is also the standard chart for the mid-tropospheric flow pattern and for locating cold pools.
MRB1bMFFDQOWNNpRwYUv: Absolute instability means a parcel keeps rising whether it is saturated or not, which requires the environmental lapse rate to exceed even the dry adiabatic rate of 1 C per 100 m. Such superadiabatic layers are shallow and short-lived, typically just above a strongly heated surface on a hot afternoon, because the resulting convection quickly overturns and stabilises the layer.
msCYXzv9wrvo39vnSfA2: Relative humidity is the actual water vapour content of a parcel expressed as a percentage of the amount it could hold at saturation at that temperature. Because the saturation capacity rises steeply with temperature, simply warming air lowers its relative humidity without removing any water at all, and cooling it raises the value to 100% at the dewpoint.
mvOnnFjGEzLw8UuqlKVl: The pressure gradient force does start the air moving from high toward low pressure, but as soon as it moves, the Coriolis force - an apparent force arising from the earth's rotation - deflects it, to the right in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern. The two forces come into balance with the wind blowing PARALLEL to the isobars rather than across them. Friction only modifies this near the surface.
mx0QKsVCvWtM1tnC70wJ: Take the temperature error first: FL100 with an ISA deviation of -15 C gives 10,000 x (1 - 4 x 15 / 1000) = 10,000 x 0.94 = 9400 ft. Now the pressure: QNH 983 is 30 hPa below 1013, and at 27 ft per hPa that is 810 ft, and since the QNH is LOWER the 1013 datum lies below sea level, so the altimeter over-reads by that amount. True altitude = 9400 - 810 = 8590 ft. Low pressure and low temperature both put you lower than indicated.
mZEd4ZTuT60cJCbTQrFJ: The geostrophic wind blows with low pressure (low contour heights) on its LEFT in the northern hemisphere. A crosswind from the left means the wind vector points across the track to the right, and low heights lie to the left of that vector - which is directly AHEAD of the aircraft. Flying at a constant flight level into progressively lower contour heights means the pressure surface is descending, so the true altitude decreases.
MZl85l71vLuhP6Sqbimp: Descending into the friction layer, the wind slows because of surface friction, and the weakened Coriolis force lets the pressure gradient force turn the flow toward low pressure - which in the northern hemisphere is a BACKING. So the surface wind is backed and weaker relative to the 2000 ft wind, by about 30 degrees and half the speed over land, or 10 degrees and a smaller reduction over the sea. Climbing out, the reverse: veers and increases.
MzvuffmCJ7YgYS3pNvuf: A blocking anticyclone is a WARM-cored high extending through the depth of the troposphere, quasi-stationary and sited unusually far north, typically between 50 N and 70 N over Scandinavia, Greenland or the north Atlantic. Because it is warm-cored it persists at altitude and diverts the polar front jet and its depressions around it, north or south - hence 'blocking'. Cold anticyclones, such as the Siberian high, are shallow and confined to low levels.
N15i9TG9oY4vjwuGZWue: The high-level outflow from a tropical revolving storm spreads out as a vast shield of dense cirrus, which is thrown out ahead of the system and can be seen 300-500 NM before the storm itself arrives. Long-period swell and a falling barometer are the other classic early indicators. The cumulonimbus of the eyewall is not visible at that range.
n9UqQeEzezu058FH0efZ: Wind speed increases with height through the troposphere because the horizontal temperature gradient that drives it accumulates with altitude (the thermal wind). That growth stops at the tropopause, where the gradient reverses, so the strongest winds - the jet streams - are found immediately BELOW the tropopause, around 30,000-39,000 ft over central Europe. Above it in the stratosphere the wind falls away again.
NhKC7tc4C54yGci9fxXF: Advection fog forms when warm, moist air is carried horizontally over a surface colder than its dewpoint and is chilled from below to saturation. It needs a wind of roughly 10-15 kt: enough turbulence to deepen the fog, but not so much that it lifts into stratus. Unlike radiation fog it forms over the sea or over cold or snow-covered land, and it can persist by day and night.
ni3Ct6lqzTjJBR3hxMqB: Every other jet stream - polar front, subtropical, arctic - is a WESTERLY flow, arising from the poleward temperature gradient. The equatorial (tropical) easterly jet blows from the EAST, because in the northern-hemisphere summer the heated Tibetan plateau puts the warm air on its poleward side, reversing the temperature gradient and hence the thermal wind. Direction is the essential distinction.
nJ8NdGIPVr0uidUST6Cm: Showers require convective cloud with strong updraughts and limited horizontal extent - towering cumulus and cumulonimbus - which is why shower precipitation begins and ends abruptly and varies rapidly in intensity. Nimbostratus and altostratus form in stable air with gentle widespread ascent and give continuous, steady precipitation over a wide area instead.
Nk8DoBV7JtzxN3txP84u: The height interval corresponding to 1 hPa grows with altitude because the air becomes less dense: about 8 m (27 ft) near sea level, about 15 m (50 ft) at 5500 m (the 500 hPa level), and around 32 m (105 ft) near 10 km. This is why the 27 ft per hPa rule is only valid for low-level altimetry problems and must not be applied at cruise levels.
nOTHi5mgZk53HtQfO3wC: An ageing anticyclone is maintained by slow, widespread subsidence. The descending air warms adiabatically, and where it meets the turbulent, cooler air of the boundary layer it forms a subsidence inversion at a few thousand feet. That inversion caps convection and traps haze and pollution beneath it, giving the poor visibility typical of a stagnant high. A radiation inversion, by contrast, is surface-based and forms overnight.
NpXirdKxotMDXoCtYRNT: QNH is derived from the measured aerodrome pressure precisely so that an altimeter set to it reads the aerodrome elevation on the ground. That is exact at the aerodrome by construction, regardless of temperature - the ISA assumption only introduces error at heights ABOVE the reference level. Setting QFE, by contrast, makes the altimeter read zero on landing.
nr09MXXl3jOpCrpRT4xV: Freezing rain is defined by rain arriving as SUPERCOOLED liquid, which happens when liquid rain descends into a layer whose temperature is below 0 C, becomes supercooled, and freezes on impact. Snow melting in an above-freezing layer produces ordinary rain; it is only the subsequent fall into sub-zero air beneath that makes it freezing rain. The classic setting is a warm layer aloft over a cold surface layer ahead of a winter warm front.
nwHfzR6cxZtccXpctbUm: The layer's temperature falls 2 C in 100 m, an environmental lapse rate of 2 C per 100 m. That exceeds even the dry adiabatic rate of 1 C per 100 m, so a displaced parcel - saturated or not - always ends up warmer and less dense than its surroundings and keeps accelerating upward. The layer is therefore ABSOLUTELY unstable. Conditional instability would require the ELR to lie between the saturated and dry rates, i.e. below 1 C per 100 m.
NwzCJBD89LaaRfjfz6t2: Advection is horizontal transport - the movement of air, and with it heat and moisture, from one place to another. Convection is vertical transport driven by buoyancy, and subsidence is slow widespread descent. Advection is what brings warm or cold air masses over a region, and advection fog is named for exactly this mechanism.
nynwtDhXOM0RB8YEiNNL: A thunderstorm requires three ingredients together: sufficient moisture, an unstable lapse rate so a saturated parcel keeps accelerating upward through a deep layer, and a trigger to lift the air to its condensation level. Stability is fatal to convection - it damps the vertical motion - and surface pressure is not a requirement at all; airmass thunderstorms form quite happily within a high.
O4TlCApFY7OrPp00A8TB: An isothermal layer has the same temperature throughout its depth, so its environmental lapse rate is zero. It is very stable: a parcel displaced upward cools at its adiabatic rate while the surroundings do not cool at all, so it becomes colder and denser and sinks back. A layer in which temperature actually INCREASES with height is an inversion, which is more stable still.
oaXSWwLMJFxCjznLBBVo: Tropopause height follows the depth and mean temperature of the troposphere beneath it, so it is highest where the surface is warmest. In the northern hemisphere it therefore descends going north: about 16-18 km over the equator, 11 km in mid-latitudes and only about 8 km over the pole. It also varies seasonally, being higher in summer than in winter at any given latitude.
oDdTNGt2pGbTgBvsKXsY: Take the pressure error first. QNH 1019 is 6 hPa above 1013, so the 1013 datum sits about 162 ft ABOVE sea level and FL135 corresponds to 13,500 + 162 = 13,662 ft above sea level in standard conditions. The actual true altitude is only 13,500 ft, i.e. lower than it should be, and air that is colder than ISA contracts and lowers the pressure surfaces. The air mass is therefore colder than ISA.
ohoefHQCOoNL7Me07Ns0: The Icelandic low, centred between Iceland and southern Greenland, is the dominant mean surface low of the North Atlantic and is at its deepest and most persistent in winter. Its pressure difference with the Azores high to the south sets the strength of the North Atlantic westerlies and steers the depression tracks. The Azores is a HIGH, and the Siberian high is a winter anticyclone.
oJtay41il94vGeXPD6KK: Above the friction layer the wind blows parallel to the isobars and there is no net inflow. Near the surface, friction slows the air, weakening the Coriolis force so that the unchanged pressure gradient force turns the flow inward across the isobars. That cross-isobaric component is what produces convergence at the centre of the low, and hence the ascent that gives its cloud and rain. Without friction there would be no low-level convergence.
OKL6H3d68iNbXImfCqXK: Surface synoptic charts plot mean sea level pressure computed using the ACTUAL temperature profile, which is QFF - the value that makes pressure patterns from stations at different elevations directly comparable. QNH uses the ISA profile and is an altimetry setting, not an analysis quantity; QFE is aerodrome-level pressure; QNE is the pressure altitude reading with 1013 set.
omGQMi45RrMhYV1msM1X: Cumulonimbus is the only cloud with enough vertical energy to overshoot the tropopause. A vigorous updraught arrives at the tropopause with momentum and punches a few thousand feet into the stable stratosphere before sinking back, producing the 'overshooting top' above the anvil - a reliable visual and satellite indicator of a severe storm. All the other cloud types are confined well within the troposphere.
OOPo3I2Et6FDSaebaDVw: On a clear, calm night the ground radiates its heat away and cools rapidly, chilling the air in contact with it far more than the air a few hundred feet up. The result is a surface-based inversion, typically a few hundred feet deep, which is very stable, traps moisture and pollution, and gives rise to radiation fog, mist and marked low-level wind shear at its top.
OSFqBcDnQGVNW81EArZz: A layer in which temperature increases with height is an inversion, and it is absolutely stable. A parcel lifted into it cools at its adiabatic rate while the surroundings get warmer, so the parcel becomes very much colder and denser than its environment and is forced straight back down. Inversions therefore act as lids, capping convection and trapping haze, smoke and moisture below them.
Ou3RkCgZyeP4CI7gpD7a: Warm air overriding cold air is the warm front mechanism: a shallow slope of about 1:150 with gentle, widespread ascent of stable air. That produces layer cloud, and the cloud lying at LOW level nearest the surface front is nimbostratus, thick and deep enough to give the continuous rain or snow. Altostratus lies above and ahead of it at medium level, and cumuliform cloud requires instability, not this gentle overriding.
oxxDYXTjwX4x7fCZqSra: A katabatic or mountain breeze blows DOWN the slope at NIGHT. The slope radiates heat away after dark, chilling the air in contact with it; that air becomes denser than air at the same level out over the valley and drains downhill under gravity, pooling cold air in the valley floor. The daytime reverse, driven by slope heating, is the anabatic or valley breeze, which blows up the slope.
oXzNLqQZ6uwEIyrb6jhH: Medium-level cloud in temperate regions has its base between about 6500 ft and 23,000 ft, and carries the prefix 'alto': altostratus and altocumulus. Cirrus, cirrocumulus and cirrostratus are high cloud; stratus, stratocumulus, cumulus and nimbostratus are classed as low cloud by their base height, even though nimbostratus can be very deep.
OzVuYOMWnuFk5CRJYx3R: The Foehn is the general name for a warm, dry downslope wind. Air forced up the windward side cools at the saturated rate once it condenses and loses its moisture as precipitation, then descends the lee side warming at the faster dry adiabatic rate, so it arrives both warmer and much drier than the air it started as. Local names include the Chinook in the Rockies. The Mistral and Bora are COLD fall winds and the Harmattan is a dusty trade wind.
P15vForRzKLXLTesuEY1: A secondary depression forms on a trailing front of a primary low and is embedded in the primary's circulation, so it is carried round the parent centre in the same cyclonic (anticlockwise in the northern hemisphere) sense, usually moving faster than the parent. Secondaries frequently deepen at the primary's expense and can eventually replace it, but they do not simply hold station or merge on the spot.
p7T7TZjISfHpS37dMK28: Unsaturated ascending air cools at the dry adiabatic lapse rate of 3 C per 1000 ft. Over 10,000 ft that is a fall of 30 C, so 15 - 30 = -15 C. Note this is much faster than the ISA environmental rate of about 2 C per 1000 ft, which is exactly why a rising dry parcel becomes colder than its surroundings and the atmosphere is normally stable to dry ascent.
pAau0ZoqAUYGWxUmuJIu: The TAF is valid 1000-1900. The main body gives 9999 (10 km or more). The TEMPO group carries no times of its own, so it applies throughout the validity period and forecasts 6000. The BECMG group with its 4000 does not begin until 1500, so it does not apply at an ETA of 1430. The lowest visibility applicable at 1430 is therefore 6000 m - 6 km. TAF visibilities are always in metres.
paeWrru1ORefM02HFhkm: As the parcel rises it expands and cools, but no water is added or removed, so the mass of vapour it carries per unit mass of air is unchanged: specific humidity and mixing ratio stay constant. What changes is how close that fixed amount is to saturation, because the saturation capacity falls steeply as the parcel cools - so RELATIVE humidity rises, reaching 100% at the condensation level.
pbRxzH8y4og5oAGo9Lvq: Sublimation is the change of state directly between vapour and ice without passing through the liquid phase, and in meteorological usage the term covers both directions. It is the process that builds cirrus, that deposits hoar frost on a cold airframe, and by which ice crystals grow at the expense of supercooled droplets in the Bergeron process that produces most mid-latitude precipitation.
pdcMMpG0nTlPG6okEv5n: Changing the subscale changes the reading by about 27 ft per hPa. Going from 1013 to 1000 is a decrease of 13 hPa, so the indication falls by 13 x 27 = 351 ft: 8000 - 351 = about 7650 ft. With QNH below 1013 the QNH altitude is always lower than the corresponding flight level - the aircraft is closer to the ground than the flight level number suggests.
pEOWmsxQvW2YDGnPa4aP: A thunderstorm is by definition a cumulonimbus with electrical discharge. Only CB has the depth and updraught strength to carry supercooled water and ice high enough for the charge separation that produces lightning, and to generate hail, severe turbulence and the downdraughts that create gust fronts and microbursts. This is why any CB, at any level, prohibits CAVOK.
Pl1pbXb7SSSeSQMmugUS: The ICAO Standard Atmosphere specifies a temperature decrease of 0.65 C per 100 m (6.5 C per km, or 1.98 C per 1000 ft) from 15 C at sea level up to 11 km, where it reaches -56.5 C and then stays constant to 20 km. The 1 C per 100 m alternative is the dry adiabatic lapse rate, which describes a rising parcel rather than the standard environment.
pTDWiC95NlUGTsOkfIuO: A thermal or heat low is created by intense surface heating, which requires a surface that warms rapidly - land - and strong insolation - summer. The heated air expands and rises, lowering the surface pressure and drawing in a converging inflow. The sea has a huge heat capacity and warms far too slowly to do this. The Iberian and Saharan summer heat lows, and the monsoon low over India, are the classic examples.
PV0h6w6cHK1UR2hO33M6: The dry adiabatic lapse rate is 3 C per 1000 ft, equivalently 1 C per 100 m. It is a fixed constant set by the thermodynamics of an expanding parcel, not by the state of the surrounding atmosphere. Compare 2 C per 1000 ft, which is the ISA environmental rate, and the saturated adiabatic rate, which is variable and always less than 3 C per 1000 ft.
q02QyFbQkbfQzkDxjw9k: BR is mist - a suspension of water droplets reducing visibility to between 1000 m and 5000 m - so the visibility of 2000 m is being reduced by water droplets. Reading the rest: R26R/P1500 means the RVR exceeds the maximum assessable value, while R26L/1500 is exactly 1500, so the two runways differ. The trailing N on each is the tendency indicator meaning No distinct change, which rules out both 'increasing' and 'distinct change'.
Q1bIiKBpxkvyNUl9Swj0: An inversion is any layer in which temperature increases with height, reversing the normal profile - no minimum rate of increase is required. Inversions are extremely stable, so they cap convection and trap moisture, smoke and dust beneath them, giving haze and poor visibility. Common types are radiation (nocturnal, surface-based), subsidence (aloft, in an anticyclone), frontal and turbulence inversions.
QAFJCsgrwVe4OCl7qmP3: 2000 ft AGL is above the friction layer, so the wind there is the gradient wind. Reversing the over-land friction rule - surface wind backed about 30 degrees and roughly half the speed - means going up you VEER about 30 degrees and DOUBLE the speed. 160 becomes about 190 and 20 kt becomes about 40 kt, giving 19040KT. Over the sea the change would be only about 10 degrees with a smaller speed increase.
qALHIEtI6vqBmHr8k36k: Altostratus carries the 'alto' prefix, which marks medium-level cloud: a base between about 6500 ft and 23,000 ft in temperate regions. It is a stratiform cloud formed by gentle widespread ascent, typically ahead of a warm front, and it renders the sun as a diffuse bright patch as though seen through ground glass - the standard way of distinguishing it from stratus, through which the sun's outline stays sharp.
qBn5iNLX2D7TcnbjWYQg: The ITCZ follows the overhead sun with a lag, but over the open Atlantic its excursion is small because the ocean's thermal inertia damps the seasonal swing - far less than over the continents. In January it sits at its southernmost Atlantic position, close to and just north of the equator, roughly 0-7 N, moving to about 10 N by July. A Dakar-Rio track crosses it in that band.
qe46ov7PVkQXTPbjqJLj: A TAF has no single fixed length: standard validities are 9, 18, 24 or 30 hours, and the actual period is given in the TAF itself as a day-and-hour group such as 0606/0706 or 1524. Always read the validity from the message rather than assuming. The 2-hour figure belongs to the TREND (BECMG/TEMPO/NOSIG) group appended to a METAR.
qfg0ggiCnKTR0vc5Mwit: Work through the groups for an ETA of 1200. The main body gives SCT050 BKN080. The TEMPO group carries no times of its own, so it applies throughout the 1000-1900 validity and forecasts BKN015 BKN030. The BECMG 1518 group with its OVC010 does not begin until 1500, so it does not apply. The lowest base applicable at 1200 is therefore 1500 ft. TAF cloud heights are always in feet above aerodrome level.
qgKItIwm4brj9BOb4hJb: Altocumulus carries the 'alto' prefix, marking it as medium-level cloud with a base between roughly 6500 ft and 23,000 ft above sea level in temperate regions. With the terrain itself only 1600 ft up, the base above the ground works out at roughly 7000-15,000 ft. Cloud classification is always by base height, and the band boundaries vary with latitude.
QhDA3UmI0t1F8PSs7CRB: A tornado is a very small but extremely intense vortex: the funnel is typically only 100-150 m across, with a track a few kilometres long, yet wind speeds inside can exceed 200 kt. Its small size is precisely why it is so destructive locally and so hard to forecast. Larger diameters of several kilometres belong to the parent mesocyclone, not the tornado itself.
qjevgmKkNqaHGTXpwDn1: Tropospheric depth follows the mean temperature of the air column, which varies systematically with latitude: about 16-18 km over the warm equator, 11 km in mid-latitudes and only 8 km over the cold poles. It also varies with season and with the passage of warm and cold air masses, but latitude is the primary control. Longitude and the earth's rotation have no direct effect.
QjwlZOel6ybyW1TgGXgm: At -25 C most of a layer cloud has glaciated into ice crystals, leaving very little supercooled liquid water, and crystals bounce off a cold airframe rather than adhering. Severe icing is therefore unlikely at this temperature. The serious risk lies between 0 C and about -15 C, where large supercooled droplets are abundant - which is why -5 C in dense cloud would be a real concern.
qKFifk1S0SzX51KFsI2o: Stable air resists vertical motion, so any lifting spreads out horizontally instead of building upward, producing flat, layered cloud: stratus, stratocumulus, altostratus, nimbostratus and cirrostratus. Cumuliform cloud - cumulus, cumulonimbus and cirrocumulus - requires instability. Nimbostratus is stratiform despite its depth, because it is formed by gentle widespread ascent rather than convection.
QkFUVszFyDtevZbjTm6F: Advection fog forms when warm, moist air is carried horizontally over a surface colder than its dewpoint and is cooled from below to saturation. It needs a wind of roughly 10-15 kt: enough turbulence to deepen the fog without lifting it into stratus. Cold air over a warmer surface does the opposite - it is heated from below, becomes unstable, and gives convection or steaming fog.
ql26QlDPtXMcfcAVpdZv: Radiational cooling is what drives the overnight temperature fall, and a complete overcast of stratus blocks it: the cloud absorbs the long-wave radiation from the ground and re-radiates much of it back down. With the sky covered all night the temperature therefore falls only a little, staying slightly below the 1800 UTC value of 3 C. Only under a clear sky would it plunge well below zero.
qlt0f1MCRkTYfB0I93WN: ISA temperature falls at 1.98 C per 1000 ft, so at FL200 it is 15 - 39.6 = about -25 C. An observed -35 C is therefore 10 C colder than standard: ISA -10. This calculation matters operationally because a colder-than-ISA air mass puts the aircraft LOWER than its indicated altitude.
qOpM48tMFgAT6bOAvQGd: A Caribbean hurricane forms in the trade wind easterlies and is steered westward on the equatorward flank of the Azores-Bermuda high. As it moves poleward round the western edge of that high it enters the mid-latitude westerlies and RECURVES, turning north and then north-east, usually accelerating as it does so. Recurvature is the standard track and is what carries storms up the US eastern seaboard.
qp4ohcs2f6CTnfdOr3Np: QNH is QFE plus the pressure equivalent of the aerodrome elevation, at about 1 hPa per 27 ft. Option A: 995 + 1600/27 = 995 + 59 = 1054. Option B: 1000 + 44 = 1044. Option C: 995 + 44 = 1039. Option D: 1003 + 44 = 1047. The greatest elevation adds the largest correction, so the 1600 ft aerodrome gives the highest QNH despite its low QFE.
qsuOGyFcyfNS1OX6jR3D: A tornado descends from the base of a severe cumulonimbus, specifically from the rotating updraught (mesocyclone) of a supercell. Only a CB has the depth, updraught strength and vertical shear needed to generate and concentrate that rotation. Ordinary cumulus, nimbostratus and stratus have nothing like the vertical motion required.
QtRlb7WFWnNKJtKW2wuh: The jet core sits at the tropopause break, on the warm-air side of the polar front and just beneath the higher warm-air tropopause - that is, within the WARM air mass, immediately above the sloping frontal surface. The strongest CAT is generally found on the cold (polar) side of the core and just below it, where the vertical and horizontal shear are greatest.
QVCB2Ltpgp6xSvSSG0aw: METAR temperatures are given in whole degrees with M prefixed for negative values, and 0.5 is rounded up. A temperature of -0.5 C rounds to zero but is still below freezing, so it is coded M00 - the special 'minus zero' form that preserves that information. The dewpoint of -1.5 C rounds up to -1 and is coded M01, giving M00/M01.
qvimJpibqVCuqevdhwgA: Friction slows the air near the surface. The Coriolis force is proportional to wind speed, so it weakens too, while the pressure gradient force stays the same, and the resultant wind turns toward low pressure. In the northern hemisphere that turn is anticlockwise, i.e. a BACKING - about 10 degrees over the sea and 30 degrees over land - accompanied by a reduction in speed.
qVPXYqSWD0iGpJYBze0H: Cirrus is a thin, high, tenuous ice cloud with a very low water content, so it produces no precipitation reaching the ground - at most fallstreaks that sublime away almost immediately. Nimbostratus is the archetypal rain cloud, cumulonimbus produces the heaviest showers and hail, and altostratus gives light continuous rain or snow.
QwkTOXlXicGWEiZGwvL4: Clear ice is the most dangerous form. It comes from large supercooled drops that only partly freeze on impact and run back over the surface before solidifying, so it is dense and heavy, adheres tenaciously, distorts the aerofoil section and spreads well AFT of the protected leading edges where boots and hot air cannot reach it. Rime is lighter and brittle, and hoar frost is a thin surface deposit.
r4djJfcMkcormPMB2H7i: The tropical easterly jet is a northern-hemisphere summer feature, running from south-east Asia across southern India and Arabia to central Africa at around 100-150 hPa. It exists because the intensely heated Tibetan plateau puts the WARM air on the poleward side, reversing the usual temperature gradient and hence the thermal wind, which is why this jet blows from the east while all the others blow from the west.
R7ldqDyob4vy33H0msQ7: A cold front passage in the northern hemisphere always produces a VEER in the surface wind - typically from south-westerly to north-westerly - together with a sharp temperature drop, a pressure rise, and a burst of showers. The two go together: the marked temperature change and the veer identify the frontal passage. In the southern hemisphere the wind backs instead.
Rblv92eKLZQZAmMYAscI: The geostrophic wind is defined as the balance of exactly two forces: the pressure gradient force and the Coriolis force. That balance is only possible with straight isobars and no friction, and it gives a wind blowing parallel to the isobars. Adding the centrifugal force, for curved isobars, gives the gradient wind; adding friction gives the surface wind.
RG0Xbp0YJJHGPTiE2u0w: A lapse rate steeper than 1 C per 100 m exceeds even the dry adiabatic rate, so a parcel displaced upward - saturated or not - is always warmer and less dense than its surroundings and keeps accelerating. That is absolute instability. Such superadiabatic layers are shallow and short-lived, typically just above a strongly heated surface, because the convection they trigger quickly overturns and stabilises the layer.
RHteyLypEdMV7fX07tja: Changing the subscale from QNH 1023 to the standard 1013 is a reduction of 10 hPa, and winding the subscale down winds the indication down with it - by about 10 x 27 = 270 ft. The reading therefore DECREASES. The general rule: with QNH above 1013 the flight level reads lower than the QNH altitude, and with QNH below 1013 it reads higher.
rMwj1XUeVKh1timYgneC: The maximum amount of water vapour air can hold - its saturation capacity - is determined solely by temperature, and rises steeply with it: warm air holds far more vapour than cold. Dewpoint and relative humidity describe how much vapour is actually present relative to that capacity, and stability has nothing to do with it. This is why cooling air to its dewpoint forces condensation.
RPhZl2N8r3gDjf7X964o: An active warm front brings extensive nimbostratus with a low, ragged base and continuous rain, and the rain falling into the cold air ahead raises its humidity to saturation, giving mist, drizzle and often frontal fog. The result at low level is a low cloud base with poor visibility - the classic marginal-VFR trap. Thunderstorms and severe turbulence belong to the cold front, whose slope is far steeper.
Rqg5Mdyjdi9h132CBHrb: Decode carefully. 25020G38KT is a mean wind of 20 kt from 250 with gusts to 38 - the 38 is a gust, not the top of a mean range. +TSGR is a thunderstorm with HEAVY hail, not moderate. 23/18 is temperature 23 C and dewpoint 18 C. So the only fully correct reading is gusts to 38 kt, thunderstorm with heavy hail, dewpoint 18 C.
rR86eoGKKhmNJdVNVaJr: Flying a constant pressure surface, you gain true altitude when the contour heights increase ahead. Use Buys Ballot: in the northern hemisphere, face downwind and low pressure is on your LEFT. Heading west with the wind from the NORTH, the wind blows toward the south; facing south, the low heights are to the east - behind you - so the heights rise ahead and you gain altitude. A pure head or tailwind means you are flying along the contours, so the altitude would not change at all.
rrh69XBldKbpFkSaxsTx: The Caribbean hurricane season runs roughly from June to November, peaking in September, and July to November covers the active part. The controlling factor is sea surface temperature: the ocean needs at least about 26.5 C through a deep layer, which it only reaches after a full season of solar heating - which is why the peak lags the June solstice by about three months.
rSbGQGDEiiFP6Ef9oovd: The standard upper-air charts and their approximate ISA heights are 850 hPa near FL50, 700 hPa near FL100, 500 hPa near FL180, 300 hPa near FL300 and 200 hPa near FL390. A pressure level of 18,289 ft therefore corresponds to the 500 hPa chart, which is the standard chart for the mid-tropospheric flow and for locating cold pools.
rSCrkvNa1ZoSAYiZDjFu: Over land the ITCZ's seasonal swing is far larger than over the ocean, because the continent heats and cools much faster. Over West Africa it lies around 5 N in January and migrates to its northernmost position of about 15-20 N in July, which is what brings the West African monsoon rains inland. Its arrival and retreat define the wet season across the Sahel.
ruOar1UZ9AglIRU5dawt: The wind group in a METAR is the mean direction and speed over the TEN minutes immediately preceding the observation. If the speed varied by 10 kt or more within that period, the maximum is added as a gust (G). If the direction varied by 60 degrees or more, a variable range is appended. ATC, by contrast, passes a 2-minute mean for take-off and landing.
rVmnZOyX4XEg0hfTB3DE: By day the valley sides are heated by the sun and warm the air against them, which becomes buoyant and flows UP the slopes and up-valley toward the mountain - the anabatic or valley wind. At night the slopes cool by radiation, the air against them becomes dense and drains back down - the katabatic or mountain wind. The daytime up-valley flow is the stronger and more persistent of the two.
rw6UWj9CZ5aOdPW1FqG7: At the transition level on descent the subscale is changed from 1013 to the local QNH. Going from 1013 down to 1009 is a reduction of 4 hPa, and winding the subscale down winds the indication down with it - by about 4 x 27 = 108 ft. The reading therefore decreases. Whenever QNH is below 1013, the QNH altitude is lower than the corresponding flight level.
S1zqsr0uo2t0sokL5v3a: Ice pellets (PL) are frozen raindrops. They form where snow melts in a warm layer aloft and the resulting raindrops then freeze completely while falling through a deep sub-zero layer beneath. That is exactly the profile that gives FREEZING RAIN where the cold layer is shallower - so ice pellets at the surface are a direct warning that supercooled rain, and severe icing, exist at a higher level.
s6ccMQcDBTG5O0JiSC1D: An inversion is very stable and decouples the air above it from the surface. The layer beneath stays light or calm under friction, while the air just above retains the full gradient wind, so speed and direction can both change markedly across a few hundred feet - differences of 30 kt or more are common. That is precisely why a nocturnal inversion with a strong wind above it is a low-level wind shear warning.
sC1Uu4ztY19ZUaGHda8P: The Bora is a cold fall (katabatic) wind, most frequent in winter, in which dense cold air pooled over the Balkan tableland spills through gaps in the coastal range and accelerates down to the Adriatic, often in violent gusts. Unlike the Foehn it arrives COLD, because the air starts so cold that the adiabatic warming on descent is not enough to offset it.
sc6Iz1QGWF9yBVIvKiaD: The Bora is a cold katabatic wind: dense continental air spills over the coastal escarpment and accelerates downslope, and the gap-funnelling makes it extremely gusty, with peaks that can exceed 100 kt. It originates over a cold CONTINENTAL interior, not a maritime source, and it is often accompanied by clear skies rather than always by cloud and showers - which is why the qualified wording matters.
sDwPl4xLuBbwZL5zkiZK: 2000 ft AGL is above the friction layer. Reversing the over-land friction rule - surface wind backed about 30 degrees and roughly half the speed - means climbing to 2000 ft you VEER about 30 degrees and DOUBLE the speed: 080 becomes about 110 and 10 kt becomes about 20 kt, giving 11020KT. Over the sea the change would be only about 10 degrees with a smaller speed increase.
SHN9oWy8kdFCHozkZHne: Moderate turbulence gives definite changes in altitude and attitude, and occupants feel a positive strain against their seat belts, but the aircraft remains under positive control throughout and indicated airspeed varies. Severe turbulence brings large abrupt changes with the aircraft momentarily out of control, and extreme turbulence can cause structural damage. Light turbulence is the rhythmic bumpiness with no appreciable attitude change.
SK09581kSyTQMspXNXB6: The significant weather chart (SIGWX) is the flight-planning chart for en-route hazards: it depicts areas of moderate or severe icing and turbulence, CB and thunderstorm areas, jet stream cores, tropopause heights, fronts, and the height of the 0 C isotherm (freezing level). Constant-pressure charts give wind and temperature at a single level, and the surface chart gives the pressure pattern and fronts.
SkMfYNZNP8NJqdooxoBa: A tropical downpour produces a density of large raindrops far beyond anything in temperate rain, and the water film streaming over the windscreen degrades the view further. Flight visibility from the cockpit can collapse to a few hundred metres - of the order of 500 m or worse - within seconds, with no warning, which is why a go-around decision must be made before entering the shaft rather than during it.
sMx87iPUV1McwkzWUrLW: A warm front normally gives stratiform cloud because the overrunning warm air is stable. Embedded thunderstorms occur when the WARM air being lifted over the frontal surface is both moist and conditionally unstable - that is, when the environmental lapse rate exceeds the saturated adiabatic rate - so that once the gentle frontal ascent saturates it, it keeps accelerating upward on its own. The stability of the cold air below is irrelevant, since it is not the air being lifted.
smyvAFjxZMgKhnlGEUxQ: A squall line is by definition a line of active thunderstorms, typically 50-300 NM ahead of a fast-moving cold front and running for hundreds of miles. Expect severe turbulence, heavy showers and hail, lightning, strong gust fronts and severe low-level wind shear. Its length makes it hard to circumnavigate, which is why it is a mandatory SIGMET item.
Spzm2ML1TuE5i0xjCQ8Z: Descending through the friction layer in the northern hemisphere, the wind BACKS and decreases - about 30 degrees and half the speed over land. A southerly (180) at 2500 ft AGL therefore becomes about 150 at the surface, which is south-south-easterly. Backing means turning anticlockwise, so 180 goes toward 150, not toward 210.
sSp0O10sABZP62NqNDee: With 1013 set but an actual QNH of 993, the subscale is 20 hPa too high, so the altimeter over-reads by 20 x 27 = 540 ft. The indicated 1200 ft is therefore 540 ft more than the true elevation: 1200 - 540 = 660 ft. Remember that with 1013 set on the ground the reading is the PRESSURE altitude of the aerodrome, which only equals the elevation when QNH happens to be 1013.
SvfQY1cuzoHOECo5dogK: Polar continental (Pc) air forms over the great high-latitude landmasses - principally Siberia, and also northern Canada - in winter, where prolonged radiational cooling over snow-covered ground produces air that is extremely cold, very dry and stable. When it reaches western Europe it brings hard frost, excellent visibility and clear skies, though it picks up moisture and instability if it crosses the North Sea.
SwWLUDBhCs58jmZvEAUx: The ISA lapse rate is 0.65 C per 100 m. The climb from 500 m to 2500 m is 2000 m, so the temperature falls by 20 x 0.65 = 13 C. Starting from +15 C gives 15 - 13 = +2 C at the summit. Note that this uses the ENVIRONMENTAL rate, because we are comparing two points in the surrounding atmosphere, not following a rising parcel.
T0JiK2h09Q4DCNeTe5H6: Stability depends on the environmental lapse rate, so anything that warms the top of a layer or cools its bottom reduces the temperature difference across it, flattens the lapse rate and increases stability. Warm advection aloft with cold advection below does both at once. The reverse - warm air below, cold air aloft - steepens the lapse rate and destabilises the layer, which is how cold pools generate showers.
t1Sjp3e1D4f4raEgAhFD: Pressure falls steadily as an active cold front approaches and then rises sharply once it has passed - the classic V-shaped pressure trace with its minimum at the frontal passage. An altimeter reads height above the pressure set on its subscale, so falling pressure makes the indication rise and rising pressure makes it fall. A parked aircraft's altimeter will therefore first increase, then decrease.
T2ubhtys5FF0KfDMyHlc: Convection is driven by surface heating, so it peaks when insolation is strongest and the surface warmest: summer afternoons. The surface goes on gaining more heat than it loses until mid-afternoon, which is why cumulus builds through the day and airmass thunderstorms peak around 1400-1600 local, then decay in the evening. At night and in winter the surface is a heat sink and the lower atmosphere is stable.
T5HJ3gKi7nVgC7il9QhE: A cold front undercuts the warm air steeply, on a slope of about 1:50, forcing rapid ascent that in an unstable summer air mass produces towering cumulus and cumulonimbus with heavy showers, hail and squalls. The other options describe the reverse of what happens: after a cold front the pressure RISES and the temperature FALLS, and layered cloud belongs to the warm front.
T6Dds8daYfrsoCdl3ehu: Radiation fog needs four things: a clear night, so the ground can radiate its heat away; light wind, to mix the cooling through a shallow layer without dispersing it; moist air, so little cooling is needed to reach the dewpoint; and a long night. It forms over LAND, since the sea does not cool appreciably overnight. The other options describe advection fog, orographic cloud and steaming fog respectively.
t9PknzaKaU2VazJ9Tkmh: Isolated, local thunderstorms are airmass or heat storms, triggered when strong surface heating lifts a parcel to its condensation level within a single warm, moist, unstable air mass. Because the trigger is thermal, they appear in the afternoon, are scattered rather than organised in lines, and dissipate after sunset. Frontal storms are triggered by mechanical lifting and are organised along the front, at any hour.
tBFTpqpqoxBH8kGQKIXq: Forecast upper winds - on significant weather charts, wind and temperature charts and in flight documentation - are always given relative to TRUE north and in knots. Only ATC-passed surface winds for take-off and landing are magnetic, because they are being compared directly against a runway direction. Mixing the two up introduces an error equal to the local variation.
TbfUclYoGCG93BUtpWSQ: A clear desert night produces a very strong surface radiation inversion. Climbing out of the cool surface layer into the much warmer air above sharply reduces air density, so both engine thrust and wing lift fall away just as the aircraft is heavy and slow - the rate of climb can drop to zero. The performance penalty is a density effect; low humidity actually helps performance rather than hindering it.
tdNKKbIwaqGTD5ccSxHU: At 2055Z three groups are live. The main body forecasts 9999 (10 km or more). TEMPO 1822 forecasts 5000 m in showers of rain and snow. PROB30 TEMPO 1821 forecasts 1500 m in a thunderstorm with hail. So the visibility could be anything from the 1500 m worst case up to in excess of 10 km - the TEMPO groups describe temporary deteriorations, not a replacement of the prevailing conditions.
TIvNv2ZAKpZg92TaxQn3: On a clear night the ground cools by radiation and forms a strong surface-based inversion. That very stable layer decouples the calm air beneath it from the air above, which retains the full gradient wind, so speed and direction can change sharply across a few hundred feet. Nocturnal low-level jets frequently form just above such inversions, and the resulting shear is a real hazard on early-morning approaches all year round.
tl2w7CKNxmm8wv6ylTGY: Rime ice is white, opaque, rough and granular, and it builds forward from the leading edge. It forms when SMALL supercooled droplets freeze essentially instantly on impact, trapping air between them, which is what makes it look powdery and keeps it light and brittle - so it is readily shed by de-icing boots. Clear ice is transparent and glassy, and hoar frost is a thin crystalline deposit from vapour.
tLjAxn1gPTUdFvntbt2Y: A warm front has a very shallow slope, about 1:150, because the advancing warm air is less dense and can only ride gently up over the retreating cold air. That shallow slope is why its cloud and precipitation extend so far ahead of the surface position - typically 300-500 NM - and why its weather changes so slowly. A cold front is roughly three times steeper at about 1:50, giving its sharp, brief, vigorous weather.
tm4ASSSEphCALeQ4qN4B: The Gulf of Guinea sits on the northern side of the equator, so its wind regime follows the ITCZ. In the northern summer the ITCZ migrates north to 15-20 N, and the south-east trades cross the equator, are deflected to the right and arrive as the moist SOUTH-WEST monsoon that brings the West African rains. In winter the ITCZ retreats south and the region falls under the dry NORTH-EAST trades - the dusty Harmattan.
TR02MLb493IsEOIwnn5Q: QNH is QFE plus the pressure equivalent of the aerodrome elevation. 200 m is about 656 ft, and at roughly 27 ft per hPa that is 656 / 27 = 24 hPa. QNH = 1000 + 24 = about 1024, so approximately 1025 hPa. QNH is always higher than QFE for an aerodrome above sea level, and the two coincide only at sea level.
TvxWcAC42IskB94Z8O8h: The two classic sources of severe low-level shear are a strong surface inversion, which decouples a calm surface layer from a much faster flow just above, and a thunderstorm, whose downdraught outflow and gust front can reverse the wind by 50 kt or more within seconds. Both put the shear exactly where an aircraft is slow, heavy and close to the ground. Mountain and valley effects also cause shear, but are neither as sudden nor as severe.
tyVTjUosk6vl4FMRRTcZ: ATIS carries both. The operational part gives the runway in use, approach type, transition level, and any significant aerodrome conditions or works; the meteorological part gives surface wind, visibility or RVR, present weather, cloud, temperature, dewpoint and QNH. Broadcasting all of it continuously is precisely what relieves the frequency congestion ATIS exists to solve.
tzB0NkxMel3EwYl7ac65: The SIGWX spatial-coverage terms are precise: ISOL (isolated) means individual cells covering less than 50% of the area; OCNL (occasional) means WELL-SEPARATED cells covering 50-75%; FRQ (frequent) means cells with little or no separation, over 75%. EMBD describes CB embedded in other cloud layers and hence not visually avoidable, which is a separate axis from coverage.
u3aXRrkL04zF6Onkhked: Severe turbulence, including severe CAT, is one of the phenomena for which a SIGMET is mandatory, along with thunderstorms, severe icing, severe mountain wave, volcanic ash, sandstorm and tropical cyclone. A SIGMET is a warning of en-route weather hazardous to aircraft, valid for up to 4 hours (6 for volcanic ash and tropical cyclone). A SPECI is a special observation of aerodrome conditions, and meteorology does not close airspace.
u73HaX2899KkTdMyaapB: Relative humidity is the actual vapour content expressed as a percentage of the saturation capacity at that temperature. If the temperature is held constant, the capacity is fixed, so adding water vapour raises the numerator and therefore raises the relative humidity - up to 100% at saturation. Removing vapour lowers it. Temperature affects it too, by changing the denominator.
UaenEsaMwmxgwBhuaNOv: Warming air raises its saturation capacity steeply while the amount of vapour actually present is unchanged, so the ratio - the relative humidity - falls. This is why the afternoon is normally the driest part of the day in relative terms, and why heating an aircraft cabin makes it feel dry. Cooling does the reverse, raising relative humidity to 100% at the dewpoint.
UBX03wPfTYKckqlk3niQ: Water vapour is the key weather constituent even though it makes up under 4% of the atmosphere by volume. It is the only substance that changes phase at ordinary atmospheric temperatures, so it forms all cloud, fog and precipitation; its latent heat powers thunderstorms and tropical cyclones; and it is the dominant greenhouse gas. Nitrogen and oxygen dominate by volume but are meteorologically inert.
UErRRudQfe264U1ge1gj: The runway state group runs DRDR ER CR eReR BRBR. Here 01 is runway 01, 6 is the deposit (slush), 5 is the extent (51-100% covered), 04 is the depth in millimetres, and 28 is the measured friction coefficient of 0.28. That figure feeds directly into landing distance calculations. Note 0.28 corresponds to MEDIUM to POOR braking action, not medium to good - the medium band starts at about 0.30.
uG39kzAAfl1sSSfMR6vL: TEMPO describes temporary fluctuations expected to last LESS THAN ONE HOUR in each instance, and in aggregate less than half of the period covered by the group. If a change is expected to persist for an hour or more, the forecaster must use BECMG or a new time-referenced group instead. That one-hour ceiling is what distinguishes a TEMPO deterioration from a lasting one when assessing alternate requirements.
uge64S6dVw13QEf9uO9K: The altimeter is set to the correct QNH of a sea-level airport, so there is no pressure error - only a temperature error. Air 10 C warmer than ISA is less dense and expands, so the aircraft is physically HIGHER than the altimeter indicates. To be truly at 12,000 ft you read less: correction = 4 ft per 1000 ft per degree = 4 x 10 x 12 = 480 ft, giving 12,000 - 480 = 11,520 ft indicated. Warm air is the safe case; cold air is the dangerous one.
UGwWpw1y72BlgapfvHus: The Foehn is a warm, dry downslope wind that forms whenever air is forced over a range: it loses its moisture as precipitation on the windward side, then descends the lee side warming at the faster dry adiabatic rate. Because it depends only on which way the air is being forced, in the Alps it can blow from the south or from the north depending on the synoptic pattern. The Mistral and Bora are cold, and the Scirocco is a southerly off North Africa.
ujpE74pAT58f06hvS2vl: The friction layer is as deep as turbulence can mix surface drag upward, so it depends on the roughness of the surface (mountains and cities mix far deeper than open sea), the wind speed (stronger wind means more mechanical turbulence), and the stability (an unstable layer mixes readily and deepens the layer, while a stable layer or inversion confines it). Typical depths run from a few hundred feet over the sea at night to several thousand feet over rough terrain by day.
uK91q5QXI6LjDEuINE6o: Pressure altitude equals true altitude only when the whole atmosphere matches the standard model - that is, sea-level pressure 1013.25 hPa AND the temperature profile matching ISA. Either condition alone is not enough: correct pressure with non-standard temperature still gives a temperature error, and standard temperature with a non-standard QNH still gives a pressure error.
ULwlQTB0MHvRtWEOvLfo: A flight level is a constant-PRESSURE surface, so at FL180 the pressure is fixed at about 500 hPa whatever the weather. Density then depends only on temperature. ISA at FL180 is about -21 C, so an actual -35 C is 14 C colder than standard, and colder air at the same pressure is DENSER. Hence the density exceeds the ISA value for that level, and the QNH is irrelevant to the comparison.
ULyzn9ndj07jUdoOMoUX: A microburst is an intense, small-scale downburst from a convective cloud, driven downward because evaporating precipitation has chilled the air, making it denser and COLDER than its surroundings. It spreads violently outward on striking the ground. On approach it produces a performance-increasing headwind, then a severe downdraught, then a sudden performance-decreasing tailwind - all within a minute or two.
uMAaW9GDCyVkAX7A7rqf: Sublimation is the change of state directly between solid and vapour, bypassing the liquid phase entirely - and in meteorological usage the term is applied in both directions. It builds cirrus and hoar frost, and it drives the Bergeron process, in which ice crystals grow at the expense of supercooled droplets to produce most mid-latitude precipitation. Solid to liquid is melting, and liquid to vapour is evaporation.
URAOdlfnDs4DkzjytAH9: A significant weather chart is a fixed-time forecast: it shows the significant weather expected AT the validity time printed on the chart, not averaged over a window and not an observation. Charts are issued for standard times (typically 0000, 0600, 1200 and 1800 UTC) and depict fronts, CB and thunderstorm areas, moderate or severe turbulence and icing, jet cores, tropopause heights and the freezing level.
us5YQVMChTd00WmWkbKa: Wind is air moving from higher to lower pressure, so the fundamental cause is a horizontal pressure difference - itself created by differential heating of the earth's surface. The earth's rotation (Coriolis) and surface friction only modify the direction and speed of that flow once it exists; without a pressure gradient there would be no wind for them to act on.
UsfqXenBAIDEMzI5GKZ5: Decode it group by group: 0400 is the meteorological visibility of 400 m; R16/1000N is the RVR for runway 16, 1000 m with no distinct change; FZFG is freezing fog; VV003 is a vertical visibility of 300 FEET (cloud heights are always in feet); and M02/M02 gives a temperature and dewpoint of -2 C each. Note R14/P1500 means the RVR exceeds 1500 m, so quoting it as exactly 1500 would be wrong.
UXYKIxvEf61ZqdUwoie4: Airborne weather radar detects precipitation-sized particles by the energy they reflect, and reflectivity rises very steeply with droplet size and with the liquid state - so it maps zones of rain and wet hail and their intensity, colour-coded by returned power. It does NOT see cloud droplets, dry snow, dry hail or clear air turbulence, which is why radar-quiet does not mean hazard-free.
uyGAHB3aVAYs3etjFbuD: Subsiding air warms adiabatically as it is compressed, and where it meets the cooler, turbulent boundary layer beneath it a subsidence inversion forms across a wide area. That inversion caps vertical mixing, so cloud dissolves above it while moisture, smoke and dust accumulate below, giving the widespread haze and mist typical of a stagnant anticyclone. Extensive layer cloud and thunderstorms both require ascent, not descent.
UzrX3QqCHTo9CMFGNQvO: Typhoons are the north-west Pacific's tropical revolving storms, and the season runs broadly July to November with a peak around August-September, when the sea surface temperature is highest after a full summer of heating. Southern Japan lies on the recurvature track, where storms turn north and then north-east into the mid-latitude westerlies.
v7zqTs9vNIW2KdDfpsRF: Above the tropopause the temperature stops falling. Through the lower stratosphere, from about 11 km to 20 km in the standard atmosphere, it stays almost constant at around -56.5 C; only higher up does absorption of ultraviolet radiation by ozone warm the air, so the temperature rises toward the stratopause at about 50 km. This isothermal, very stable layer is what makes the tropopause such an effective lid on convection.
VcwpSsxqPojrKHIR5VPn: Serious icing needs abundant supercooled liquid water, sub-zero temperatures and long exposure. Nimbostratus is deep, water-rich and horizontally extensive, so an aircraft stays in it long enough to accumulate moderate to severe ice. The upper part of a cumulonimbus is glaciated into ice crystals which do not adhere, clear air holds no liquid water at all, and altostratus is thinner and higher so icing there is usually lighter.
VHx6SW9cRMX5XQbslyDz: Cumulonimbus capillatus is the mature form of a thunderstorm cell: the top has glaciated into ice crystals and lost its sharp cauliflower outline, taking on a fibrous, striated, hair-like appearance, usually spread into the classic anvil (incus). It is the visual marker that the cell has reached the mature stage, with precipitation, downdraughts, lightning and possibly hail. Cumulonimbus calvus is the earlier stage, with the top still smooth and rounded.
ViFnEQpUvZMe6mVJxQ58: The winter (north-east) monsoon blows off the cold, dry Asian landmass, where a huge shallow anticyclone builds over Siberia. The air arrives over India as a north-easterly that is dry, stable and dusty, giving hazy skies and little or no rain over most of the subcontinent. The moist south-westerlies belong to the summer monsoon, when the flow reverses.
vjWDzMKVDDyF17ViQpwe: A Foehn blows on the LEEWARD side. Air forced up the windward slope cools at the dry rate to its condensation level, then at the slower saturated rate while it precipitates out much of its moisture. Having lost that water, it descends the lee side warming at the full dry adiabatic rate the whole way, so it arrives both warmer and much drier than the air at the same level upwind. The moisture loss is the essential mechanism.
vNYoxjikFPdmnAuenZ2j: Clear air turbulence is caused by wind shear, so its intensity scales with the strength of the vertical and horizontal shear in the airflow - which is why CAT is worst near a sharply curved jet stream, on the cold side and just below the core, and around a deep trough. Solar radiation drives convective turbulence, not CAT, and stability alone determines whether shear breaks down into turbulence rather than how severe it becomes.
VPcbLyxgEkZC3X27YjWj: An active cold front undercuts unstable warm air on a steep slope of about 1:50, forcing rapid ascent. Once saturated, that unstable air keeps accelerating upward on its own, building cumulonimbus - so the precipitation is showery, heavy, brief and often accompanied by thunder, hail and squalls. Continuous rain and drizzle come from the stratiform cloud of stable air at a warm front.
VQDU9hJtPeiItmFdeRdM: This is the freezing rain structure: warm air overriding the front holds the cloud and its rain above the 3000 ft freezing level, while everything below 3000 ft is sub-zero, reaching -5 C at the surface. Rain falling out of that cloud enters the cold layer, becomes supercooled and freezes on impact - so severe icing is expected from the ground up to 3000 ft. Note that being clear of cloud is no protection: the drops are already liquid and already supercooled.
VsXkJeVgrwUoD7jQuSxC: Altocumulus lenticularis is the standing lens-shaped cloud that forms at the crest of a mountain wave, where the rising air cools to saturation; it appears stationary while the air flows through it. Its presence confirms a stable layer, a strong cross-ridge wind and a standing wave train downwind, with severe turbulence in the rotor zone beneath the wave crests.
VT9xESvgpAI0W1n89RSp: Supercooled droplets need only a temperature below 0 C and an absence of freezing nuclei, and sub-zero temperatures exist aloft all year round - the freezing level in mid-latitudes is around 10,000 ft even in high summer. So supercooled water, and the airframe icing it causes, can be met in any season and at any altitude above the freezing level, not just in winter.
VtAowZ101sjhyah19uEK: QFE is QNH reduced by the pressure equivalent of the aerodrome elevation. Using the stated 1 hPa = 8 m, 200 m corresponds to 200 / 8 = 25 hPa. QFE = 1015 - 25 = 990 hPa. The 8 m per hPa figure is the metric equivalent of the familiar 27 ft per hPa, and like it applies only near sea level.
vZNQuZnlBUn1f6NxZD6r: Heavy rain (+RA) needs a deep, water-rich cloud with sustained ascent over a wide area, which is nimbostratus - the archetypal continuous-precipitation cloud of a warm front. Stratus and stratocumulus are too shallow and give at most drizzle or light rain, and altocumulus is a thin medium-level cloud. Heavy SHOWERS (+SHRA) would come from cumulonimbus instead.
wAKNPtW5GUZ9tHzY5oIS: The ITCZ is by definition where the trade wind systems of the two hemispheres converge: the north-east trades of the northern hemisphere meeting the south-east trades of the southern. The convergence forces deep ascent in warm, very moist air, giving the near-permanent line of cumulonimbus and heavy showers. Monsoons are the seasonal reversals that occur where the ITCZ migrates far over land.
wgJYY0oLXDJzn2Q1HtnK: Icing needs supercooled LIQUID water, so any cloud with 'cirro' in its name is ruled out - cirrostratus and cirrocumulus form above about 20,000 ft at temperatures near -40 C and are pure ice crystal. That leaves the medium-level water clouds, altocumulus and altostratus, which typically give light to moderate icing.
wgwKsZRf1BNDTqCdKpqq: With regional QNH 1013 set there is no pressure error, so only temperature matters. Very cold air is dense and contracts, so the pressure surfaces are lower than standard and the aircraft is physically LOWER than the altimeter indicates. Flying level with the summit, the instrument therefore shows an altitude greater than the summit's elevation - the classic cold-weather mountain trap: 'from hot to cold, look out below'.
WHtCPF8fyoOuybEoCVqP: Steady, continuous precipitation comes from stratiform cloud formed by gentle, widespread ascent in STABLE air, so there is little vertical motion and hence little turbulence, and the precipitation covers a large area and changes only slowly. Showery precipitation is the convective counterpart: brief, sharply varying and locally intense, with the turbulence that the updraughts imply.
WL3ftROpzPS4jrQBYxZ5: The 200 hPa surface lies near 39,000 ft, which is above the ISA tropopause at 36,090 ft, so the standard temperature there is the constant tropopause value of -56.5 C. A reading of -55 C is therefore within about 1.5 C of standard - well inside plus or minus 5 C. Always compare an upper-air temperature with the ISA value for that level rather than judging the raw number.
Wlo0Ebn2UwQXSPDKIr28: The significant weather chart marks jet streams explicitly, with a bold arrow along the core, the flight level of the core, the maximum speed, and double bars where the speed changes by 20 kt. It also shows the tropopause heights and CAT areas that go with it. An upper wind and temperature chart shows the flow at one level and requires interpretation of the isotachs to locate the core.
wmyvUvnVf9njCZriqQsl: Both parcels cool by expansion as they rise, but in a saturated parcel the water vapour is condensing, and condensation RELEASES latent heat back into the parcel. That heat partially offsets the expansional cooling, so the net rate of cooling is lower - the saturated adiabatic rate, roughly 1.2-2.8 C per 1000 ft, against the dry rate's fixed 3 C per 1000 ft. This is exactly why saturated air is more unstable than dry air.
wNR86rjuCWoRxCDz8jbH: QFE is QNH reduced by the pressure equivalent of the aerodrome elevation, so the elevation is the only extra information required - at about 1 hPa per 27 ft (or 8 m). Temperature does not enter, because both QNH and QFE are defined on the ISA relationship. It is QFF that uses the actual temperature, which is why QFF and QNH differ in non-standard air.
Wo3DT2BGDPT8TDRUSwmC: In a stratiform cloud the liquid water content increases with height above the base, because the air has been rising and condensing throughout the cloud's depth, so the largest supercooled droplets accumulate near the top. With a surface temperature near 0 C the whole depth of a thick stratocumulus layer is in the icing band, and the upper part - biggest drops, highest water content - is where severe icing occurs. Stratocumulus in northern Europe in winter is water, not ice crystals.
Wp3vJJc4d3JJeRFvFSrD: An inversion is a layer in which temperature increases with height, and it is extremely stable: a parcel lifted into it cools at its adiabatic rate while the surroundings get warmer, so it becomes much colder and denser and is forced straight back down. Inversions therefore cap convection, suppress storms, and trap moisture, smoke and dust beneath them, giving haze and poor visibility.
wr04ToKGplApM4nXDtJ9: RVR is assessed against high-intensity runway lights, which stay visible through fog long after unlit dark objects have disappeared, and it is measured close to the runway surface. Meteorological visibility is assessed against unlit objects by day, so in homogeneous fog it is generally LESS than the RVR. That difference is precisely why RVR, not visibility, is the controlling value for low-visibility take-off and landing.
wsQwoNOsstlSqjYInkjr: RVR is defined as the range over which the pilot of an aircraft on the centre line of a runway can see the runway surface markings, or the lights delineating the runway or identifying its centre line - so it is a LENGTH OF RUNWAY, specific to that runway, not a general visibility. It is measured by transmissometers or forward-scatter meters sited alongside the runway, and reported when visibility or RVR is below 1500 m.
WtZ7dVtvOfX1HOnxS4tp: Smoke and other pollutants only accumulate when they cannot be dispersed vertically, so the critical ingredient is a low-level inversion capping the layer. Under a nocturnal radiation inversion or a subsidence inversion in a stagnant anticyclone, industrial smoke builds up beneath the lid and visibility collapses. A strong gusty wind, afternoon convection or a passing cold front all mix or sweep the pollutants away.
wuWWWkl8biKbzv5oKdBa: An easterly wave is a shallow trough moving westward through the trade wind belt. Ahead of the trough line the air subsides and the weather is fine; behind it there is convergence and ascent, giving a broad band of deep convective cloud with thunderstorms and heavy rain. Easterly waves are the seedlings from which many tropical revolving storms develop. There is no frontal weather - fronts require the temperature contrasts of higher latitudes.
WvpiSXysnW00uYuTeKGB: Airmass and orographic thunderstorms are largely stationary, tied to the heated surface or the terrain that triggers them. Frontal thunderstorms are embedded in and steered by the frontal system, which is itself driven along by the upper flow, so they move with the front - often at 30-40 kt or more. That speed makes them harder to circumnavigate and is why they can arrive at an aerodrome with little warning.
Wy7TPMj86bzEjpK3B4r2: Ahead of a warm front, rain from the overrunning warm air falls through the cold air trapped beneath the frontal surface. Some of it evaporates into that cold air, raising its dewpoint until it saturates, and the result is very low ragged stratus and frontal fog. The key point is that it is the COLD air that becomes saturated - the warm air aloft is already at saturation inside its own cloud.
WYvLAnAkMjb2pE2LyN0c: The warm front cloud sequence approaching from the cold side runs CI, CS, AS, NS. Seeing it in REVERSE - nimbostratus first, then altostratus, cirrostratus and cirrus - means you are flying out from under the frontal cloud shield into the cold air AHEAD of the warm front. Leaving warm air for cold air means the outside temperature falls. Strong gusty winds would be the signature of a cold front, which has quite different cloud.
Wz7NKQ42Q3RdGEJ0cemy: SIGMET covers en-route phenomena hazardous to aircraft in flight: thunderstorms, tropical cyclone, severe turbulence, severe icing, severe MOUNTAIN WAVE, heavy duststorm or sandstorm, volcanic ash and radioactive cloud. Aerodrome conditions - runway ice, local fog, a sudden change to a METAR - are handled by METAR, SPECI, TREND, TAF and aerodrome warnings, not by SIGMET.
X2Bj3Ou7kg4bfAuSfwhg: Hoar frost forms when a COLD airframe meets air that is warmer and moist, so that water vapour deposits directly as ice crystals on the skin. Taking off through a significant ground inversion does exactly that: the aircraft has been cold-soaked in the chilled surface layer and then climbs into the warmer, moister air above. The same happens on a rapid descent from cruise into warm humid air, where the danger is a frosted windscreen at a critical moment.
x6f3MpT9R5oagsBWqDqh: The pampero is a sudden, vigorous surge of cold polar air from the south sweeping across the Argentine pampas, effectively a South American cold front outbreak. It brings a sharp temperature drop, strong squally southerly winds, line squalls and thunderstorms, followed by clear, cold, very good visibility - the southern-hemisphere counterpart of a North American norther.
XfzYTKb6pUYaSRxJkcD3: An inversion is very stable and prevents vertical exchange between the air beneath it and the air above. Moisture, smoke, dust and industrial pollution released at the surface therefore accumulate in the shallow layer below the lid instead of being dispersed upward, and visibility degrades to moderate or poor - typically as haze or mist. The effect is usually worst at night and in the early morning, when the inversion is strongest.
XjJKFJktUXEBffYTpeGV: At 1500 UTC the BECMG 1315 group has completed, so the wind is 25025G45KT; the TEMPO 1720 with its 4000 m and heavy showers has not yet begun; and the main body's 9999 and SCT012 BKN030 still apply. The ceiling is the lowest BROKEN or overcast layer, so the main cloudbase is 3000 ft, not the scattered 1200 ft. The T1815Z group gives 18 C at 1500 UTC. That makes option A correct on every count.
xkAQ0XCfq5m90oCq3Ohx: Around 99% of atmospheric water vapour is in the troposphere, and most of that in its lowest few kilometres. The source is evaporation from the surface, and the temperature falls rapidly with height so the air's capacity to hold vapour drops away sharply. The tropopause then acts as a lid on vertical moisture transport, which is why the stratosphere is extremely dry and cloud-free.
xliWtvnnRj7Gl9bWpnMn: Evaporation requires energy to break the molecular bonds of liquid water, and that latent heat is taken FROM the surroundings - which is why evaporation cools. The vapour added also raises the relative humidity, since the amount present increases while the saturation capacity (fixed by temperature) does not. The heat is given back later, when the vapour condenses, and that release is what powers thunderstorms.
XLl6EljrdG3YCuf3IHlh: A stationary winter high over land gives light winds, clear skies and strong subsidence. The long nights allow intense radiational cooling of a damp surface, and the subsidence inversion caps the layer so the moisture cannot disperse upward - so fog and low stratus form readily and, with little insolation to burn them off, can persist for days. This is the classic 'anticyclonic gloom' of a European winter.
Xm6MMIbJdtfjq4TzrNW3: Supercooling requires only a temperature below 0 C and the absence of a freezing nucleus, so it can occur in any liquid water suspended or falling in the atmosphere: cloud droplets, fog droplets (freezing fog, FZFG) and precipitation (freezing rain and freezing drizzle, FZRA and FZDZ). All three are icing hazards - freezing rain being the most severe of all.
XMxmG63luF2sfmXKe1J8: Compare the sounding with ISA at each level. ISA at 10,000 ft is -4.8 C against an observed -2 C, and the whole column runs 3-12 C warmer than standard. Warm air is less dense and expands, so the pressure surfaces sit HIGHER than standard and the aircraft is physically above its indicated altitude. Checking the other options: the freezing level is near 9000 ft (interpolating between +2 at 8000 and -2 at 10,000), and 16,000-18,000 ft loses only 1 C in 2000 ft, which is very stable, not unstable.
xNja3bOBOqBT8VZjQw1W: The steepest wind shear around a polar front jet is on the polar (cold) side, because the jet's speed falls away much more sharply toward the cold air than toward the warm air. In the northern hemisphere the cold air is to the LEFT looking downstream, so that is where CAT is most probable - and slightly below the core rather than in it. The standard escape is to climb or descend, and to move toward the warm side.
xOfOw6j1W7uodorHmH4e: A frontal depression forms on the polar front and is steered by the flow in its own warm sector, which runs broadly west to east along the front. So the centre travels ALONG the front, eastward, with the low pressure on its left in the northern hemisphere - which is why Atlantic depressions track from west to east across Europe rather than moving across the frontal zone.
xQ7T9ofmRa5kPIaPUIWu: With calm and clear synoptic conditions the diurnal land-sea circulation dominates. By day the land heats faster than the water, forming a shallow thermal low over the land, and the wind blows from the water inland - the sea breeze. At night the land cools faster, the gradient reverses, and the weaker land breeze blows from the land out over the water.
xrRPpDWGCAAP8o9W7VhT: Subsidence is slow, widespread DOWNWARD motion of air, the defining feature of a large anticyclone. The descending air is compressed and warms adiabatically, so its relative humidity falls, cloud dissolves and a subsidence inversion forms, trapping haze beneath it. Convection is localised upward motion, convergence is inflow, and advection is horizontal transport.
XS5gXJNe0fQncGpy7yjM: A cold pool is a mass of cold air aloft. In summer over land the surface beneath it is strongly heated, so the temperature difference between bottom and top of the column becomes very large - a steep lapse rate and marked instability. The result is vigorous convection with heavy showers, hail and thunderstorms, often more severe than a front would produce, and with little or no signature on the surface chart to warn of it.
xsMnW0exX91GaPoRURBf: Ground temperature continues to fall all night and reaches its minimum around or just after sunrise, because the surface only stops losing more heat than it gains once the sun is properly up. That is when the air is most likely to be cooled to its dewpoint, so radiation fog typically forms or reaches its greatest density shortly after sunrise - and often thickens briefly as the first heating stirs moist air upward before finally burning off.
XTD1w7rjMxHyqjl4NtCa: Tropopause height follows the depth and warmth of the troposphere beneath it, so it is lowest over the cold poles - about 8 km - and highest over the warm equator, at 16-18 km, with about 11 km in mid-latitudes. It is also higher in summer than in winter at a given latitude, which rules out the seasonal option offered.
XV7hCl5mr9KajkvIKgdU: Hill or orographic fog is simply cloud that forms when moist air is forced up a slope and cools to its dewpoint, and to those on the hill it appears as fog. It needs high humidity, a wind driving the air against the high ground, and STABILITY, so that the air spreads as a layer against the slope rather than breaking into convective cloud. Instability would give cumulus, and clear calm conditions with low humidity give no cloud at all.
Y37JTxtGwHRQAw6xpkXB: PROB followed by 30 or 40 gives the percentage probability of the conditions in the associated group occurring. Only 30 and 40 are used: a probability below 30% is not considered significant enough to include, and 50% or more would be forecast outright with BECMG or TEMPO instead. PROB30 TEMPO combines the two - a 30% chance of temporary conditions.
y6WP87hlyZSvKRowfRbD: Pressure at a level is the weight of the air above it, so the pressure change over a given height interval depends on the density of the air in that interval. Air becomes less dense with height, so the same 100 m of climb removes progressively less weight: the pressure decrease per 100 m is SMALLER at high levels. In feet-per-hectopascal terms, about 27 ft per hPa near sea level rises to about 50 ft per hPa at 18,000 ft.
y7Yw9Wx3WgBPdSw2eolt: A trend forecast is a short landing forecast appended to a METAR or SPECI, valid for the two hours following the observation and written with BECMG, TEMPO or NOSIG. It covers only wind, visibility, weather and cloud. The 9-hour aerodrome forecast is a TAF, and a METAR by itself is a report, not a forecast.
Y9oOTuztVez3WcuVYd0v: The cumulus, or building, stage is defined by updraughts throughout the cell, drawing in warm moist air while the cloud grows vertically and all precipitation is still held aloft. Downdraughts appear only when precipitation begins to fall, which marks the start of the mature stage; by the dissipating stage downdraughts dominate throughout and the cell decays.
yAgajFIcIMLc75YgfIQU: The 300 hPa surface is at about FL300, so -48 C applies there. Below the tropopause the temperature falls at roughly 2 C per 1000 ft, so climbing 3000 ft to the tropopause at FL330 gives -48 - 6 = -54 C. ABOVE the tropopause the temperature stops falling and becomes isothermal, so FL350 is still about -54 C. Note that -56.5 C is the ISA tropopause value and does not apply when the actual tropopause is at a different level.
yaRjAX8EFCo7qJbzVaez: A warm front normally gives stratiform cloud because the overrunning warm air is stable. Embedded thunderstorms occur only when the WARM air - the air actually being lifted up the frontal surface - is convectively unstable, so that once the gentle frontal ascent has saturated it, it keeps accelerating upward under its own buoyancy. The stability of the cold air beneath is irrelevant, since it is not the air being lifted.
