Yc7KHSO6d6WTJGCr6DUq: Large supercooled drops carry a lot of latent heat, so only part of a drop solidifies on contact; the remainder runs back over the surface and freezes progressively, building a dense, transparent, tenacious layer well aft of the leading edge - clear ice, the most dangerous form. Small drops freeze essentially instantly, trapping air and giving opaque, brittle RIME, and hoar frost is a deposit from water vapour.
YEGrvrNZyBdWRKmlA4es: Vertical wind shear is quoted in knots per 100 ft, since it expresses the change in the horizontal wind over a vertical interval. The usual severity bands are light below 4 kt/100 ft, moderate 5-8, strong 9-12 and severe above 12. Values around and above the strong band on final approach are what make a go-around the correct decision.
YEHJu9PtL8O4Erq8K6py: Simple interpolation between two charts 200 hPa apart is unreliable because the wind does not vary linearly with height - a jet core between the two levels would be missed entirely, and FL250 lies squarely in the band where polar front jets are found. So interpolate, but cross-check against the maximum wind and jet core data on the significant weather chart before using the figure.
YG5ks1a0ijPmgxxp8N8v: A cold front is driven by dense cold air actively undercutting lighter warm air, so it moves fastest - typically 20-30 kt, often overtaking the warm front ahead of it and forming an occlusion. A warm front is slower, around 15-20 kt, because the warm air can only ride gently up over the cold air. An occlusion, having lost the warm sector that drove it, is slower still and decays.
yJMwTy8pOiVeLOICn1BH: Crossing at RIGHT ANGLES means the wind must be a crosswind - a headwind or tailwind is geometrically impossible. Below the core, the cold air lies on the polar side, so a FALLING outside air temperature means you are tracking northward. The jet blows from west to east, so on a northerly heading it arrives on the aircraft's left. (Reverse the temperature trend and the wind comes from the right.)
YoFDP0NXRNF5Khtf1Jim: Drizzle (DZ) is made of very small droplets, under 0.5 mm, with almost no fall speed, so it can only reach the ground from a cloud with a very low base, no significant updraught to hold the drops up, and plenty of small droplets - which describes stratus, and stratocumulus. Cumulus and cumulonimbus give showers, and cirrocumulus is high ice cloud that produces nothing at all.
YogDYnMnBEAJwJV4Nyk3: Work forward through the groups to 1200 UTC. The BECMG 1012 change is complete by 1200, so its conditions - 23005KT, 2500 m, BKN005 - are what prevail. The earlier BECMG 0810 with 0800 m has been superseded, and the TEMPO 1316 with 6000 m does not begin until 1300. So expect 2.5 km visibility, a 500 ft cloudbase and 5 kt of wind.
ytxvNiyOQ3qn7xAsRlSp: Warm sector air over Central Europe is tropical maritime: warm, very moist and stable after its long sea track. In winter the land beneath is COLDER than the air, which cools it further from below and reinforces the stability, so the moisture is trapped in a shallow layer as extensive stratus with drizzle and poor visibility. Only in summer does surface heating break that stratus up into fair weather cumulus.
YufiLPykUsAOHj2jk37R: Friction backs the surface wind relative to the gradient wind in the northern hemisphere and reduces its speed. Over the SEA, where friction is light, the rule of thumb is to back about 10 degrees and reduce the speed to roughly 70-80%: 060 backs to about 050 or 045, and 15 kt becomes about 12 kt. Over land the effect roughly doubles - back 30 degrees and halve the speed.
yXOcm7Eh7klIhszAM534: Runway contamination is reported in the runway state group appended to the METAR, coded DRDR ER CR eReR BRBR - runway designator, deposit type, extent of contamination, depth, and either the friction coefficient or a braking action code. It is a report of current aerodrome conditions, which is why it belongs to the METAR rather than to a forecast (TAF) or an en-route warning (SIGMET).
YYeJvCBgVEKGo75Cnwjz: Freezing rain requires a specific vertical structure: a layer of above-zero air aloft in which precipitation is liquid, sitting over a layer below 0 C. The rain falls out of the warm layer, becomes supercooled in the cold layer without freezing, and then freezes instantly on impact. That structure occurs where warm air overrides cold air - classically ahead of a winter warm front - and it produces the most severe icing conditions there are.
Yz8jcMkqJXGer4wspiRl: The significant weather chart is the flight-planning chart for en-route hazards and depicts areas of moderate or severe CAT as scalloped boxes with a number keying them to a table of levels and intensity, alongside jet cores, tropopause heights, CB areas, icing and fronts. Constant-pressure charts show wind and temperature at a single level and do not identify turbulence areas as such.
Z17DgKuvJjIV6OGI5l94: Freezing fog (FZFG) is made of SUPERCOOLED water droplets - still liquid despite being below 0 C - which freeze on contact with any surface, so it deposits rime on the airframe and glazes the runway. That is exactly what makes it hazardous. Fog composed of particles that have already frozen is ice fog, a different phenomenon of very cold climates, which presents no icing risk.
Z4US1gmBAH8jEgmzZXZk: The QNH is identical at both ends, so there is no pressure change to explain the drift. A flight level follows a constant-pressure surface, and that surface sits HIGHER over warm air, because warm air is less dense and expands. A true altitude that falls steadily along the route therefore means the air is getting progressively colder - i.e. Marseille was the warmer end. Nothing is wrong with the altimeter.
Z5M0HOgj2hQaFG7nKQu2: QNH is QFE plus the pressure equivalent of the aerodrome elevation, at about 1 hPa per 27 ft (or 8 m), so the elevation is the only additional information needed. Temperature does not enter, because both QFE and QNH are defined on the ISA relationship. It is QFF that uses the ACTUAL temperature, which is why QFF and QNH differ whenever the air is not standard.
z60iGqtgOmU7vmK6VcL9: The Harmattan is the dry north-easterly trade wind that blows off the Sahara across West and North-West Africa in the northern winter, when the ITCZ has retreated south. It carries fine dust and sand, often reducing visibility to a few kilometres or less over a huge area, and it is markedly dry - the opposite of the moist south-west monsoon that replaces it in summer.
ZedsSGgGB9YU5WP3bQJ9: The layer cools 2 C in 1000 m, an environmental lapse rate of only 0.2 C per 100 m. That is far less than the saturated adiabatic rate, let alone the dry adiabatic rate of 1 C per 100 m, so a parcel displaced upward - saturated or not - immediately becomes colder and denser than its surroundings and sinks back. The layer is absolutely stable, which is consistent with the absence of cloud.
zeiLXrN6gyi4qhqv49an: At 2400 UTC the BECMG 1821 change is long complete, giving 2000 m as the prevailing forecast. The PROB30 BECMG 2124 change to 0500 m in fog is also complete by 2400 - but only with a 30% probability. So the forecast at 2400 is not a single figure: the visibility is expected to be 2000 m, with a 30% chance of being as low as 500 m, i.e. somewhere between 500 m and 2000 m. A PROB group qualifies the forecast, it does not replace it.
ZeQOvw0uXZfzQyvQJY26: Cloud, fog and dew are all simply liquid water that has come out of the vapour phase, so the one thing that must happen in every case is CONDENSATION. Water vapour being present is not enough - it must be brought to saturation and then condensed. A relative humidity of 98% or a small temperature-dewpoint spread makes condensation likely but does not guarantee it; only condensation itself always produces the result.
zF26LWRQEkdDzstmRP64: Warming unsaturated air raises its saturation capacity steeply while the vapour actually present is unchanged, so the relative humidity falls. The dewpoint, however, depends only on how much vapour is present - it is the temperature to which THIS air would have to be cooled to saturate - so as long as no moisture is added or removed, the dewpoint stays the same. That is why the temperature-dewpoint spread widens as the day warms.
ZGmy3IahZPckZfDIGkbB: The turbulence here is jet stream CAT, and a jet is only a few thousand feet deep, so the quickest escape is vertical, moving away from the core. With the core forecast at FL310 and the aircraft at FL270, descending increases the separation, while climbing would take it toward the strongest shear. Moving toward the warm (equatorward) side also helps, since the sharpest shear is on the cold side.
ziqUfmG6kWZOAi0wkNmK: Heavy freezing rain accretes clear ice faster than any de-icing system can shed it, and it forms well aft of the protected leading edges. With no de-icing capability and no landing option, staying in it or continuing is not survivable for long. Descending only takes you into colder air nearer the surface, and the warm layer is above - but climbing through the supercooled layer to reach it means prolonging the exposure. The correct action is to turn back out of the affected area immediately, while control authority remains.
zJF72VUdHqZ5sUvUC8TM: The vertical distance between two pressure levels depends on the mean temperature of the layer: warm air is less dense, so a given pressure interval spans a greater height. Use the 4 ft per 1000 ft per degree rule on the nominal 6000 ft thickness: 4 x 10 x 6 = 240 ft, giving 6000 + 240 = 6240 ft. This thickness-temperature relationship is exactly why contour heights on upper charts are higher over warm air.
ZJsvIJYB7LeEOTSPgGIb: The standard upper-air charts sit at roughly 850 hPa near FL50, 700 hPa near FL100, 500 hPa near FL180, 300 hPa near FL300 and 200 hPa near FL390. FL290 is therefore closest to the 300 hPa chart, which is also the standard chart for locating the polar front jet.
ZlKLenH5yV2GyGY7rbr7: The Indian monsoon is a seasonal reversal driven by the differential heating of the Asian landmass. In July the heated continent generates a deep thermal low, drawing the moist SOUTH-WEST monsoon in off the Arabian Sea and giving the west coast its torrential rains. In January the continent is cold, a high builds over Siberia, and the dry NORTH-EAST monsoon blows offshore.
znRVxFLyyqZFvXJA4ha4: QFE is the pressure at aerodrome level and QNH is that same pressure reduced to sea level, so the two differ by exactly the pressure equivalent of the aerodrome elevation. When the elevation is zero the aerodrome IS at sea level, there is nothing to reduce through, and QFE, QNH and QFF are all identical. Temperature is irrelevant to this - it affects QFF, not the QNH-QFE relationship.
zPi7Ck6mfMFZGQyPIL54: An occlusion is classified by comparing the two COLD air masses either side of it. In a cold occlusion the air arriving behind the cold front is colder than the air that was ahead of the warm front, so it undercuts both and ends up at the surface behind the occlusion, with the less cold air ahead. The warm sector air, having been lifted off the ground by the cold front catching the warm front, sits aloft above them both.
ZsAmpBKkbHKjmVNNSjE3: The geostrophic wind is the speed at which the Coriolis force balances a given pressure gradient force, and Coriolis is proportional to the sine of the latitude. Nearer the equator Coriolis is weaker, so a HIGHER wind speed is needed to achieve the balance. For the same isobar spacing the geostrophic wind is therefore greater at 30 N than at 60 N - which is why isobar spacing alone cannot be used to estimate wind speed without knowing the latitude.
ZSjPw3Jr8xHQUfSTBhJf: Hurricanes form over the warm tropical Atlantic and Caribbean and are steered westward, then recurve north and north-east around the western edge of the Azores-Bermuda high. That track carries them onto the south-eastern seaboard - Florida, the Gulf coast and the Carolinas. The west coast faces the cold California current, which keeps sea temperatures well below the 26.5 C needed, and the northern coasts are far too cold.
ZuWT5Amg0R6vniqILz3o: Cumulonimbus concentrates every serious hazard in one cloud: severe turbulence, hail, lightning, severe icing, heavy precipitation, microbursts and gust fronts, with tops that can exceed FL450. Its hazards also extend outside the visible cloud - hail thrown from the anvil and gust fronts 15-20 NM ahead - which is why the standard rule is to avoid a CB by at least 10 NM rather than to fly between cells.
ZxziU31mpnzviCQQ7BWZ: An occlusion is cold when the air behind the cold front is colder than the air ahead of the warm front. Over Europe that comparison is decided by the continent: in SUMMER the land ahead of the system is warm, so the maritime air arriving behind is the colder of the two and cold occlusions predominate. In winter the continental air ahead is very cold and the milder maritime air behind rides over it, giving warm occlusions instead.
ZZ8EMRatx9UVBOSr0Mao: ISA temperature falls at 1.98 C per 1000 ft from 15 C at sea level, so at 10,000 ft it is 15 - 19.8 = -4.8 C, taken as about -5 C. The handy mental shortcut is 2 C per 1000 ft, giving 15 - 20 = -5 C directly. This is the reference against which any ISA deviation is measured.
03sJPEOPCg3InGqK6dCj: CS-25.107 sets two floors on VR: it may not be less than V1, and not less than 105% of VMCA. The V1 floor prevents rotation before the decision speed, and the VMCA margin guarantees directional control is available if an engine fails at rotation. The 1.05 multiplier attaches to VMCA, not to V1 - reading it the other way round is the usual trap.
06aWHm4Bg6leFig6VCFZ: A slat opens a slot ahead of the wing that ducts high-energy air from beneath onto the upper surface, re-energising the boundary layer and delaying separation to a much higher angle of attack - typically an extra 5-10 degrees of stalling angle. CLmax therefore rises without changing the basic aerofoil. Note that slats raise the critical (stalling) angle, whereas trailing-edge flaps normally lower it.
0cRQjvSNAZO0EDJdqGES: A fixed-pitch propeller is optimised for exactly one combination of airspeed and rpm and its efficiency falls away rapidly either side of that point. A constant-speed unit varies blade angle to hold the chosen rpm, so the blades stay near their optimum angle of attack across the whole speed range - climb, cruise and descent - giving near-maximum efficiency throughout. Its peak efficiency is no higher than a fixed-pitch prop's; it simply holds it over a far wider range.
0fXfIPuyEdIFWxPbodSC: Wing loading is weight (a force, in newtons) divided by wing area, so N/m2. Dynamic pressure q = 1/2 rho V2 is a pressure, and a pascal is by definition one newton per square metre, so it is also N/m2. Both quantities share the same units, which is why wing loading and dynamic pressure can be compared directly in the lift equation.
0QW52e6aikKs75YMlzZ7: In a steep wind gradient the headwind decreases rapidly as the aircraft descends. The aircraft's inertia means that lost headwind comes straight off the airspeed, so IAS decays on final. Unless speed is deliberately controlled, the result is a low, slow approach that undershoots the aiming point - or, if the loss is severe enough, a stall. The standard defence is to add a margin to the approach speed when a marked gradient is reported.
1ccJZBowvlMlqGl2wjCa: Power is the rate of doing work: work is force times distance (newton-metres, or joules), so power is newton-metres per second - equivalently the watt or joule per second. N/m is a force gradient, Pa/m2 is meaningless here, and kg m/s2 is the newton, a force rather than a rate of work.
1GaKujnydz225ctTldFO: At a normal cruising angle of attack an efficient aerofoil generates far more lift than drag - lift-to-drag ratios of 15 to 20 are typical for a transport aeroplane. Since both forces share the same 1/2 rho V2 S term, the ratio of the coefficients equals the ratio of the forces, so CL is much greater than CD. Only near the stall, where CD climbs steeply, do the two approach each other.
1glRrRo3M1aruDyX7rLT: CS-25.113 requires the certified take-off distance to be the GREATER of the one-engine-inoperative distance and 115% of the all-engines-operating distance. Here that is the greater of 1720 m and 1.15 x 1547 = 1779 m, so 1779 m is used. The 15% factor exists because an all-engines take-off is flown routinely, so it needs its own safety margin rather than being covered by the engine-out case.
1Ik07QBo9MQkMAXjnQMZ: Beyond Mcrit a shock wave forms on the upper surface, and the separated flow behind it produces the airframe shaking known as Mach buffet. The shock also moves the centre of pressure aft and reduces the downwash reaching the tailplane, and both effects generate a nose-down pitching moment - Mach tuck. The insidious part is that the nose-down pitch increases the Mach number further, so the tendency is self-reinforcing.
1J9hNYz7W2O1GqdZePG8: A tyre's speed limit is a structural limit on how fast the carcass can rotate, so it is governed by how fast the wheel is actually moving over the ground - the GROUNDSPEED. Airspeed of any flavour is irrelevant to the tyre. This is why a strong tailwind or a hot-and-high aerodrome, both of which raise the groundspeed for a given IAS, can make tyre speed the limiting factor for take-off.
1mu7vPUeztlmtehDTfx6: Take each quantity in turn. Load factor n = 1/cos(bank), so it depends only on bank angle - both are at 20 degrees, so the load factors are identical and option A fails. Turn radius = V2/(g tan bank), so the slower aircraft A turns in a tighter circle, not a larger one. Rate of turn = g tan(bank)/V, so the slower aircraft A turns FASTER - that is the correct statement. And with the same lift required at a lower speed, A must fly at the higher CL, not the lower.
1puaWhvVjeRZmZhDfxH5: Selecting fine (decreased) pitch with the engine at idle makes the propeller windmill faster and presents a larger effective disc to the airflow, so it generates considerably more drag. Total drag rises while lift is unchanged at constant IAS, so L/D falls and the glide angle steepens - the rate of descent increases. This is why the drill for a forced landing is to select COARSE pitch, minimising windmilling drag and extending the glide.
1RhomxOIwI5DbrmaF6TE: The ground run shortens if the aircraft is lighter (less inertia and a lower lift-off speed), if the air is denser (more thrust and more lift at a given TAS), and if flap is increased (a higher CL means lift-off at a lower speed). All three of those act in the same direction here. High pressure altitude, high temperature and high mass all lengthen the run.
1tlKvPaC5LI5ZHHStQMC: The stall recovery is: unstall the wing first by moving the stick centrally forward to reduce the angle of attack, keeping the ailerons NEUTRAL because aileron input at high alpha can provoke a wing drop or spin; apply full power to minimise height loss; and level the wings with RUDDER, since rudder remains effective when the ailerons are not. Waiting passively for a nose-down tendency, or leaving the power at idle, both cost far more height than necessary.
1TTc3LpAQpg4bXOG5rfK: Drag = CD x 1/2 rho V2 x S. With the shape unchanged, CD is unchanged, and the frontal area S appears to the FIRST power - so tripling the area triples the drag. The square-law in the drag equation applies to SPEED, not to area; confusing the two is what produces the factor-of-9 answer.
26Q5H8BiXuva2IRynrKW: Drift down is the procedure following an engine failure at cruise level, where the aeroplane can no longer hold altitude and descends at the speed for best gradient until it reaches the level-off altitude. The requirement it addresses is TERRAIN: the net flight path during that descent must clear obstacles by the prescribed vertical margin, which is what determines whether an escape route is needed along the airway.
2eTL9oAO2Tf3JwxGwZFx: VLO is the landing gear OPERATING speed - the maximum speed at which the gear may be moved, extended or retracted. It is distinct from VLE, the landing gear EXTENDED speed, the maximum at which the aircraft may be flown with the gear already down and locked. VLO is normally the lower of the two, because the doors and moving gear are more vulnerable in transit.
2Fbw95wE43vM7b5ZPAv8: At the speed for minimum glide angle the aircraft is exactly at (CL/CD)max. Reducing mass while holding the SAME speed reduces the lift required, so CL falls and the aircraft is no longer at the best-ratio point: CL/CD decreases. Since tan(glide angle) = CD/CL, the glide angle increases, and with speed unchanged and the path steeper, the rate of descent increases too. The correct response to lower mass is to fly SLOWER, back to the new best-glide speed.
2IdV7hnxAJiVqQtIoGJH: A turbulent boundary layer mixes fast-moving air from the free stream down toward the surface, so it carries more kinetic energy close to the skin. That extra energy lets it fight an adverse pressure gradient for longer, so it separates LATER than a laminar layer, not sooner. The price is that it is thicker and gives higher skin friction drag - the trade that vortex generators deliberately accept.
2OUNbaxaizTd3oQVKVXB: In subsonic flow through a converging tube the mass flow must be conserved, so the air speeds up as the area reduces. Bernoulli's theorem says total pressure is constant, so the rise in dynamic pressure must be paid for by a fall in STATIC pressure. This is exactly the mechanism by which the accelerated flow over a wing's upper surface produces its suction. Note that above M1.0 the relationship reverses.
2YsZ8DS0KVI5EKUbt90C: Turn radius = V2 / (g tan(bank)), which contains no mass term at all - so two aircraft at the same TAS and the same bank angle fly identical radii regardless of weight. The same is true of rate of turn. What the heavier aircraft needs is more LIFT to generate the same load factor, hence a higher CL or a higher speed to sustain the turn, but the geometry of the turn itself is unchanged.
32plJ4joxyD12tB5LbYy: Reduced (assumed-temperature or derated) thrust is only permissible when there is a genuine performance margin to give away - that is, when the actual take-off mass is BELOW the performance-limited mass, of which the field-length limit is the relevant one here. Reducing thrust when the aircraft is already at or above a limiting mass would erase the certified margins. Reduced thrust is also prohibited on contaminated runways and with anti-skid inoperative.
36gOqlCJa1MtOBDOlPcE: Descending at a constant Mach number, the temperature rises so the local speed of sound increases and TAS increases with it; density also increases rapidly, so IAS climbs steeply. VMO is an indicated-airspeed limit, so it is the limit that gets exceeded first. This is why the descent profile changes from a constant Mach to a constant IAS at the crossover altitude - and the aural warning to expect is the overspeed clacker.
3A0mbyfrrGgYsrqjWB0C: A servo tab is the tab used for manual reversion: the pilot's controls move only the tab, and the aerodynamic force the tab generates then flies the main surface into position. Because the pilot never has to move the large surface directly, the stick forces stay manageable with the hydraulics off. The trade is reduced effectiveness at low airspeed, where the tab has little dynamic pressure to work with.
3afu2PTisOU2oFo0pK5m: Bernoulli's theorem states that static pressure plus dynamic pressure equals a constant total pressure along a streamline. If one falls the other must rise, so a decrease in static pressure means an increase in dynamic pressure. At a stagnation point the velocity is zero, so the DYNAMIC pressure there is zero and the static pressure equals the total - the reverse of what two of the distractors claim.
3jWbzUvC5CIbEYuMg0IX: Sweeping the wing means only the component of the airflow perpendicular to the quarter-chord line does the aerodynamic work, so the effective velocity over the aerofoil section is reduced by the cosine of the sweep angle. The flow therefore reaches sonic speed at a higher free-stream Mach number: Mcrit is raised. Vortex generators delay shock-induced SEPARATION but do not change the Mach number at which the shock first appears; dihedral affects lateral stability only.
3maCqt7C4RSxWbfJy8qn: Buffet margin is the gap between the low-speed and high-speed buffet boundaries at a given weight and altitude, and it widens as altitude decreases. Descending at a constant IAS reduces the Mach number and moves the aircraft away from both boundaries, so the margin increases. A step CLIMB does the opposite - it takes the aircraft higher and narrows the margin, which is precisely why step climbs are delayed until fuel burn has reduced weight enough.
3O7uL0Lj5MZcvMaRsQYl: Endurance is time aloft, so for a piston engine - whose fuel flow is proportional to POWER - maximum endurance comes at the speed for minimum power required. That is slower than the minimum-drag speed (which gives maximum range) and it coincides closely with the speed for best rate of climb, since best ROC is where excess power is greatest. Note the contrast with a jet, where fuel flow follows thrust, so maximum endurance is at minimum DRAG.
3oPFNXY2r8CjeW22s1we: At constant IAS the dynamic pressure is fixed, so a lighter aeroplane needs a smaller CL and therefore flies at a lower angle of attack. A lower angle of attack means less acceleration of the flow over the upper surface, so the local flow reaches M1.0 only at a higher free-stream Mach number - Mcrit increases. This is why Mcrit is quoted against angle of attack, and why it falls as weight, load factor or altitude increase.
3pihDhKKny6mjLW7NHCy: Higher pressure altitude means lower air density, which cuts thrust, reduces the lift generated at a given TAS and lengthens the take-off run, while also degrading the climb gradient. Every one of those effects works against the aeroplane, so the allowable take-off mass must be reduced to restore the certified margins. The reduction is continuous, not stepped - there is no altitude below which it can be ignored.
3rKNHRQMPxaKYxn60WFX: Long range cruise is flown at approximately a constant lift coefficient for a given weight, which means approximately a constant IAS. As altitude decreases at constant IAS the TAS falls, and at the same time the warmer air raises the local speed of sound - both effects reduce the Mach number. So below the optimum altitude the LRC Mach number decreases continuously as the aeroplane descends.
3SrhsTQA6ucguHMpWkgz: Vortex generators are small vanes that trip the boundary layer into a turbulent state, mixing high-energy free-stream air down toward the skin. That extra energy lets the layer survive the steep adverse pressure gradient behind a shock wave, so shock-induced separation - and the buffet and control problems that come with it - is delayed to a higher Mach number. They do not change stalling speed by altering tangential velocity, and they add a little parasite drag rather than exploiting it.
3yfgZfNKOnIZlqyJCwN8: Excess thrust is unbalanced force, and by Newton's second law an unbalanced force produces acceleration. If the pilot holds altitude, that excess goes into accelerating the aeroplane; if instead the speed is held, the excess is converted into potential energy and the aeroplane climbs. Which of the two happens is entirely a matter of what the pilot chooses to hold constant.
3Zc7xGpIcDuypbvmq19K: Increasing the load factor increases the lift required and therefore the angle of attack, so the aeroplane stalls at a higher speed than its 1g value - an accelerated stall. Decelerating at the same time closes the gap from the other side. At high cruise altitude the low-speed and high-speed buffet boundaries are already close together, so quite a modest g increase can take a buffet-free aeroplane straight into the low-speed boundary.
3ZIYsxPTerf7EKTd3PPf: In identical flying conditions the thrust required is unchanged, so the fuel flow - and hence the fuel burnt per nautical mile - scales directly with specific fuel consumption. New fuel mileage = 14 x (0.035 / 0.06) = 8.17 kg/NM. The 42% cut in SFC produces exactly the same 42% cut in fuel per mile, which is why SFC improvements dominate the economics of engine development.
41f93bdeKBdQWy5nBAZ0: Climbing at a constant Mach number, the falling density outweighs the falling speed of sound, so the dynamic pressure decreases and the IAS decays steadily. To keep generating the same lift with less dynamic pressure the aeroplane must fly at a higher CL - a higher angle of attack. That climbing CL is precisely why the buffet margin narrows with altitude and why the aeroplane eventually reaches its aerodynamic ceiling.
41tn3hxaLhNSCHnnVwHS: From Newton's second law, force = mass x acceleration, so the SI unit of force is the kilogram-metre per second squared, given the name newton. For comparison: the pascal is N/m2 (pressure), the joule is N m (work or energy), and the watt is J/s (power). Recognising the base-unit combination is the quickest way to identify which quantity is being described.
44wDkCKg50OqCLRRWwuf: The neutral point is the CG position at which the aeroplane has zero longitudinal static stability. For positive stability the CG must lie AHEAD of it, and the distance between them is the static margin. Certification requires a minimum static margin, which is what sets the aft CG limit; loading behind the neutral point would make the aeroplane divergently unstable in pitch.
495LWSMeRgXfncq6vzKa: Induced drag is the penalty for the tip vortices produced by spanwise flow around the wing tip. A high aspect ratio wing is long and narrow, so the tips are a much smaller proportion of the span and their influence over the wing as a whole is reduced, cutting downwash and induced drag - CDi is inversely proportional to aspect ratio. This is why gliders and long-range aircraft use slender wings.
4D6W3Qh7ibUd15oP1fNv: With a servo tab system the pilot's controls move only the tab, and the tab then flies the elevator. If the ELEVATOR itself jams, the tab still responds to the stick - but now it is acting as a tiny control surface in its own right, and its aerodynamic force acts in the OPPOSITE sense to the elevator deflection it would normally command. The result is pitch control that is much weaker and reversed in direction, a genuine trap for the unwary.
4dnSh49BP7A8iHc15i6S: Both factors reduce air density. High temperature expands the air directly, and water vapour is less dense than dry air, so humid air is lighter still - and in a piston engine the vapour also displaces oxygen in the charge, cutting power further. Lower density means less thrust, less lift at a given TAS, a longer ground run and a shallower climb gradient. Cold, dry air is the best combination for performance.
4eaMjNe0U8aMYRmE8VWh: An auto-slat system extends the slats automatically once the angle of attack exceeds a preset value, restoring the stall margin at a moment when the crew may be fully occupied - typically during a windshear escape or an aggressive manoeuvre with the flaps at a take-off setting. It is a protection device driven by AoA, not by the ground/flight logic and not part of the roll control system.
4KwENJr48mWJxvTOoXIw: The trimmable stabiliser setting for take-off is scheduled against CG, and an aft CG calls for a setting toward the nose-DOWN end of the permitted band - precisely because an aft CG already needs less nose-up trim to rotate. So an aft CG paired with the maximum permissible nose-down THS position is the correctly scheduled combination, and rotation using the normal technique will be normal. A mismatch between the two is what produces under- or over-rotation.
4PmFXfHJjvWoDfTZFrVH: Total drag is the sum of induced drag, which varies as 1/V2 and dominates at low speed, and parasite drag, which varies as V2 and dominates at high speed. Adding the two gives the classic U-shaped curve: drag falls as speed rises from the stall, reaches a minimum where the two components are equal (VMD, the best L/D speed), then rises again toward VNE.
4u1advm7xhLR0ko00oeq: A flapper-switch stall warner is a small vane set in a slot on the wing leading edge, positioned just below the stagnation point in normal flight. As the angle of attack increases, the stagnation point migrates DOWN and aft along the lower surface; once it passes below the slot the local flow through it reverses, lifting the flapper and closing the warning circuit. The device is therefore triggered by movement of the STAGNATION point.
4vNtZLcOJBoRAEWTpZGn: If sin(climb angle) varies inversely with mass, then gradient x mass is constant. So mass x 2.6% = 110,000 x 2.8%, giving mass = 110,000 x 2.8 / 2.6 = 118,455 kg. Sense-check the direction: the required gradient is LOWER than the gradient currently achieved, so the aeroplane can afford to be HEAVIER - an answer below 110,000 kg would be the wrong way round.
59ZWC8bdaFbGkzKF3BwH: TAS = Mach number x local speed of sound, and the speed of sound depends only on temperature. In the troposphere the temperature falls steadily with altitude, so the speed of sound falls too, and at a fixed Mach number the TAS must decrease. Above the tropopause the temperature is constant, so a constant-Mach climb there gives constant TAS.
5JPWZQzo3Imn5DumSd69: Propeller efficiency is the ratio of useful power out to power in - thrust horsepower delivered to the airflow divided by the brake horsepower supplied at the shaft. Typical peak values are around 85%. The difference between geometric and effective pitch is propeller SLIP, and the distance actually advanced per revolution is the effective pitch; neither is an efficiency.
5k2cNC11r05xXzlNpYn4: In a level turn the lift must support n times the weight, and since lift varies with the square of speed, the stalling speed rises with the SQUARE ROOT of the load factor: Vs(turn) = Vs x sqrt(n). At 60 degrees of bank n = 2, so the stall speed rises by sqrt(2), about 41%. Flap extension does the opposite - it raises CLmax and therefore lowers the stall speed.
5PsQSPp2BmxfCkFWQo0G: Clearway may be counted toward the take-off distance available only up to a maximum of HALF the take-off run available. With a 3000 m runway, at most 1500 m of the 2000 m clearway may be used, giving a TODA of 3000 + 1500 = 4500 m. Clearway is also counted at one end only, for the direction of take-off - it is not added twice.
5VV74juG1ppI8zT3EPGp: Dihedral is the upward angle of the wing measured between the quarter-chord line and the lateral (pitch) axis, i.e. the spanwise horizontal. Its purpose is lateral static stability: in a sideslip the lower wing meets the relative airflow at a greater effective angle of attack, generates more lift, and rolls the aircraft back toward wings-level. Sweep and high wing position produce a similar effect.
5wc0kBTAMUxcJjqTnH2M: A positively cambered aerofoil carries more of its lift toward the rear of the chord, so even when the net lift is zero the pressure distribution still produces a couple. That couple is nose-down, so Cm at CL = 0 is negative - and because it is essentially independent of angle of attack it is a fixed characteristic of the section. A symmetrical aerofoil has Cm0 = 0, and a reflexed section can achieve a positive value.
5WfvaqKRfBPiLaalLGGD: For a turbojet the dry landing field length required is the demonstrated landing distance divided by 0.6, i.e. plus 67%. For a WET runway a further 15% is applied on top: 1.67 x 1.15 = 1.92, so the required field length is the demonstrated distance plus 92%. Note that this factoring is a dispatch requirement, assessed before departure.
5YasUMVOV9DJYfQWdStx: With the CG aft, the moment arm to the tailplane is short, so a small elevator deflection produces a large pitching moment and the aeroplane responds quickly - manoeuvrability is at its best and trim drag at its least. The price is reduced longitudinal stability and lighter, less informative stick forces, which is why certification sets an aft limit. A forward CG gives the opposite trade: very stable but sluggish and draggy.
5zKSkGUoil800OsEaZyC: Long range cruise deliberately gives up 1% of the maximum specific range in exchange for the HIGHER of the two speeds that deliver 99% of it. That buys typically 3-5% more speed for a 1% fuel penalty, which is almost always worth it once crew time, maintenance and schedule are costed in. Maximum range cruise itself is rarely flown, because near the optimum the specific range curve is very flat.
5ZLsHjtC3ZJJMpr3LYUv: In a steady glide tan(glide angle) = CD/CL, so the shallowest glide - and therefore the greatest distance covered per unit of height lost - occurs at the angle of attack giving (CL/CD)max. Note the contrast with minimum SINK rate, which is a different condition, (CL^3/CD^2)max, flown at a lower speed and used when the aim is to stay airborne longest rather than to go furthest.
63N3f4CeRCtG3jcBlibb: The lateral axis runs spanwise, from wingtip to wingtip, and rotation about it is PITCHING, controlled by the elevator. For completeness: rolling is rotation about the longitudinal axis (nose to tail, controlled by ailerons) and yawing is rotation about the normal or vertical axis (controlled by the rudder).
6Ihh8LXVH0bwLwmzAo7k: Lower atmospheric pressure means lower air density. Less dense air reduces the thrust the engine can produce and reduces the lift generated at any given TAS, so the aeroplane must accelerate to a higher TAS before it will fly - the take-off distance lengthens. The same thrust loss cuts the excess thrust available for climbing, so the initial climb gradient degrades too. Both effects work against the aeroplane.
6IMDoAr9yL17tI6JTQ52: A shock wave is an abrupt compression: the flow decelerates violently and much of its kinetic energy is converted into heat, so the static temperature RISES sharply across the wave. The local speed of sound depends only on temperature (a is proportional to the square root of absolute temperature), so it increases. Static pressure and density also rise, while total pressure falls - the energy lost as wave drag.
6rATg478cDarJwE4vtE3: V2 must give an adequate margin above the stall with an engine failed, and the required margin depends on how much the aeroplane can reduce its power-on stall speed. For two- and three-engined turboprops the floor is 1.2 VS. Turboprops with more than three engines, and jets with provisions to significantly reduce the one-engine-inoperative stall speed, are allowed the lower figure of 1.15 VS. V2 must also be at least 1.1 VMCA.
6tMudOGed3y1Ogja9DT9: Leading-edge ice reduces CLmax and, critically, lowers the angle of attack at which the wing stalls. The highest angle of attack of the whole take-off occurs at the END of rotation, just as the aircraft is unstuck at minimum speed - so that is where the reduced stalling angle bites first and hardest. In the subsequent climb the angle of attack is lower and the margin correspondingly greater.
6upC5GmnhD11kwkXyptb: VY is the speed for the best RATE of climb - the greatest height gain per unit TIME, found where excess POWER is greatest. VX is the speed for the best ANGLE of climb, the greatest height gain per unit DISTANCE, found where excess THRUST is greatest, and is the speed used for obstacle clearance. V2 is the take-off safety speed.
6vvBI46fEfZahoHHZC9Q: Minimum sink rate is flown at (CL^3/CD^2)max and best glide ANGLE at (CL/CD)max, and the minimum-sink condition always occurs at the lower speed of the two - typically around 76% of the best-glide speed. Fly slower to stay airborne longest; fly faster, at best glide, to travel furthest. Both are TAS relationships and the ordering never reverses between aeroplane types.
71nJD5B35WOYBmFq9PXy: V1 is a decision speed, and a decision to continue is only meaningful if the aeroplane can actually be kept straight on the runway after the failure - which requires V1 to be at least VMCG, the minimum control speed on the ground. At the other end, V1 may not exceed VR. Together these bracket V1 between the speed at which control is assured and the speed at which rotation begins.
78bA6tuzNltk3dbPH7d5: Moving the CG aft shortens the moment arm to the tailplane, so a given elevator deflection generates more pitching moment and less stick force is needed to produce a given g - manoeuvre stability, measured as stick force per g, falls. Beyond the aft limit that figure drops below the certified minimum, so the aeroplane becomes dangerously easy to over-stress and gives the pilot almost no force cue that it is happening.
7bDU8Di0upeXR1Td6hSS: This is Newton's second law in its rotational form: an unbalanced moment produces an angular acceleration about that axis, just as an unbalanced force produces a linear acceleration. Steady flight - straight and level, or a steady turn or descent - therefore requires the sum of moments about ALL THREE axes to be zero, which is what trimming achieves.
7BzyGarICnZdLrPIIGHj: With altitude the falling density means a given indicated airspeed corresponds to an ever-higher true airspeed, and in TAS terms both VX and VY increase. In IAS terms they move toward each other - VX rising slightly and VY falling - until they meet at the absolute ceiling, where the only remaining climb speed produces zero rate of climb. The two framings are often confused, so note which the question is using.
7DpvFCxvFoX6U8dSmECC: A constant-speed unit works by sensing rpm and adjusting blade angle to hold the selected value. Medium turbulence produces small, transient changes in the airflow through the disc and hence small rpm excursions, so the governor responds with correspondingly small blade angle changes. The whole point of the system is that the pitch changes are gentle and continuous, never large or abrupt.
7hjxtMjfmyByd3pDdBG8: Slush adds two penalties: displacement drag as the wheels plough through it and spray impingement drag on the airframe, both of which slow the acceleration and lengthen the run. It also degrades braking if the take-off is rejected, which is why contaminated-runway take-off performance is separately certified. Headwind, lower mass and a downhill slope all SHORTEN the take-off distance.
7jsw5K5i1ffoltMW26rU: Newton's second law states that force equals mass times acceleration, F = m a. Rearranged, a = F/m - which is why a heavier aeroplane accelerates more slowly for the same thrust, and why take-off mass has such a direct effect on the ground run. The SI unit of force follows from this: 1 newton is 1 kg m/s2.
7N64lFaDTtvS1ARmL0i3: The best lift-to-drag ratio occurs at a fixed angle of attack and therefore a fixed lift coefficient, whatever the mass. A heavier aeroplane needs more lift at that same CL, and since lift depends on 1/2 rho V2 S CL, the only way to get it is to fly FASTER. So the best-glide speed increases with mass. The glide ANGLE, however, is unchanged - the heavier aeroplane covers the same distance, just more quickly.
7swc4ECxFHxFpztTbXPA: Close to the ground the surface interferes with the formation of the wing tip vortices, so the downwash behind the wing is reduced. Less downwash means a smaller induced angle of attack, which tilts the lift vector less far rearward and cuts induced drag - by as much as 40-50% at very low height. The aeroplane consequently floats, and the reduced downwash over the tailplane also produces a nose-down trim change.
7W8tap5AejMXlUFt3q4Z: Rate of climb is the climb gradient multiplied by the speed along the path. 100 kt is 100 x 6076 / 60 = about 10,130 ft/min, and 3.3% of that is roughly 330 ft/min. A useful rule of thumb follows: gradient in percent times groundspeed in knots, times about 1.013, gives the rate of climb in feet per minute - so roughly 'percent times knots' is close enough for a mental check.
7Wf9wxKLNHTRsgpdRSug: In a right turn the outside of the turn is to the LEFT, so a ball displaced left has swung to the outside - the classic SKID, meaning the rate of turn is too high for the bank angle. There are two coordinated fixes: reduce the rate of turn with less right rudder, or match the bank to the rate by rolling in MORE right bank. Of the options offered, more right bank is the coordinating input.
7wX9NgKn9RzSOemiMP6V: Maximum range for a jet means the most nautical miles per kilogram of fuel, and since fuel flow follows THRUST, that means minimising drag per unit of speed - i.e. minimising D/V, which is maximising V/D. Geometrically, the minimum of D/V is where a straight line from the origin just touches the total drag curve. That tangent point lies at a higher speed than VMD, which is why jet maximum-range speed is faster than minimum-drag speed.
7XFbQGRWQMNkxEdHHYL8: In a steady level turn the lift must support the weight and provide the turning force, so L = W / cos(bank), i.e. the load factor n = 1/cos(bank). At 45 degrees, cos 45 = 0.707, so n = 1.41 - a 41% increase in lift. Useful reference points: 30 degrees gives n = 1.15, 45 degrees n = 1.41, and 60 degrees n = 2.0.
7XorvdEuG6fRZub7qk3M: The same angle of attack means the same lift coefficient, and in level flight the lift must still equal the weight. Since L = CL x 1/2 rho V2 S, holding CL and L constant while density FALLS with altitude requires V - the true airspeed - to increase. The indicated airspeed, which is what the dynamic pressure determines, stays the same: this is the basis of flying by IAS at all altitudes.
81JOPMiudtblE59CBVWk: The centre of pressure moving aft in the transonic region increases the distance between it and the CG, lengthening the restoring moment arm. A larger restoring moment for a given disturbance is by definition greater static longitudinal STABILITY - the aeroplane resists pitch changes more strongly. It also produces the nose-down Mach tuck, since the increased download aft pitches the nose down.
8bzBUMjMBS0nXyxjiDA4: The CS-23 positive manoeuvring limit load factors are 3.8 for the Normal category, 4.4 for Utility, and 6.0 for Aerobatic. The Utility category permits limited aerobatics such as spins and steep turns, so it carries a structure stronger than Normal but lighter than a full aerobatic aeroplane. The 2.5 figure is the large-aeroplane (CS-25) minimum.
8EiTVOvxcTgxmIs8fpta: Less flap means a lower CLmax, so the approach and touchdown speeds are higher and more energy has to be dissipated: the landing distance increases. But less flap also means much less drag, so if a go-around becomes necessary the climb gradient available is significantly better. This is exactly the trade a reduced-flap landing buys - runway length for go-around performance.
8fzOnAhunBmM3ldWuUYw: A plain flap simply hinges the rear portion of the aerofoil downward, which increases the effective CAMBER of the section. More camber raises CLmax and shifts the whole lift curve up and to the left, so the wing generates the same lift at a lower speed. It also lowers the stalling ANGLE of attack and increases drag markedly - unlike a slat, which raises the stalling angle.
8i5klJCVjPE2xJRYN9f6: CS-25.113(b) defines the take-off run for the all-engines case as the horizontal distance from the start of the take-off to a point equidistant between the point at which VLOF is reached and the point at which the aeroplane is 35 ft above the surface - in effect, half the airborne segment is counted. It is not the same as the accelerate-stop distance, nor a distance measured to V2, nor the take-off DISTANCE (which measures the full run to 35 ft).
8L4JQnKBiJCYyViXS8nr: Both climb performance figures depend on excess power or excess thrust, and both shrink as altitude increases: thrust falls with density while drag at a given IAS does not, so the excess available for climbing steadily disappears. The best angle and the best rate therefore both decrease, reaching zero rate of climb at the absolute ceiling.
8ODBVcKJU1edwWO6rU9X: In level flight the lift must equal the weight regardless of speed, so in L = CL x 1/2 rho V2 S the product CL x V2 is fixed. Doubling the indicated airspeed multiplies V2 by four, so CL must fall to a QUARTER of its original value - achieved by lowering the angle of attack. This inverse-square relationship is why the angle of attack falls away so rapidly as an aeroplane accelerates.
8wATAXuXdoCUXh1PSyOm: A stabiliser jammed at the cruise setting leaves the aeroplane trimmed nose-down relative to what a normal flap-down approach needs, so the elevator has to hold a large out-of-trim pull force. Landing faster reduces the elevator deflection required, and selecting less flap reduces the nose-up trim change that has to be countered in the first place. Both measures reduce the residual out-of-trim force to something manageable in the flare.
8xnFoDvLY7JEYFJZAvEO: Drift down is the procedure used when an engine fails at a cruise level above the one-engine-inoperative maximum altitude, so the aeroplane can no longer hold height. It descends at the speed for the best gradient, at maximum continuous thrust on the remaining engine or engines, until it reaches the level-off altitude - and the requirement it must satisfy is obstacle clearance along the net flight path during that descent.
8Z56fYPpauXkJYy7V4sw: VA is defined as the speed at which the aeroplane will stall at exactly the limit manoeuvring load factor - so at or below VA a full elevator deflection produces a stall before it produces structural damage. Where a single fixed value is published rather than a weight-dependent one, it is computed at maximum take-off mass. Note that VA protects only against a single full deflection in ONE direction from 1g, not against rapid reversals.
8ZKxwyJ0soSEJikW4sck: Certified performance data assume a fully serviceable anti-skid system, because braking is used both in the accelerate-stop distance (take-off) and in the landing distance. Anti-skid may therefore be credited for BOTH. The corollary matters operationally: with anti-skid inoperative the AFM penalties must be applied to both take-off and landing figures, and reduced-thrust take-offs are prohibited.
90XKVymQWxEqwPT64ubl: Deep stall - a stable, unrecoverable stall - needs two things together. A swept wing tends to stall at the tips first, which moves the centre of pressure forward and pitches the nose UP, driving the angle of attack higher still. A T-tail then sits directly in the low-energy turbulent wake shed by the stalled wing, so the elevator loses effectiveness exactly when it is needed to push the nose down. Aircraft with this combination are fitted with stick pushers.
94iNoHCgbPh6YnpIC6JU: Bernoulli's theorem gives total (pitot) pressure = static pressure + dynamic pressure, where dynamic pressure is 1/2 rho V2. Total pressure is what a pitot tube facing the airflow senses; static pressure is what a flush port parallel to the flow senses. The ASI works by measuring the difference between the two, which is the dynamic pressure and hence the indicated airspeed.
97atGVIikeB0RH6KuTl2: A shock stall is separation caused by the steep adverse pressure gradient behind a shock wave, and shock waves appear once the LOCAL flow goes supersonic - which at high cruise Mach numbers happens at quite a low angle of attack. Low-speed and deep stalls, by contrast, require the wing to be taken to a high angle of attack. This is the essence of the coffin corner: at high altitude the aeroplane can be close to both boundaries at once.
9GBvVk3eabuzpxAy9zuK: Below VMD the aeroplane is in the region of reversed command, where induced drag dominates and rises as speed falls. Slowing down therefore INCREASES the total drag and so requires MORE thrust - the reverse of normal intuition. This is why an approach flown behind the drag curve is unstable: any speed loss increases the drag, which loses more speed unless thrust is added promptly.
9Gqm4CovmapKTq8KcyYS: For turboprops the required landing distance at the destination and at any alternate must not exceed 70% of the landing distance available - equivalently the landing distance is factored by 1/0.7, about 1.43. Turbojets use the more demanding 60% (a factor of 1.67), and a further 15% is added to either figure if the runway is forecast to be wet.
9hhEW2jd3HNVePs8e0oD: In the throat the area is reduced, so continuity requires the flow to speed up - which means the DYNAMIC pressure there is higher than in the undisturbed flow, so statement 1 is false. Bernoulli's theorem says total pressure is conserved along a streamline in an ideal subsonic flow, so statement 2 is true: the rise in dynamic pressure in the throat is paid for exactly by a fall in static pressure.
9iZYlCdRbmutJ5MMNnji: In a steady climb the weight can be resolved into a component perpendicular to the flight path (balanced by lift, so lift is slightly LESS than weight) and a component acting backwards along the flight path - the uphill component. Thrust must overcome both the drag and that rearward weight component, which is why a climb needs more thrust than level flight at the same speed.
9K2YBGj5kL4EIWQ8aW0I: Two effects combine to produce Mach tuck. First, the shock wave forming on the upper surface moves the centre of pressure AFT, lengthening the nose-down moment arm about the CG. Second, the shock-induced separation reduces the downwash reaching the tailplane, which DECREASES the tailplane's effective angle of attack and hence its download, removing some of the nose-up moment it was providing. Both act nose-down.
9Np6IJ0hSkG0HoWCozC9: Stick POSITION stability - the relationship between elevator position and airspeed - is set by the CG position and the configuration, not by the trim setting. Moving the trim tab changes the speed at which the stick force is zero, and hence the whole stick FORCE curve, but the elevator still has to sit in the same place to hold a given speed. So stick position stability is unaffected.
9OEtfKka0trQ0OG6uOtJ: Dutch roll is a coupled oscillation in which yaw and roll feed one another, common on swept-wing aircraft where strong dihedral effect combines with relatively weak directional stability. A yaw damper senses yaw rate with a rate gyro and applies rudder to oppose it, breaking the coupling at source. Roll spoilers and rudder limiters serve quite different purposes.
9oYYSlHfzix1qYdajVtz: Manoeuvre stability is quoted as stick force per g, so the force required is the figure multiplied by the CHANGE in load factor, not by the final load factor. Going from n = 1 to n = 2.5 is a change of 1.5 g, so the additional force is 150 x 1.5 = 225 N. Multiplying by 2.5 to get 375 N is the standard trap.
9R1KeYjNP2Uar8eYUcGB: A symmetrical aerofoil has no camber, so at zero lift the pressure distributions on the upper and lower surfaces are mirror images and there is no residual couple: Cm0 = 0. This is why symmetrical sections are used for tailplanes and fins, where a pitching moment that varies with nothing is desirable. A positively cambered section, by contrast, has a constant negative (nose-down) Cm0.
9T5wRN7iaopbpOG3T3oA: The gust envelope in CS-25 is built on three reference gust velocities in the clean configuration: 66 ft/s at VB (the rough air / design gust speed), 50 ft/s at VC (design cruising speed) and 25 ft/s at VD (design dive speed). The gust velocity reduces as the design speed increases because the load a gust produces rises with airspeed, so the same structural limit is reached by a smaller gust.
9TNmIWLGFZsuqG3RqI8N: Outboard ailerons give a long moment arm and hence powerful roll control, which is wanted at low speed with the flaps out. At high speed the same long arm applied to a flexible outer wing risks aileron reversal and imposes large wing bending loads, so the outboard surfaces are locked out once the flaps and slats are retracted or the speed rises above a threshold, leaving roll control to the inboard ailerons and spoilers.
9XBuECLFkCZB3v0wHwSj: Stall speed rises whenever more lift is demanded or less CLmax is available. An increase in load factor raises the lift required (Vs increases with the square root of n); a forward CG shift increases the tailplane download, so the wing must generate more lift than the weight alone; and a loss of thrust removes both the vertical thrust component and, on a propeller aircraft, the slipstream over the wing. Higher flap settings and slats do the opposite - they raise CLmax and lower Vs.
9YKfHkgRUXdxU4oALd38: Wet snow reduces the friction coefficient available to the wheel brakes and, on a contaminated surface, raises the risk of reverted-rubber or viscous aquaplaning. Braking is therefore less effective and the landing distance increases - which is why AFM contaminated-runway data carry substantial penalties and why a contaminated landing must be assessed before dispatch.
A6rQmvbSHepPaHgneDhs: On a propeller aeroplane, a large part of the lift from the wing section behind the engine comes from the accelerated slipstream. Lose that engine and the slipstream disappears, so that wing suffers a sudden and substantial loss of lift on top of the asymmetric thrust - producing a marked roll toward the dead engine. A jet's exhaust does not wash over the wing in the same way, so its engine failure is predominantly a yaw problem.
a7Hoosuo8pAx7czjpmPQ: The ground interferes with the formation of the tip vortices, so the downwash behind the wing is reduced. Less downwash means the effective angle of attack at the wing INCREASES for a given attitude, so more lift is produced, while the lift vector is tilted less far rearward, so induced drag falls - by up to 40-50% at very low height. More lift and less drag together are why an aeroplane floats in the flare.
A9brc9kf6gG4S2G0dUtU: The optimum altitude rises steadily as fuel burns off, so economics always argue for climbing higher. What stops you is the buffet boundary: the 1.3g altitude is the height at which only a 1.3g manoeuvre margin remains before buffet onset, and it is the practical ceiling for a step climb regardless of what the fuel figures suggest. A continuous cruise climb would in fact be more economical still, but ATC will not normally allow it.
A9WHsJY4eXFswLjSLMqL: The pitching moment coefficient of a cambered aerofoil about its aerodynamic centre, Cm0, is essentially CONSTANT with angle of attack - that is what defines the aerodynamic centre. A constant moment cannot generate a restoring moment that varies with disturbance, so camber contributes nothing to longitudinal STABILITY. It affects the trim condition (a nose-down moment the tailplane must balance), but not the stability itself.
aa7AqETEsPvehqnQq8Nl: Density is mass per unit volume, so its SI unit is the kilogram per cubic metre; ISA sea-level density is 1.225 kg/m3. The distractors are all pressure units: psi is pounds per square inch, kg/cm2 is a metric pressure unit, and the bar is 100,000 pascals.
AAB9IwSVQTNAs5nifx1m: Pressure is force per unit AREA, so the units must be a force over a length squared - psi (pounds per square inch) fits, as do the pascal (N/m2) and the bar. kg/m3 is density (mass per volume), kg/dm2 is a mass over an area rather than a force, and lb/gal is a density in imperial units.
AAUjm0N0uHoL2te8WMoX: Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for the deviation from standard temperature - in effect, the altitude in the standard atmosphere at which the prevailing density would be found. It is the figure that actually governs aircraft and engine performance: on a hot day at a high-elevation aerodrome the density altitude can be thousands of feet above the physical elevation.
AKeEmn90l43XO3YQBJDn: In level flight lift equals weight, and minimum drag occurs at the fixed angle of attack giving (L/D)max. So Dmin = W / (L/D)max - with (L/D)max a constant for the airframe, the minimum drag is directly PROPORTIONAL to mass. Altitude does not change the value of the minimum drag; it changes the SPEED at which that minimum occurs.
ALv3JGPiN3U9NzdCjyZD: Brakes absorb the aeroplane's kinetic energy as heat, and their capacity to do so depends on starting cool. Brakes already hot from a previous landing or from taxiing have far less energy absorption left, so in a rejected take-off - the most demanding braking case there is - they may fade or fail, or the fuse plugs may melt and deflate the tyres. Hence the brake temperature limit and the mandatory cooling schedule before departure.
aMecZiL7GU1J6tHl8tg4: An expansion wave is the opposite of a shock: the supersonic flow turns around a convex corner and ACCELERATES, and because the process is isentropic, static pressure, density and temperature all DECREASE steadily through it. There is no Mach number above which the trend reverses - that monotonic decrease is what distinguishes an expansion fan from a shock wave, where all three properties rise abruptly.
aMJIsjM6qWwDFT37QshL: Parasite drag = CDp x 1/2 rho V2 S, and with CDp essentially constant it therefore varies with the SQUARE of the speed - double the speed and parasite drag quadruples. Induced drag does the opposite, varying inversely with V2. Adding the two produces the U-shaped total drag curve, with the minimum at the speed where they are equal.
aMoNPwTEIAQfUhHSlpN9: In a no-gyro approach the aircraft has lost its heading reference, so the controller issues 'turn left' and 'stop turn' instructions and the pilot flies them by timing on the turn coordinator. On the initial vectors turns are made at STANDARD rate, but once handed to the final controller they are made at HALF standard rate, so that the smaller, more frequent corrections needed on final do not overshoot the centreline.
ams0aSRf7l4QiYmuB4kP: Traffic load is what is left of the maximum take-off mass after the operating mass and the fuel have been accounted for. A longer desired range needs more fuel, and that fuel comes straight out of the payload allowance - the classic payload-range trade. The other limits work differently: maximum zero fuel mass caps the traffic load rather than the fuel, and reserve fuel, being fuel, also reduces the payload available.
ANbbsKvbVH0JJzc7hbzq: The gust load factor increment is inversely proportional to wing loading, so a LIGHTER aeroplane has less inertia to resist the gust and suffers a larger load factor - statement 1 is correct. Altitude works the other way: as height increases the gust alleviation factor falls, so at a given IAS the gust load DECREASES with altitude - statement 2 is incorrect. This is why turbulence penetration is more punishing when light and at low level.
AnpejvbyYjkCjjtfeYfH: A turbulent boundary layer continuously mixes fast-moving free-stream air down toward the surface, so the velocity climbs very steeply in the first fraction of a millimetre before levelling off. A laminar layer changes velocity gradually and smoothly through its whole depth. The steeper wall gradient is exactly why the turbulent layer produces more skin friction drag - and also why it carries more energy and separates later.
ANVkifdfZPzcgGTW4Vaz: The gross flight path is the aeroplane's demonstrated performance; the NET flight path is that gradient reduced by a mandatory margin (0.8% for a twin, 0.9% for three engines, 1.0% for four) to allow for variations in technique, airframe condition and the atmosphere. The net gradient is therefore always smaller, and it is the net path that must clear obstacles.
ANX0K3JhGpuP2R785hmD: Dutch roll arises when lateral stability (dihedral effect) is strong relative to directional stability: a sideslip generates a powerful rolling moment before the fin has straightened the aeroplane out, so roll and yaw feed each other in an oscillation. Increasing lateral stability therefore worsens the tendency. The opposite imbalance - strong directional, weak lateral - gives spiral instability instead.
AoBUOmcc6fESpDcopOUD: Descending at a constant Mach number, both the rising temperature and the rapidly increasing density mean the IAS climbs steadily. Higher dynamic pressure needs a smaller lift coefficient to support the same weight, so the angle of attack decreases - and with it the pitch attitude. This is why a constant-Mach descent has to be flown to a crossover altitude and then continued at a constant IAS.
aoZsNlB2TyrdXQP17jFF: In fully supersonic flow the pressure over each surface is essentially constant between the shock waves, so the pressure distribution is broadly rectangular rather than the peaked, rounded subsonic shape. Because the loading is spread evenly along the chord, the centre of pressure sits at about 50% chord - well aft of the subsonic quarter-chord position, which is the source of the transonic trim change.
ARIG9WSRBwXYxmfwrxSm: The flow accelerates most over the UPPER surface, because that is where the curvature is greatest and the suction peak highest, so the local flow reaches M1.0 there first. That is the definition of the critical Mach number, and the shock forms just downstream of the suction peak, around mid-chord, then strengthens and moves aft as Mach increases. A lower-surface shock appears only at a higher Mach number.
ArIMPgAQel8pbCU27h2P: A Fowler flap travels rearward on tracks first, increasing the wing AREA, and only then rotates downward to add CAMBER. Because it does both, it produces the largest CLmax increase of any trailing-edge device for a given drag penalty - which is why the first stages of Fowler flap give a big lift gain with little drag, ideal for take-off, while the final stages add mostly drag.
aswNozoQZobBagf2ZIEt: The horizontal stabiliser provides LONGITUDINAL (pitch) stability. Its long moment arm behind the CG means that if a disturbance raises the nose, the tailplane's angle of attack increases, generating an upward force aft of the CG and a restoring nose-down moment. Lateral stability comes chiefly from dihedral and sweep, and directional stability from the fin.
AxewD2T5EYHgSu9TBXdx: A headwind does not change the aeroplane's airspeed, rate of descent or air-relative glide angle - but it reduces the groundspeed, so for each foot lost the aeroplane covers less ground. The descent path traced over the ground is therefore STEEPER and the distance covered shorter. A tailwind flattens the ground path and extends the glide.
Axyoq2khOtGB70oXGHLg: Gyroscopic precession makes an applied force take effect 90 degrees onward in the direction of rotation. For a propeller turning clockwise as seen from the cockpit, a pitch-up input precesses into a YAW to the RIGHT, and a yaw to the right precesses into a PITCH DOWN - so both statements hold. The familiar tailwheel case is the same rule: raising the tail (pitching nose down) yaws the aeroplane left.
AyZvh0exoqNkUKvKqfZ3: Behind a shock wave the pressure rises steeply against the flow, and the boundary layer separates. The separated region destroys the suction peak over the rear of the upper surface, so lift falls sharply while drag rises steeply - the shock stall. The separation is also unsteady, which is what produces Mach buffet, and it can render ailerons in the affected region ineffective.
b18PEezcLcq5gB2DFb9S: VS is the stalling speed, or the minimum steady flight speed at which the aeroplane remains controllable. It is the reference from which many operating speeds are derived - V2, VR and VREF are all defined as multiples of a stall speed. Note the variants: VS1 is for a specified configuration and VS0 for the landing configuration.
b1SjnWH0vU5WLJVCzrvG: Statements 2, 3 and 4 hold. The tailplane load, whether up or down, forms part of the aeroplane's total lift; a tailplane CAN stall before the wing when ice has reduced its stalling angle and a large flap setting has increased the downwash meeting it - the classic tailplane icing stall, recovered by RAISING the nose and reducing flap; and balancing the total pitching moment is the tailplane's fundamental job. Statement 1 fails on the word 'always': with an aft CG the tailplane load can be positive.
b1YFpeb1ztYlJ87J5Z79: The tailplane dominates because it combines a useful area with a very long moment arm behind the CG - and stability contribution scales with area multiplied by arm. A pitch disturbance changes its angle of attack and generates a restoring moment large enough to overcome the destabilising contributions of the fuselage and, usually, the wing. This is why tailplane size is set by stability rather than by control requirements.
B5YjGn2WAbjkirFap5X9: V2 is defined as a multiple of the stall speed in the take-off configuration. A larger flap setting raises CLmax and therefore lowers the stall speed, so V2 comes down with it. The qualifier matters: V2 must also be at least 1.1 VMCA, and VMCA does not improve with flap, so at high flap settings VMCA can become the limiting floor.
bbLvcHPmMoSRwze9yihb: Both statements are false. The gust load factor is inversely proportional to wing loading, so a lighter aeroplane suffers a LARGER load factor - decreasing mass increases the gust load. And the gust alleviation factor increases as altitude decreases, so descending makes gust loads WORSE, not better. The practical lesson is that turbulence penetration is most punishing when light and at low level.
BbtxWjkQmZvgMJBpFqRD: The third climb segment is the level acceleration segment, in which the aeroplane accelerates from V2 to the flap retraction speed while retracting flap. Regulations set a minimum acceleration height of 400 ft above the take-off surface, so the aeroplane must have completed the second segment climb to at least that height before levelling off. Noise abatement procedures may raise it, but never lower it.
BcaCWSaAViWkESEVtVBq: A propeller aeroplane's fuel flow is broadly proportional to POWER, and power required is drag times speed - so maximum range means minimum drag, which is (L/D)max. A jet's fuel flow follows THRUST, so its maximum range comes at the tangent-from-the-origin point, faster than (L/D)max. For propeller maximum ENDURANCE the target is minimum power, which is slower still.
bey3sVTUaaGgZlrkdJy5: V1 must be at least VMCG, the minimum control speed on the ground: below that speed the rudder cannot hold the aeroplane straight after an engine failure, so a decision to CONTINUE would be meaningless. At the top end V1 may not exceed VR. The sequence to remember is VMCG, V1, VR, VMU, VLOF, V2.
bNNQL8gsSb1vmqnDmBlI: The slot between the extended slat and the wing forms a converging duct, so air from the high-pressure region beneath the wing is ACCELERATED as it passes through and emerges as a fast-moving jet over the upper surface. That jet re-energises the boundary layer, letting it resist separation to a much higher angle of attack - typically an extra 5-10 degrees of stalling angle. The slat does not reduce wing loading, and the flow through the slot speeds up rather than slowing down.
bqgZJAZWFqipzYOipgyL: With fully powered controls the pilot feels nothing of the real aerodynamic loads, so an artificial feel unit generates them. It reproduces what an unpowered system would give: force proportional to how far the surface is deflected and to the DYNAMIC pressure (q-feel), so the controls become progressively heavier as speed increases. That speed-dependence is what discourages large deflections at high speed.
BT4UmJx2XQM74y5fGiaZ: Two effects stack. A forward CG needs a larger nose-up balancing moment from the tail, which means a bigger tail DOWNLOAD, and the wing must generate the weight plus that download. Idle thrust removes the nose-up couple that a below-CG thrust line normally supplies, so the tail has to provide even more download. Forward CG with idle thrust therefore demands the greatest wing lift - and gives the highest stall speed.
bV9YkxM7NLVOLHudV1cW: Both statements are false. The ELLIPTICAL spanwise lift distribution is the theoretical optimum, producing uniform downwash across the span and therefore the MINIMUM induced drag for a given lift - a rectangular distribution produces more, not less. And induced drag is inversely proportional to aspect ratio, so REDUCING aspect ratio increases it, which is why long slender wings are used where efficiency matters.
bVFPBHJDZS4dpzxkfi1X: A force acting below the centre of gravity produces a nose-up couple about it, so on an aeroplane with underslung engines a sudden thrust increase pitches the nose up - and a thrust reduction pitches it down. This coupling is why a go-around from a low-speed, high-drag configuration demands prompt forward pressure, and why the effect is most pronounced on aircraft with large-diameter engines slung well below the wing.
BVOkTxjK9Vv2od4CCs53: Losing an engine hurts twice over. The failed engine, unless feathered, windmills and adds substantial drag, and the asymmetric thrust must be balanced by rudder and a small bank, which adds further drag from the deflected surfaces and the sideslip. Both increase the power required from the remaining engine or engines at the very moment when less power is available.
bVrORMisgr3ggbYp3xwT: Large transport aeroplanes certified under CS-25 have a positive limit manoeuvring load factor of 2.5 (with the negative limit at -1.0), reflecting an operating regime in which deliberate manoeuvring is gentle. The ultimate load is 1.5 times the limit, i.e. 3.75. The higher figures of 3.8, 4.4 and 6.0 belong to the CS-23 Normal, Utility and Aerobatic categories.
bXXGENzz2CalZqu42mrO: Turn radius = V2 / (g tan(bank)), so at the same bank angle the slower aeroplane flies the tighter circle - A's radius is less than B's. Checking the others: load factor is 1/cos(bank), identical for both; rate of turn is g tan(bank)/V, so A's is HIGHER; and with the same lift required at a lower speed, A must fly at the HIGHER lift coefficient.
c3grizWklNMagXLb0l1u: V1 is bounded below by VMCG and above by the accelerate-stop capability. With anti-skid inoperative the braking available is much reduced, so the accelerate-stop distance lengthens dramatically and V1 must be REDUCED to keep the stop case within the runway available. Increased mass or temperature push the take-off distance up and generally raise V1, and an inoperative FMS has no performance effect at all.
cCqJLGFtEH9nj6ZE0PXR: Lateral and directional stability are strongly coupled, because a sideslip excites both. If DIRECTIONAL stability is strong relative to lateral, the fin swings the nose into the sideslip faster than the dihedral effect can raise the lower wing, so the bank persists and steepens - spiral instability, a slowly tightening descending turn. The reverse imbalance, strong lateral effect with weak directional, gives Dutch roll.
CeqTM88PWVqr1XqHlMOT: For a turbojet at the planning stage, the landing distance required must not exceed 60% of the landing distance available on a dry runway - so multiply the LDA by 0.60. Expressed the other way round, the demonstrated landing distance is factored UP by 1/0.6 = 1.67. Turboprops get the less demanding 0.70, and a wet runway adds a further 15% to the required distance.
cgfDVVmLp0iaB6dy5KQi: The glide angle relative to the AIR is set by L/D and is unaffected by weight or wind. What a tailwind changes is the ground track: the aeroplane is carried along while it descends, so it covers more ground for the same height loss - the glide path over the ground flattens. A headwind does the reverse. Weight changes the SPEED at which the best glide occurs, but not the distance achieved.
CkPD4ZES3vOmtzMhq5qV: A rate-one turn is 3 degrees per second, and rate of turn = g tan(bank)/V - so holding the rate fixed means the required bank angle depends entirely on TAS. The familiar rule of thumb follows: bank angle is roughly TAS in knots divided by 10, plus 7. Weight does not enter the turn equations at all, and load factor is itself a consequence of bank rather than an independent input.
cletUfFkAuGtmoM9QRzG: The blade's angle of attack is the fixed blade angle minus the helix angle of the airflow it meets, and that helix angle is set by forward speed divided by rotational speed. Reducing forward speed or increasing rpm both flatten the helix, so the blade meets the air at a LARGER angle of attack. This is why a fixed-pitch propeller is efficient over only a narrow band and can be stalled at high power and low airspeed.
ClOmc0YPfcIGvROuvvqk: The total pressure lost across a normal shock rises very steeply with the Mach number ahead of it - the loss is negligible just above M1.0 but severe by M2. So an efficient intake keeps the shock weak, decelerating the flow gradually through a series of oblique shocks before a final weak normal shock, rather than allowing one strong shock at high Mach. A shock cannot exist at all below M1.0.
ClpYv1ekJX5PUg9S5nZ0: V1 is the maximum speed at which the pilot must take the FIRST action to stop, and the minimum speed at which the take-off may be continued after a failure - and the aeroplane is still on the ground at that point. It is deliberately distinguished from VEF, the speed at which the engine actually fails: V1 is one reaction time LATER, which is what makes V1 a decision speed rather than a failure speed.
CMFNduO0XNiXmcm7Tdy5: Both statements have the direction wrong. In tuck under (Mach tuck) the centre of pressure moves AFT as the shock wave forms, not forward, lengthening the nose-down moment arm. And the shock-induced separation REDUCES the downwash reaching the tailplane, it does not increase it, which removes some of the tailplane's nose-up contribution. Both effects pitch the nose down.
cmQZ2FYHFG5FaZI0zSEE: An uphill slope means gravity opposes the acceleration throughout the take-off run, so the take-off distance grows substantially. The accelerate-stop distance is affected less, because although the acceleration to V1 is slower, the same slope then HELPS the deceleration during the stop - the two effects partly cancel. So the take-off distance suffers more than the accelerate-stop distance, and the allowed take-off mass falls.
CpAqNKa3eCeFNfoJd3ES: The obstacle limit of 4630 kg is below the estimated 5000 kg, so it is the obstacle case that must be improved. Less flap means less drag and therefore a better climb gradient, which raises the obstacle-limited mass - but less flap also means a longer ground run, which lowers the runway-limited mass. Selecting 5 degrees therefore trades runway limit for obstacle limit, and with 640 kg of runway margin in hand that is the trade to make.
cqCjQU2VO339cT981tmm: Induced drag coefficient is proportional to CL squared divided by aspect ratio, so INCREASING aspect ratio reduces it directly. A long, slender wing has tips that are a smaller proportion of the span, so the tip vortices influence less of the wing and the downwash is reduced. This is why gliders and long-range aircraft carry high aspect ratio wings, and why winglets - which effectively increase the aerodynamic span - are fitted.
cr0BlnNSDiConKgboQMr: In subsonic flow the aerodynamic centre of a conventional aerofoil sits at about 25% chord. Once the flow is fully supersonic the pressure distribution becomes essentially uniform along the chord, so the centre of the load - and the aerodynamic centre - moves back to about 50%. That rearward shift is what lengthens the nose-down moment arm and produces the transonic trim change known as Mach tuck.
CRHJdgw76czeDnsmf1tO: Both statements are correct. The gust load increment is proportional to the wing's lift curve slope, and a higher aspect ratio gives a steeper lift curve slope, so the same gust produces a bigger change in lift and a larger load factor. And the increment is directly proportional to airspeed, so flying faster in turbulence increases the load - which is exactly why a turbulence penetration speed is published and flown.
ctOKsvZM6d2vdkgFe4Uj: As Mach number rises toward Mcrit the centre of pressure moves aft, producing the nose-down tuck.
