The Mach trim system senses Mach number and automatically applies a compensating nose-up input - usually by repositioning the trimmable stabiliser or biasing the elevator feel - so the stick force gradient stays positive and the aeroplane retains apparent speed stability. It corrects the pitching moment, not the drag.
CUjp1YeM8zNBAq2WkYDs: Convert the speed to the same units: 194 kt is 194 x 6076 / 60, about 19,650 ft/min. The gradient is then 1000 / 19,650 = 5.1%. Since the tangent of a small angle in degrees is roughly the percentage divided by 60 x ... more simply, arctan(0.051) is about 2.9 degrees, so 3 degrees. Note the useful rule: 1 degree is approximately a 1.75% gradient.
CW508DVxB5LbRdect7k8: Turn radius = V2 / (g tan(bank)) and rate of turn = g tan(bank) / V - neither expression contains mass, so two aeroplanes at the same TAS and bank angle fly identical turns regardless of weight. What differs is the LIFT the heavier aeroplane must generate to achieve the same load factor, and hence the higher lift coefficient or thrust it needs to sustain the turn.
cWwpzX6Ufuez2JhWh9nD: VMCA is set by the balance between the asymmetric yawing moment from the live engine and the rudder's ability to oppose it. At higher pressure altitude the live engine produces less thrust, so the yawing moment to be countered is smaller and a lower speed suffices - VMCA decreases with altitude. Note the exception: a flat-rated engine holds full thrust to a certain altitude, so VMCA stays constant until that point.
cxZMjrAtyZN2uMZC69IO: A lower pressure altitude means DENSER air, which improves everything at once: more thrust, more lift at a given TAS, a lower TAS needed for a given IAS, and a better climb gradient. The take-off distance required therefore decreases, as do the ground run and the accelerate-stop distance. It is high pressure altitude, not low, that penalises performance.
CyDQP3HsvaUvPUpoTRzD: A shock wave is a violent, irreversible compression: the flow decelerates abruptly and part of its ordered kinetic energy is converted into random thermal energy, raising the static temperature. That conversion is a loss of available energy, and it shows up as a drop in TOTAL pressure across the wave - which is the source of wave drag. Static pressure, density and temperature all RISE across the shock; only total pressure falls.
d0Iwii3pa6KmyheoFLqK: Reduced thrust relies on the certified performance margins remaining intact, and a contaminated runway destroys the assumptions behind them: braking action is degraded and displacement drag is unpredictable, so the accelerate-stop case can no longer be guaranteed. Reduced thrust is therefore prohibited on contaminated runways, and also with anti-skid or reverse thrust inoperative, or when windshear is reported.
d3fplXkQzQUEWDgpwrSL: In the first part, descending at constant Mach, the IAS climbs steadily as density increases. Above VMD more speed means more drag, and with idle thrust the descent angle is essentially D/L, so the path STEEPENS. In the second part the IAS is held constant, so the angle of attack, CL, CD and therefore L/D are all constant - and so is the descent angle. Increases, then constant.
D3kXQ9za22ihUifZGAvx: On a typical aerofoil of moderate thickness the adverse pressure gradient is steepest toward the rear of the upper surface, so as the angle of attack increases the boundary layer first separates at the UPPER SURFACE TRAILING EDGE. The separation point then creeps forward with increasing alpha until it reaches the point where lift collapses - the gentle, progressive trailing-edge stall with good buffet warning. Thin aerofoils behave differently, stalling abruptly from the leading edge.
D3VdPQLzr8A7rSilysng: Rolling is rotation about the LONGITUDINAL axis, which runs from nose to tail through the centre of gravity, and it is controlled by the ailerons and roll spoilers. Pitching is rotation about the lateral axis (wingtip to wingtip) and yawing about the normal or vertical axis. There is no 'wing axis' in the standard set.
d4mMn3MZYx7ikxaEZNlb: Extending take-off flap raises CLmax, so every speed defined by reference to the stall - including VX and VY - comes down. The climb gradient and rate also fall, because flap adds more drag than lift at these speeds, which is precisely why flap is retracted once the acceleration segment is complete. Both speeds are therefore lower than clean, but so is the performance they deliver.
DaQN7KrI85u99QhsPIhc: A take-off toward an obstacle IS permitted with a tailwind, provided the performance calculation accounts for it - and it must, because a tailwind lengthens the take-off distance and flattens the climb path over the ground, both of which reduce the obstacle-limited mass. Wind is therefore very much a factor. Bank angles up to 15 degrees are permitted in the net take-off flight path, subject to height and speed conditions.
DbmgTKolFPWnpevpSYNU: Work in two steps. Dry: the landing distance required must not exceed 60% of the LDA, so 0.60 x 3000 = 1800 m. Wet: a further 15% is added to the required distance, so the maximum permissible landing distance becomes 1800 / 1.15 = 1565 m. The two factors compound, they are not applied side by side.
dDC03VSL1Korgs1HIjUH: Significant turbulence produces gust-induced load factor excursions, and any load factor above 1 raises the speed at which the wing stalls - an accelerated stall. At high cruise altitude the low-speed and high-speed buffet boundaries are already close together, so an aeroplane that is buffet-free in smooth air can be taken into the low-speed boundary by a modest gust while decelerating.
dDOOjE80IyjhNetoYVcJ: As fuel burns the aeroplane gets lighter, so it needs less lift, flies at a lower drag for the same speed, and requires less thrust. Fuel flow therefore DECREASES and the distance flown per kilogram of fuel - the specific range - INCREASES. This steady improvement through the cruise is why optimum altitude rises with time and why step climbs pay.
DgmcA70MVAVM6Ap9oz2l: In laminar flow the air moves in smooth parallel layers that slide over one another without mixing, so there is no velocity component perpendicular to the surface. That absence of mixing is exactly why a laminar layer produces low skin friction but carries little energy near the wall - and therefore separates far more readily than a turbulent layer under an adverse pressure gradient.
dieIpTt7JBRcWqupIWJL: Aspect ratio is wing span divided by the mean geometric chord - equivalently, span squared divided by wing area, which is the form to use on a tapered wing. A high aspect ratio wing is long and slender and produces less induced drag, since induced drag is inversely proportional to aspect ratio. Gliders run around 20-30; a fighter may be as low as 3.
DPpJTHAlSJw4wJYvWbmx: Optimum cruise altitude is the pressure altitude at which the aeroplane achieves its best specific range - the most nautical miles per kilogram of fuel - for its current weight. Because it depends on weight, it rises steadily as fuel burns off, which is why step climbs are flown. It is limited in practice by the buffet boundary and by available thrust.
dqIbgzIJutMkax7xmXzV: Behind the drag curve, below VMD, drag INCREASES as speed falls. So any speed loss increases the drag, which loses more speed - the divergence feeds itself and the speed is unstable. Above VMD the opposite holds and speed is self-correcting. This is why an approach flown too slow demands constant thrust attention, and why the region of reversed command is treated as a hazard rather than a curiosity.
DqmwmnajHaZSVQ6NLp7Q: TAS = IAS divided by the square root of the density ratio, so the gap between them is created entirely by density falling below sea-level value. Descending increases density, the ratio approaches 1, and the two converge - at sea level in ISA they are equal. Climbing does the reverse: at FL350 the TAS can be more than 70% above the IAS.
dQTX4W8sXmkBZyvYPXON: Taper ratio is the TIP chord divided by the ROOT chord, so it is always a number between 0 (a pointed tip) and 1 (a rectangular wing). Taper is used to approximate the elliptical lift distribution and so reduce induced drag, and to save structural weight - but excessive taper concentrates loading at the tips and encourages tip stalling, which is why washout is usually added with it.
DR0XPXwnt8oKpHgecoPH: Mach trim counters tuck under. As Mach number rises toward Mcrit the centre of pressure moves aft and the downwash at the tail reduces, both pitching the nose down; the system senses Mach number and applies an automatic nose-up input so the stick force gradient stays positive. It does not prevent the shock wave or the buffet that follows - only the trim change.
DRe8FO6lQv1gcJJrRC5i: Both statements are correct. Vortex strength depends on the pressure difference between the upper and lower surfaces, which is governed by lift coefficient - so a lower angle of attack means weaker vortices, which is why the heaviest, slowest, cleanest aircraft generates the strongest wake. And a low aspect ratio wing has tips that dominate a greater proportion of the span, so the vortices are stronger and induced drag higher.
DspUiAUtPknhHtsHbGXv: Higher atmospheric pressure means DENSER air, which improves everything at once: the engine produces more thrust, the wing produces more lift at a given TAS, and the TAS needed to reach a given IAS is lower. The take-off distance therefore shortens and the excess thrust available for climbing increases, improving the initial climb gradient.
Dt9dwpR8d831oiaXxW8d: A positively cambered aerofoil is asymmetric - the upper surface is more curved than the lower - so it still accelerates the flow over the top and generates lift even at zero geometric angle of attack. The CL-alpha curve therefore crosses the vertical axis ABOVE the origin, and the zero-lift angle is a small NEGATIVE alpha. A symmetrical section passes through the origin.
dtDceDNaEyUSKKiepmFh: Statement 1 is correct: the elliptical distribution produces uniform downwash across the span and is the theoretical minimum-induced-drag case, so it beats a rectangular distribution. Statement 2 is incorrect: induced drag coefficient is inversely proportional to aspect ratio, so REDUCING aspect ratio INCREASES induced drag. That is why efficient aircraft use long, slender, taper-approximating-elliptical wings.
DVgrVcTQ0ajbs7EqJH9c: The lift gain from trailing-edge flap tails off with deflection while the drag penalty accelerates, so the final stages are almost all drag. Going from 30 to 45 degrees therefore harms CL/CD most - which is exactly why take-off uses a small flap setting (lift with little drag) and landing uses a large one (drag is wanted, to steepen the approach and slow the aeroplane). Slats hurt CL/CD least of all.
DvJbe6aY339o4F8ie8Ho: Anti-skid maximises braking by modulating pressure to keep each wheel just below the point of locking. Without it the pilot must brake conservatively to avoid locking and blowing tyres, so the deceleration achieved is far lower and the accelerate-stop distance increases substantially. The AFM carries specific penalties, V1 must be reduced, and reduced-thrust take-offs are prohibited.
DXWdl0K1RQq3uNLlTzxT: Optimum altitude is by definition where specific range is greatest, so flying above it cannot improve fuel mileage. What happens in practice is that ATC assigns discrete flight levels rather than a continuous cruise climb, so the aeroplane spends most of the cruise slightly BELOW optimum as the optimum rises with fuel burn - and immediately after a step climb it may be slightly ABOVE it. Both excursions are ATC-driven, not economics-driven.
dzJmoHST1pfAM1bwiWmd: Bernoulli's theorem states that total pressure equals static plus dynamic pressure: pt = ps + q. Rearranged, ps = pt - q, which is what the pitot-static system exploits: a pitot tube senses pt, a static port senses ps, and the ASI measures the difference q = 1/2 rho V2 to derive the indicated airspeed.
E0Twg20vcEJwyqpCSc3n: In incompressible terms the stalling IAS would be constant at all altitudes, since IAS is a direct measure of dynamic pressure. But at high altitude the true airspeed for a given IAS is much higher, so compressibility effects appear: local shock waves reduce the achievable CLmax, and the stalling speed in IAS therefore INCREASES with altitude. This rising low-speed boundary, meeting the falling high-speed one, is what creates coffin corner.
E5TzgXBRKeVK1YtLy1BZ: The maximum cruise altitude is set by requiring a residual manoeuvre margin - conventionally 1.3g - before buffet onset. The reason for insisting on that margin is that turbulence produces gust-induced load factor excursions, and without a margin a routine gust would take the aeroplane straight into Mach buffet. The limit is about the buffet boundary, not about exceeding the structural limit load.
Ead9VSJ5KugAVA8UiheG: Convert first: 300 kt is 300 x 0.5144 = 154.3 m/s. Then r = V2 / (g tan(bank)) = 154.3 squared / (10 x tan 45) = 23,808 / 10 = 2381 m. Note that tan 45 = 1, which simplifies the arithmetic, and that mass does not appear - turn radius depends only on speed and bank angle.
eBBoMt1iUjzFofoHoWPD: A normal shock wave always decelerates the flow from supersonic to SUBSONIC - that is its defining property. Static pressure, density and temperature all rise abruptly across it, while total pressure falls (the energy lost as wave drag). An OBLIQUE shock, by contrast, can leave the flow still supersonic, which is why efficient supersonic intakes use a series of oblique shocks before a final weak normal shock.
ebGEoa6uBbnRhvSrJvvn: All three can be limiting, and the take-off mass used is the LOWEST of them. The field length limit comes from TODA, ASDA and TORA; the climb limit comes from the one-engine-inoperative gradient requirements of the take-off segments; and the brake energy limit caps VMBE, the maximum speed from which the brakes can absorb a rejected take-off. Obstacle clearance, tyre speed and structural limits complete the list.
Ed5m2OBN2tlbtCb9SAI9: A wing stalls at a fixed ANGLE OF ATTACK, not at a fixed speed - so as long as alpha stays below the critical angle, the wing cannot stall, whatever the airspeed, attitude, weight or load factor. This is why an aeroplane can be stalled at high speed in a steep turn, or in a nose-down attitude during a recovery, and why angle of attack is the parameter stall warning systems actually measure.
edC3pMBWHPOdVNoOg5wI: In a no-gyro approach the heading reference has failed, so the controller issues 'turn left/right' and 'stop turn' instructions which the pilot flies by timing against the turn coordinator. On the initial vectors, turns are made at STANDARD rate unless otherwise advised; only after handover to the final approach controller are they reduced to half standard rate, so that corrections on final do not overshoot.
EfnWaPV0hlLhUAFR0peV: For a jet, fuel flow follows thrust, so maximum range means minimising drag per unit of DISTANCE - the tangent-from-the-origin point on the drag curve, which lies at a speed about 1.32 times VMD. Flying faster than the minimum-drag speed means a smaller lift coefficient and therefore a LOWER angle of attack than the (L/D)max condition. The (L/D)max angle gives maximum range for a PROPELLER aeroplane, and maximum endurance for a jet.
ege8Xqz04epXyNIiuxB0: Subsonically the centre of pressure sits around the quarter-chord. Once the flow is fully supersonic the pressure distribution becomes essentially uniform along the chord, so the centre of the load moves to roughly MID-CHORD, about 50%. That rearward migration lengthens the nose-down moment arm about the CG and is the origin of the transonic trim change, Mach tuck.
EHiSlOqkBVhK0NGtTpGA: The maximum operating altitude of a pressurised aeroplane is simply the highest pressure altitude for which it has been certified for normal operation - a structural and systems limit, driven chiefly by the maximum permissible cabin differential pressure, and published as a fixed figure in the AFM. The aerodynamic ceiling and the buffet-limited altitude are separate, weight-dependent limits that may be lower on any given day.
EHWVObCbyMslHx6dharQ: Retracting flap reduces the wing's camber and therefore its lift coefficient at a given angle of attack. Since lift must still equal weight and the speed is being held constant, the lost CL has to be recovered by raising the angle of attack. This is the source of the sink that accompanies flap retraction if the attitude is not adjusted promptly.
EifBm3pMqVhdN3uvh9A0: Mach number is TAS divided by the LOCAL speed of sound - local because the speed of sound depends on the ambient temperature, which varies with altitude. It is emphatically not based on IAS, nor on the sea-level speed of sound. Note the consequence: at a fixed TAS, warmer air raises the speed of sound and therefore LOWERS the Mach number.
el3vRxycFkDK8tNJ67Yd: Higher pressure altitude means less dense air, so the engine produces less thrust and the wing produces less lift at a given TAS - the aeroplane must accelerate to a higher true airspeed before it will fly, and it does so more slowly. The take-off distance REQUIRED therefore increases. The distances 'available' are physical properties of the aerodrome and do not change with the weather.
elM5ivg85irBl5eNFzFX: Lift and drag are defined relative to the RELATIVE AIRFLOW, not to the airframe or the horizon: lift acts perpendicular to it and drag parallel to it, opposing the motion. This is why they rotate with the flight path, and why in a climb the lift vector is tilted forward of vertical while part of the weight acts along the flight path.
EmzJFq4YdbYbyL8kTjOW: Mach number is TAS divided by the local speed of sound, so the speed of sound is TAS divided by Mach number: 400 / 0.8 = 500 kt. That figure is consistent with a temperature around -20 C, since the speed of sound depends only on temperature - roughly 39 times the square root of the absolute temperature, in knots.
eoneAWHqfcmHZA5hRWd1: Static directional stability is the tendency to weathercock into the relative airflow. In a sideslip to the right the airflow arrives from the right, striking the fin and generating a sideforce that pushes the TAIL to the left - which swings the NOSE to the right, into the sideslip, until the slip is eliminated. The fin's long moment arm behind the CG is what makes this restoring moment effective.
EpkluG0fEZ1n1dhNMSRk: Power required is drag multiplied by speed, so a tangent drawn from the origin touches the power curve where P/V - which is simply the DRAG - is at its minimum. That point is VMD, the minimum drag speed. For a jet, whose fuel flow follows thrust, minimum drag means minimum fuel flow and therefore maximum ENDURANCE. (Maximum specific range for a jet lies at a higher speed, found from the tangent to the DRAG curve instead.)
EUphXQTJRIV0TaI6FII1: In a power-ASSISTED (boosted) system the pilot's muscular effort and the hydraulic power act together on the surface, so a proportion of the real aerodynamic load is still transmitted back up the control run to the column. That residual feedback gives genuine feel, which is why no artificial feel unit is required - unlike a fully powered system, where the pilot is completely isolated from the surface. Trimming is still very much required.
Exqn94lpwCBlcbxAiWSg: Climb angle depends on excess THRUST divided by weight, so anything that adds drag flattens the climb. Flap adds a great deal of drag - and beyond the first stage it adds far more drag than lift - so the angle of climb with flap extended is always smaller than clean. This is why flap is retracted on schedule after take-off and why an obstacle climb is flown in the minimum practicable configuration.
ezWoEBVubgysRnVpvJHZ: In severe turbulence the aeroplane is squeezed from both sides: a gust can raise the load factor toward the structural limit, while the same gust can raise the angle of attack toward the stall. That is why a turbulence penetration speed is published - it sits between the two. Extending flap is exactly the wrong response, because the flap-extended structural limits are much LOWER than the clean ones.
F175IKuw77Lw4thjW3IK: The approach climb requirement is a go-around case with one engine inoperative, assessed in the approach configuration (gear up, approach flap) at the go-around thrust available. It sets a minimum gradient - 2.1% for a twin, 2.4% for three engines, 2.7% for four - and it frequently limits the landing mass. The all-engines, full-flap, gear-down case is the separate LANDING climb requirement.
f5bygPYrhlaSLR7gXu1c: Excess power can be spent in only two ways: gaining height or gaining speed. Accelerating at a constant power setting therefore diverts energy that would otherwise have gone into the climb, so both the rate of climb and the angle of climb fall while the acceleration lasts. This total-energy view is why a level acceleration segment is scheduled after take-off rather than trying to do both at once.
FAaFlFz1n6iWk35PFVGm: A symmetrical aerofoil has an essentially constant pitching moment coefficient about its aerodynamic centre at 25% chord, so as angle of attack changes the lift grows but its point of application barely moves. That is why symmetrical sections are used for tailplanes and fins, where a wandering centre of pressure would upset the balance the surface exists to provide. A cambered section's CP moves forward as alpha increases.
Famdf4ybA8jqTlxmzk65: Slats raise the stalling angle of attack, typically by 5-10 degrees, by ducting high-energy air through the slot onto the upper surface to re-energise the boundary layer and delay separation. Trailing-edge flaps do the opposite - they raise CLmax but LOWER the stalling angle by increasing camber. Spoilers and speed brakes destroy lift rather than enhance it.
FAUIWW0elGITt3oBJq01: Long range cruise deliberately accepts a specific range 1% below the maximum, and takes the HIGHER of the two speeds that deliver it. Because the specific range curve is very flat near its peak, that 1% fuel penalty buys typically 3-5% more speed - which is almost always worth it once crew time, maintenance and schedule are costed. Taking the lower of the two speeds would give the 1% penalty for no benefit at all.
fBHjTBe4mfObb3I8KIxH: Mach buffet is the airframe shaking produced by shock-induced separation, and a shock wave cannot exist until the LOCAL airflow reaches M1.0 - which by definition is the critical Mach number. So Mach buffet is uniquely a supercritical phenomenon. Speed instability occurs at low speed behind the drag curve, and Dutch roll is a lateral-directional oscillation independent of Mach number.
Fc6QIe6gBkj7B1KTT4GR: A stick pusher is fitted where the natural stall is unacceptable rather than merely uncomfortable. Excessive wing drop can flick the aeroplane into a spin, and a deep stall - typical of swept wings with a T-tail, where the stalled wing's wake blankets the elevator - is unrecoverable by normal means. A benign pitch-down with a minor wing drop, by contrast, is exactly the recovery behaviour certification wants.
FCYJIyG934f3k23lWjVk: More power gives more speed, but drag rises with the square of speed, so the extra fuel burnt outruns the extra distance covered: fuel per hour and fuel per nautical mile both increase. That is the whole point of cruising at a reduced power setting - the 10% power saving buys a disproportionate gain in specific range for a modest loss of speed.
fEN97ySfzA9jujCJ3YFG: Behind the drag curve, below VMD, induced drag dominates and rises steeply as speed falls - so slowing down requires MORE thrust, not less. This reversed relationship makes the speed unstable: any decay increases drag, which decays the speed further unless thrust is added promptly. It is why an approach flown too slow demands continuous thrust attention.
fewS8R7CBjpIN4UYWQA7: Both are leading-edge high-lift devices and both raise the stalling angle of attack, so that is not the distinction. The difference is geometric: a SLAT moves forward on tracks and leaves a SLOT between itself and the wing, through which high-energy air is ducted onto the upper surface. A Krueger flap hinges down and forward from the lower surface, increasing camber but forming no slot.
FHdINP60JFF9OgrlmEFg: The climb is flown at an indicated airspeed, and wind has no effect on the aeroplane's performance relative to the AIR - so the time to climb, the fuel burnt and the height gained are all unchanged. What changes is the groundspeed: a headwind means less ground covered in the same climb time, so the top of climb occurs earlier along the route.
FiWhDgxLogYVL3U1m0mV: The dispatch rule for a turbojet is that the landing distance required must not exceed 60% of the landing distance available on a dry runway, with a further 15% added if the runway is expected to be wet. Note the other traps here: the landing distance is measured from a 50 ft screen height (35 ft is the TAKE-OFF screen); reverse thrust is generally NOT credited on a dry runway; and an anti-skid failure lengthens the required distance considerably.
fIx8LMf86nxEfNx0WcSN: A normal shock stands perpendicular to the flow, so the airflow does not change direction - it simply decelerates abruptly from supersonic to SUBSONIC. Static pressure, density and temperature all rise sharply across it while total pressure falls, and that total pressure loss is wave drag. An OBLIQUE shock does turn the flow and can leave it still supersonic; an expansion wave accelerates it.
FKGOpixQL5kKBGlrtebT: Yawing left swings the STARBOARD wing forward, so it meets the air at a higher relative speed while the port wing slows. More speed means more lift on the starboard wing, and the aeroplane rolls to PORT - the direction of the yaw. This yaw-induced roll is 'further effect of rudder', and it is one half of the coupling that produces Dutch roll.
FktZwNhP26P2f9qJ0tAX: Maximum level IAS occurs where the excess thrust or power is greatest at high speed - and for a piston engine, power output falls off steadily with altitude as density drops, while the drag at a given IAS does not change. So the greatest speed capability is at the LOWEST altitude, where the engine can produce most power. Note the contrast with maximum TAS, which occurs higher up.
fLiE6X3NBoOSaygxoZhB: Climb angle is governed by the excess of thrust over drag, divided by weight: sin(gamma) = (T - D)/W. All three quantities therefore appear. Lift does not enter, because in a steady climb lift merely balances the component of weight perpendicular to the flight path - which is why the question specifies that the required lift exists.
fLXTtUpnRPwhqhED1Cro: Dutch roll appears when the dihedral effect (lateral stability) is strong relative to the fin's weathercock effect (directional stability): a sideslip produces a powerful rolling moment before the aeroplane has straightened out, so roll and yaw drive one another in an oscillation. Swept-wing jets are prone to it, which is why they carry yaw dampers. The opposite imbalance gives spiral instability.
fNYq2K6UhlHscazezEAV: For a turbojet, the landing distance required at destination must not exceed 60% of the landing distance available on a dry runway (70% for a turboprop), with a further 15% added if the runway is expected to be wet. The certified landing distance is measured from a 50 ft screen height, not 35 ft; reverse thrust is normally not credited on a dry runway; and an anti-skid failure lengthens the distance materially.
fOvMFt78mPMzVTBVf64d: Laminar flow consists of smooth parallel layers sliding over one another with no mixing between them, so there is no velocity component perpendicular to the surface. That lack of mixing gives low skin friction but leaves very little energy near the wall, which is why a laminar layer separates far more readily than a turbulent one when it meets an adverse pressure gradient.
fQATcwJMnRrZzvM0msmf: The tyre speed limit caps the GROUNDSPEED at lift-off, and the lift-off groundspeed is set by the lift-off IAS (a function of mass and configuration) and the wind - not by how quickly the aeroplane got there. A downhill slope shortens the ground run but the aeroplane still leaves the ground at the same speed, so a tyre-speed-limited mass is unaffected. Slope matters when the limit is field length or brake energy.
FTQV1LSnWyOfrUf8p1s2: Range over the ground depends on ground nautical miles per kilogram of fuel. In a headwind, flying slower means spending longer in the wind and losing more ground for every kilogram burnt, so the optimum shifts to a HIGHER airspeed - the aeroplane cuts its exposure to the headwind. In a tailwind the reverse applies: slow down and let the wind do more of the work.
FTXTIgN2n7eBpvrHYT2y: A shock wave is a violent compression in which much of the flow's kinetic energy is converted into heat, so the static temperature rises sharply across it. The local speed of sound depends only on temperature - it is proportional to the square root of absolute temperature - so it INCREASES. Static pressure and density also rise; only total pressure falls, and that loss is wave drag.
FU9vXY7xoHhajFrkjuo8: At low subsonic speeds the flow is treated as incompressible, which means by definition that density does not change: rho1 = rho2. The continuity equation then reduces to area times velocity being constant, so a change in cross-section is accommodated entirely by a change in SPEED. Only above about M0.4 do density changes become significant enough to matter.
fupgaOftxp9xFE0vuXC2: The CS-25 gust envelope pairs a specific gust velocity with each design speed: 66 ft/s at VB (rough air speed), 50 ft/s at VC (design cruising speed) and 25 ft/s at VD (design dive speed). The gust velocity reduces as the design speed rises because the load a gust produces is proportional to airspeed, so a smaller gust reaches the same structural limit.
FV8wI82Y4ZXqtgTiG9wp: The stabiliser setting is scheduled against CG, and a FORWARD CG calls for a nose-UP setting to help rotation. Pairing a forward CG with the maximum nose-DOWN setting is therefore a mismatch that works against the pilot twice over, so the rotation demands abnormally high stick force and may be sluggish. Note the contrast with an aft CG, where the nose-down end of the band IS the correct setting.
fvqT5aFG2Yw3YpucwWSz: In incompressible subsonic flow, continuity requires area multiplied by velocity to remain constant - so an increasing area means a DECREASING speed. Bernoulli then says the static pressure rises to compensate, which is how a diffuser works. Note that above M1.0 this reverses entirely: a diverging duct accelerates supersonic flow, which is why a convergent-divergent nozzle is needed.
fz0lBlGNTKssNhSWxmJC: A spoiler is a plate raised from the upper surface that deliberately separates the flow behind it. Destroying the suction over the rear of the upper surface reduces CL, while the large wake it creates increases CD - so it does BOTH at once. That dual action is why spoilers serve three roles: roll control, in-flight speed brake, and lift dump on landing to put weight on the wheels.
fzoJweUmmt1soZkqvxx4: Statement 1 is correct: positive static longitudinal stability requires the neutral point to lie BEHIND the CG, and the distance between them is the static margin. Statement 2 is incorrect: camber produces a pitching moment coefficient that is essentially CONSTANT with angle of attack, and a constant moment cannot generate a restoring moment that varies with disturbance - so camber contributes nothing to stability. The wing's stabilising contribution comes from CG position relative to the aerodynamic centre, not from camber.
g7kpHnEzmCejEE70cbOB: A forward CG demands a large tailplane download to raise the nose, so the forward limit is set by whether the ELEVATOR can still do the job - enough authority to rotate at VR and to flare at touchdown - and, in a mechanically controlled aeroplane, by whether the stick force needed remains within certified limits. Engine thrust and location affect the pitching moment but do not define the CG limits.
g8CVY9YoxoRpbHFh5Iwl: V1 is the decision speed: at or above it, the take-off MUST be continued, because the accelerate-stop distance is no longer guaranteed to be available. Below V1 the take-off is rejected. That is the whole purpose of defining V1 - to remove the decision from the moment of the failure and settle it in advance. Rejecting above V1 is a classic overrun scenario.
GAtjIovFpSROoW0qcrpd: A forward CG requires a larger nose-up balancing moment from the tail, which means a greater tail DOWNLOAD. The wing must then generate the weight plus that download, so it flies at a higher lift coefficient and produces more induced drag - and more drag means more fuel per mile. This is why operators load toward the aft CG limit where the schedule and stability requirements permit.
gb6KaqRSdfjcseubh13r: The fuselage is destabilising in pitch: at a positive angle of attack the pressure distribution along a slender body produces a moment that tends to increase the angle further. The wing may be stabilising or destabilising depending on CG position, and the tailplane is strongly stabilising - large enough to overcome the fuselage and leave a net positive static margin.
GbGKAVpWnqSt4OLpOSNV: As angle of attack increases the oncoming flow meets the aerofoil from further below, so the stagnation point migrates DOWN and aft along the lower surface. At the same time the suction peak on the upper surface sharpens and moves FORWARD toward the leading edge, which is also why the centre of pressure moves forward on a cambered section. Stagnation point movement is what a flapper-switch stall warner senses.
gBm1646cMHSq0auYWbe2: A normal shock is an abrupt, irreversible compression: the flow decelerates from supersonic to subsonic and much of its kinetic energy is converted to heat, so static TEMPERATURE, pressure and density all INCREASE across it. Velocity decreases. The only property that falls is TOTAL pressure, and that loss is what constitutes wave drag.
GdGPbkUFMP1BI9Qj0hRE: As the centre of pressure moves aft, the distance between it and the CG grows, lengthening the arm of the restoring moment. A larger restoring moment for a given pitch disturbance is by definition greater static longitudinal STABILITY. The same rearward shift is what produces the nose-down Mach tuck, so the aeroplane becomes both more stable and harder to hold in trim.
geh1jHjGKUZRGGiCSlif: Retracting flap reduces camber and therefore reduces the lift coefficient at a given angle of attack. If alpha is held constant, the lift simply falls below the weight and the aeroplane sinks. The correct technique is to allow the aeroplane to accelerate, or to raise the angle of attack, as the flaps come in - which is why flap retraction is scheduled against speed rather than done arbitrarily.
gG9fgHEezlToZdWIfdTS: Newton's third law: the engine turns the propeller to the right, so the propeller applies an equal and opposite reaction to the airframe, rolling it to the LEFT. The effect is greatest at high power and low airspeed - take-off - where it adds to slipstream effect and asymmetric blade effect to produce the familiar left-yawing and left-rolling tendency countered by right rudder.
GIWSVlbv2EtD6kBw1TIM: Sweeping the wing means only the airflow component perpendicular to the quarter-chord line does the aerodynamic work, so the effective velocity over the aerofoil section is reduced by the cosine of the sweep angle. The local flow therefore reaches M1.0 only at a higher free-stream Mach number, raising Mcrit. Increasing aspect ratio actually lowers Mcrit slightly, and dihedral affects only lateral stability.
gKfiFwsB8ZISaBzEJrgU: Induced drag arises from the downwash produced in generating lift, and in level flight the lift is fixed at the weight - so the lift coefficient needed varies as 1/V2, and induced drag varies as 1/V2 as well. It therefore dominates at low speed and falls away rapidly as speed builds, which is exactly the opposite of parasite drag's V2 behaviour.
GoSpYoy3q12S1LTFZ1N6: A propeller aeroplane's fuel flow is broadly proportional to POWER, and power is drag times speed - so best range means least drag per mile, which is the (L/D)max condition. In level flight lift equals weight, so maximum L/D and minimum drag are the same point. Note the contrast with a JET, whose fuel flow follows thrust and whose best range lies at a higher speed, around 1.32 x VMD.
gpj0L7qz0UEO7TnZinjG: Minimum drag occurs at the fixed angle of attack giving (L/D)max, so Dmin = W / (L/D)max - reduce the weight and the minimum drag falls in proportion. The speed at which that angle of attack is achieved also falls, because less lift is needed: VMD in IAS is proportional to the square root of weight. Both therefore decrease together.
gpSoWIJ4Z3dEWkgh6KE9: Drift down performance is weight-limited, so if the calculated level-off altitude will not clear the terrain, the only way to raise it is to reduce weight - and the only weight available to shed in flight is fuel. Jettisoning must begin at the START of the drift down, so the weight reduction takes effect while the descent is still in progress; waiting until the obstacle altitude is reached would be far too late.
GR2HDZcf13OkbeDOjk7e: Drag = CD x 1/2 rho V2 x S, so drag varies with the SQUARE of the airspeed. Multiplying the velocity by 4 multiplies the drag by 4 squared = 16. This square law is why parasite drag climbs so steeply at high speed and why small speed reductions in turbulence produce large reductions in airframe loading.
gs2sXjYmE4LspDF3V1OQ: An expansion wave is an isentropic acceleration of supersonic flow around a convex corner, and static pressure, density and temperature all DECREASE steadily through it. Velocity and Mach number increase. There is no reversal at any Mach number - the monotonic decrease is precisely what distinguishes an expansion fan from a shock wave, across which all three properties rise abruptly.
gwtPiUsHsHHlOWeVCtMn: Static directional stability is the weathercock tendency. In a sideslip to the right the relative airflow arrives from the right and strikes the fin, generating a sideforce that pushes the TAIL to the left - and since the fin is well behind the CG, that swings the NOSE to the right, into the relative airflow, until the sideslip is eliminated.
gyqUMhsu56bBSV2btuQ7: Induced drag coefficient is proportional to CL squared divided by aspect ratio, so the two are inversely related: DECREASING aspect ratio INCREASES induced drag. A short, stubby wing has tips that dominate a large proportion of the span, so the tip vortices affect more of the wing and the downwash is greater. This is why efficiency-driven designs - gliders, long-range transports - use long slender wings.
h1u6hUK7aKwhXd1N6xAo: Raising a spoiler deliberately separates the flow behind it, destroying the suction over the rear of the upper surface. That reduces CL while the large turbulent wake increases CD - both at once. The dual action is what makes spoilers useful in three distinct roles: asymmetric deployment for roll control, symmetric deployment as an in-flight speed brake, and full deployment on landing to dump lift onto the wheels.
H1yT7XBkwYd5J3y6BrtF: Holding the highest possible altitude on one engine means minimising the thrust required, and thrust required is at its least where DRAG is at its least - the angle of attack giving (L/D)max. Any other speed needs more thrust than the remaining engine can spare for level flight, so the aeroplane will drift down further. Long range speed is faster than this and would cost altitude.
heEL9jGEJduCzPXVaKQX: The manoeuvring limit load factor is a fixed figure laid down in the regulations - 2.5 for a large transport aeroplane. The gust limit load factor is CALCULATED, and depends on wing loading, lift curve slope, aspect ratio, airspeed and altitude, so it varies from aeroplane to aeroplane and from moment to moment. In a severe gust at high speed it can exceed the manoeuvring figure, which is why the gust envelope may extend outside the manoeuvring envelope.
HeQ5R38dA17G3Z2kzvLV: Trimming for a higher speed means trimming nose-DOWN, which requires the elevator to sit further down. A trim tab always works in the OPPOSITE sense to the surface it drives: deflecting the tab UP generates a download at the tab that levers the elevator DOWN. So the visible change is an up-deflected tab with the elevator further down.
hGtAMHCmc56oMRVOOjyO: A higher OAT means less dense air, so a given indicated airspeed corresponds to a higher TRUE airspeed - and therefore a higher groundspeed at V1. Kinetic energy rises with the square of speed, so the brakes must absorb more energy in a rejected take-off, and the brake-energy-limited mass falls. The same density loss lengthens the take-off distance and reduces the climb-limited and field-length-limited masses too.
Hh0HlBEHDvMNc8JSJZgW: Higher pressure altitude means lower density, which reduces thrust and requires a higher TAS to achieve the lift-off IAS - so the take-off distance lengthens and the mass that fits within the available field length falls. The climb-limited mass falls too. Pressure altitude penalises essentially every take-off limit; only the tyre-speed limit can behave differently.
HjHI0vqUIwfEwe5i5txm: Both statements are correct. Flutter is a divergent oscillation driven by the coupling of aerodynamic, inertial and elastic forces, and it only occurs above a critical speed - so reducing IAS immediately is the correct and only response. Stiffening the structure raises that critical speed, which is why flutter resistance is designed in through wing stiffness and mass balancing of control surfaces.
hJIDJvY2EIJRc1kJ4DRR: Above Mcrit a shock wave forms, and the energy dissipated across it - kinetic energy converted irreversibly into heat, showing up as a total pressure loss - constitutes WAVE DRAG. Adding the boundary layer separation behind the shock, drag rises very steeply indeed with Mach number. Skin friction and interference drag are present at all speeds and do not account for the transonic drag rise.
hkwwm8GKEvsPX3uNfKH0: Power required is drag multiplied by speed, so the minimum of that product occurs at a LOWER speed than the minimum of drag alone - typically about 76% of VMD. Minimum power is the speed for maximum endurance in a PROPELLER aeroplane and for minimum rate of descent in a glide; minimum drag is the speed for maximum endurance in a JET. The two are distinct and minimum power is always the slower.
HLaqTFm2YgY98mlcm9Cp: Vortex generators are small vanes that trip the boundary layer turbulent, mixing high-energy free-stream air down toward the skin. That extra energy allows the layer to survive the steep adverse pressure gradient behind a shock wave, so shock-induced separation - and the Mach buffet and control degradation that follow - is delayed to a higher Mach number. They cost a little parasite drag, which is a price worth paying.
HLYRF8V2OzK4PWUskoao: The crossover altitude is where the constant-IAS schedule and the constant-Mach schedule give the same true airspeed. A HIGHER climb IAS reaches any given Mach number at a LOWER altitude, so raising the IAS from 280 to 290 while holding M0.74 brings the crossover DOWN. Above the crossover the aeroplane flies Mach, below it flies IAS.
hmrbYBBgNejPxgfpnfSC: Drag = CD x 1/2 rho V2 x S, so drag varies with the SQUARE of airspeed. A fourfold increase in velocity therefore multiplies the drag by 4 squared = 16. It is worth noting the contrast with FRONTAL AREA, which appears to the first power - tripling the area only triples the drag.
hnai52uUYJwcoXbFyyLK: On a positively cambered aerofoil, increasing the angle of attack sharpens the suction peak on the upper surface and draws it toward the leading edge, so the centre of pressure moves FORWARD. Because the CP moves toward the leading edge as lift increases, a cambered wing on its own is longitudinally unstable - which is one reason a tailplane is needed. At the stall the CP then jumps sharply aft.
HtcAuwQ8aJgWP5wTdnSp: Aerodynamic balance uses the airflow itself to reduce the hinge moment the pilot must overcome: servo and spring tabs generate an aerodynamic force that helps move the surface, and a seal between the wing trailing edge and the control surface leading edge preserves the pressure differential that assists deflection. MASS balance is a different thing entirely - a weight forward of the hinge line, fitted to prevent flutter, not to reduce control forces.
hTRMm84mbj8QnhlgMwer: Stall speed rises with the SQUARE ROOT of the load factor. At 45 degrees of bank n = 1/cos 45 = 1.41, and the square root of 1.41 is 1.19 - so the stall speed increases by about 19%. Note the trap: 41% is the increase in LIFT (the load factor itself), not in stall speed. At 60 degrees n = 2 and the stall speed rises by 41%.
Htrs6oPblabUdKqQJTpb: Where the thrust available curve crosses the drag (thrust required) curve, thrust exactly equals drag, so there is no unbalanced force along the flight path - the aeroplane is in equilibrium at constant speed in level flight. There are normally two such intersections, one on each side of VMD: a low-speed one behind the drag curve and a high-speed one, the maximum level speed.
HTs54Jle780KBneqMqpZ: For a jet, thrust available is roughly constant with speed, so the maximum EXCESS thrust - and hence the best climb ANGLE - occurs where drag is least, at VMD. Maximum endurance for a jet is also at VMD, since fuel flow follows thrust. Maximum range lies higher, at about 1.32 x VMD. So the ascending order is Vs, then the max angle of climb speed, then the max range speed.
Hue3fu99J4B8OK0MpSX4: Adverse yaw arises because the down-going aileron adds more induced drag than the up-going one removes, yawing the aeroplane away from the turn. Differential deflection fixes it at source by rigging the UP-going aileron to travel further than the down-going one, equalising the drag. Frise ailerons and rudder-aileron interconnects achieve the same end by other means.
HxgVbKRyqqLDCQQuEgFD: Climb gradient is height gained divided by horizontal distance travelled through the AIR, expressed as a percentage - an air-mass quantity, so it is unaffected by wind. Only when the gradient is measured over the GROUND does wind matter, and it is the ground gradient that determines obstacle clearance. Rate of climb, by contrast, is height gained per unit time.
hyZHPFiqnSvMuN5mKUBU: The standard erect spin recovery is: close the throttle, centralise the AILERONS, apply full opposite rudder, then move the control column progressively FORWARD to unstall the wing, and centralise the rudder as rotation stops. Ailerons must be neutral because any deflection at high alpha aggravates the autorotation, and the stick goes forward - holding it fully aft is what sustains the spin.
HZrtr8LIf3IdCxIZdwfv: A shock is called NORMAL when it stands perpendicular to the local flow direction, which is what distinguishes it from an oblique shock. Because it is perpendicular, it does not turn the flow - it simply decelerates it from supersonic to subsonic. Across it the static pressure, density and temperature all RISE abruptly; only total pressure falls, and that loss is wave drag.
I1JP7okftWTqVbCP8vi6: Swirling debris on final marks a thermal, and a thermal is rising air that will balloon the glider above the intended path while its outflow lower down can produce a sudden sink and airspeed loss on the far side. Closing the spoilers restores the glide performance in hand, and the extra airspeed provides a margin against the shear and sink - the same reasoning as adding a wind gradient allowance.
I6ivxB6tgBglyowHgkuF: Pushing the rpm lever forward commands HIGH rpm, which the governor achieves by selecting FINE pitch. A fine-pitched propeller windmilling at idle presents a large effective disc to the airflow and generates considerable drag, so total drag rises, L/D falls and the rate of descent increases. This is why the forced-landing drill selects COARSE pitch - to minimise windmilling drag and stretch the glide.
IAYeWjzaaIfbR4T7TjiA: Dutch roll is a coupled lateral-directional oscillation arising from strong dihedral effect relative to directional stability, and it has nothing to do with compressibility - it can occur at any speed. Mach buffet, shock stall and tuck under all require a shock wave, and a shock cannot exist until the local flow reaches M1.0, which is by definition the critical Mach number.
iBbuEU5fsgfy8RGEwbhj: Both statements are correct. VMCL is the minimum control speed in the landing configuration with the critical engine inoperative. Crucially, the certification criterion is not merely holding the aeroplane straight but retaining adequate ROLL capability - the aeroplane must be able to roll from a steady 5 degree sideslip to 20 degrees of bank in not more than 5 seconds - so roll rate can indeed be the limiting factor.
IDCHQ5thixJ1NSrQ1eMe: As Mach number rises toward Mcrit the aft shift of the centre of pressure produces a nose-down tuck, which means the pilot has to PUSH less - or even pull - as speed increases: the stick force gradient goes flat or reverses, destroying apparent speed stability. The Mach trimmer senses Mach number and applies an automatic nose-up input to restore a positive stick force gradient. It corrects the trim change, not the drag or the buffet.
iEeozKrjjumJNXPByJxT: Pulling up from a dive increases the load factor, and the stall speed rises with the square root of n - so the wing can stall at a much higher speed than its 1g value. This is the accelerated stall. The other options all reduce the stall speed: less weight needs less lift, and retracting spoilers restores lift that had been destroyed. Modest altitude changes have little effect on the stalling IAS.
ieJpV2TEIoFYSsNJfIND: Tuck under, or Mach tuck, is the nose-DOWN pitching tendency that appears as speed rises into the transonic region. Two effects combine: the shock wave moves the centre of pressure aft, and shock-induced separation reduces the downwash at the tailplane. It is insidious because the nose-down pitch increases the Mach number further, so the tendency reinforces itself - hence the Mach trim system.
IFtYnzA8G80AiYkMoL20: Sweepback exists to raise the critical Mach number: only the airflow component perpendicular to the quarter-chord line does the aerodynamic work, so the effective velocity over the section is reduced by the cosine of the sweep angle and the flow reaches M1.0 only at a higher free-stream Mach number. The penalties are a HIGHER stalling speed, tip-stall tendencies, and a strong dihedral effect that encourages Dutch roll.
IJPzezETUeluzJG8PuTu: A weight-shift wing carries substantial washout, so the tips are set at a much lower angle of attack than the root. When the root stalls the tips are still flying, which preserves roll damping and generates the nose-down pitching moment that begins the recovery automatically. That built-in tip margin is the basic stall-safety feature of the flexible-wing planform.
ILIYe8zprnhR4JG6ez3W: A higher V1 means accelerating further before the decision point, so more distance is used getting there and more speed - hence more kinetic energy - has to be dissipated in the stop. The accelerate-stop distance therefore lengthens. The continued-take-off distances all SHORTEN with a higher V1, because the failure is recognised closer to rotation. This opposition is what makes V1 a balancing act between the stop case and the go case.
IpFfJ4M5sO4fAT61MTSS: VA is the speed at which the aeroplane stalls at exactly the limit manoeuvring load factor, and since stall speed rises with the square root of load factor, VA = VS x sqrt(n). For a large transport aeroplane the positive limit load factor is 2.5, so VA = VS x sqrt(2.5), about 1.58 VS. Below VA a single full elevator deflection stalls the wing before it overstresses the structure.
iPGfmE6mdXkZGV6105t4: Relative (or percentage) thickness is the maximum thickness of the aerofoil expressed as a percentage of the CHORD - a dimensionless ratio, so aerofoils of different sizes can be compared directly. Typical values run from about 18% on a light aircraft to 8-12% on a transport jet, where thin sections are used to raise the critical Mach number.
IQjiUmEtez9SMhhBXVXL: Static stability is about the INITIAL response: the aeroplane starts back toward its original condition, so it is statically stable - if it were statically unstable it would diverge rather than oscillate. Dynamic stability is about what happens over time: an oscillation of constant amplitude neither damps nor diverges, which is dynamically NEUTRAL. Note that static stability is a prerequisite for dynamic stability, but not a guarantee of it.
Ir9DgtQW1WNdNqH3MkbN: Mach number is TAS divided by the local speed of sound, and the speed of sound depends only on temperature. Climbing in the troposphere the temperature falls steadily, so the speed of sound falls, and with TAS held constant the Mach number must INCREASE. This is why a climb at constant TAS or IAS steadily eats into the Mach margin and eventually runs into MMO.
irUe1HAN4wNsjG6NtPSJ: In a servo tab system the pilot's controls move only the tab, and the tab then flies the elevator. If the ELEVATOR jams, the tab still responds to the stick - but it is now acting as a tiny control surface in its own right, and its aerodynamic force acts in the OPPOSITE sense to the elevator deflection it would normally have commanded. The result is pitch control that is both greatly weakened and reversed in direction.
itNm2XYHOqhJAWt4kiBC: With the CG BEHIND the centre of pressure, the wing's lift acts ahead of the CG and therefore produces a nose-UP moment. To balance it, the tailplane - which is behind the CG - must generate an UPWARD force, since an upward force aft of the CG gives a nose-down moment. This is the aft-CG case, and it is why an aft CG reduces trim drag: the tail is helping to carry the weight rather than pushing down against it.
iVjOYqLZWYMoL1IVvUds: Deploying flap increases the camber of the section (and on a Fowler flap the area as well), which shifts the whole CL-alpha curve up and to the left. So at any given angle of attack the lift coefficient is HIGHER with flap out. This is why lift increases and the aeroplane balloons if the attitude is not adjusted as flap is selected. Note that flap also LOWERS the stalling angle.
IWRF5HyJ10nFQoWBivTV: Induced drag is proportional to lift squared divided by speed squared, so both effects work the same way: flying FASTER means a smaller lift coefficient and much less induced drag, and being LIGHTER means less lift required and therefore less induced drag. Both increasing speed and reducing weight decrease induced drag.
IxgrJyFFxmV754cvZ50T: Climbing at a constant Mach number, the falling density outweighs the small fall in the speed of sound, so the dynamic pressure decreases steadily. With the same weight to support and less dynamic pressure to do it, the lift coefficient - and therefore the angle of attack - must INCREASE. That rising alpha is why the buffet margin narrows with altitude and why the aeroplane eventually reaches its aerodynamic ceiling.
iy1L90ZgYglgkCXdnVy9: A left turn requires the LEFT aileron to go UP and the right to go DOWN. Differential rigging then makes the up-going aileron travel FURTHER than the down-going one, so the extra parasite drag from the raised surface offsets the extra induced drag from the lowered one - cancelling adverse yaw. Left 5 up with right 2 down satisfies both the direction and the differential.
IZfs2guCRXonvcfJGbNM: The critical (stalling) angle of attack is a fixed aerodynamic property of the aerofoil and configuration - typically around 15-16 degrees for a conventional section - and it does not change with weight, CG position, load factor or altitude. What those variables change is the SPEED at which that angle is reached. This is exactly why a wing can be stalled at any speed and in any attitude, and why stall protection systems sense alpha rather than airspeed.
IZLaGmOYyB8SDlpH631T: The turn needle shows RATE OF TURN, and the aeroplane is flying straight, so it reads zero. The ball shows the resultant of gravity and any lateral acceleration: with the wings level and a straight flight path there is no lateral acceleration and gravity acts along the aeroplane's vertical axis, so the ball is centred too. Note that centred ball with wings level does NOT mean zero sideslip - the aeroplane is in fact slipping, which is why the drag-minimising technique is a small bank toward the live engine with the ball slightly displaced.
j3vbgqBvVbKVmr7aHwfp: Static longitudinal stability is read from the slope of the pitching moment coefficient against angle of attack (or CL): a NEGATIVE slope means that an increase in angle of attack produces a nose-down restoring moment, which is stability. A positive slope is instability and a zero slope is neutral stability, the neutral point. The steeper the negative slope, the greater the static margin and the more sluggish the aeroplane in pitch.
j4hVWfOvTJogDSzp0qji: A swept wing generates a spanwise flow toward the tips, which thickens the boundary layer out there and makes the tips stall first - producing a pitch-up at the stall and a loss of aileron authority. A boundary layer fence is a chordwise plate that physically blocks that spanwise drift, keeping the outboard boundary layer thin. It is therefore a LOW-SPEED fix, addressing stall behaviour rather than compressibility.
j7kALxtuBnSo0VR1gu5V: A turbulent boundary layer continuously mixes high-energy free-stream air down toward the surface, so it has far more kinetic energy near the wall and can fight an adverse pressure gradient much longer before separating. That resistance to separation is its great advantage - and the reason vortex generators deliberately trip the flow turbulent. The price is a thicker layer and higher skin friction drag.
J7pUjbgFAuz7IC5DXxK2: With an engine out the aeroplane must descend to a lower altitude where the remaining engines can sustain level flight, and it flies there at a less efficient combination of speed and altitude. The dead engine adds drag if it is windmilling, and the rudder and small bank needed to balance the asymmetry add more. All of that reduces the miles flown per kilogram of fuel, so specific range is degraded.
j83D5tM9ulJLYVNLhRQC: A forward CG needs a larger tailplane DOWNLOAD, and the wing must then produce the weight plus that download - flying at a higher lift coefficient and therefore more induced drag. Moving the CG aft reduces the download required, so the wing carries less, induced drag falls, and the power or thrust needed comes down with it. This is why operators load toward the aft limit where the schedule permits.
J9aU0UEd5mdjU1hJEmBs: Stall speed rises with the SQUARE ROOT of the load factor. At 60 degrees of bank n = 1/cos 60 = 2.0, and the square root of 2 is 1.41 - so the stall speed increases by 41%. This is the standard reference point to memorise, along with 45 degrees (n = 1.41, stall speed up 19%) and 30 degrees (n = 1.15, stall speed up 7%).
jbhdZXNVlcoRAvqQOz2w: A Fowler flap moves aft as well as down, so it adds lift well behind the original centre of pressure - shifting the whole lift distribution rearward. A lift increment behind the CG produces a nose-DOWN pitching moment, and the increased downwash at the tailplane adds to it. This is the trim change felt on flap selection, and it is why flap is normally deployed in stages.
JC1eTcgLvrfXnwXz4Umj: Raising a spoiler separates the flow behind it, destroying the suction over the rear of the upper surface. At any given angle of attack that reduces CL while the large turbulent wake increases CD - both at once, which is what makes spoilers effective speed brakes. On landing they also do the opposite of not affecting braking: by dumping lift they transfer weight onto the wheels, which is exactly what makes wheel braking work.
JcvWa9KJ9B2ZLlHvstiL: The tyre speed limit is a structural limit on how fast the tyre carcass may rotate, so it constrains the GROUNDSPEED at which the aeroplane leaves the ground - that is, VLOF expressed as a groundspeed. Airspeed is irrelevant to the tyre. A strong tailwind or a hot-and-high aerodrome both raise the groundspeed for a given IAS, which is when tyre speed becomes limiting.
JfjaLoHniBlZJtA4Z31m: Slats give the largest single CLmax increment of any high-lift device, because they act on the mechanism that actually limits CLmax - boundary layer separation - by ducting high-energy air onto the upper surface and RAISING the stalling angle of attack by 5-10 degrees. Trailing-edge flaps raise CLmax by adding camber but LOWER the stalling angle, and each successive flap stage yields less lift and more drag than the one before.
jGlIaaJQGmSB4L55o9Bh: A large transport aeroplane has to be trimmed over an enormous range of speed, weight and CG, and a small trim tab simply cannot generate enough hinge moment to hold the elevator where it is needed at the extremes - particularly with full flap at a forward CG. Moving the entire stabiliser provides essentially unlimited trim authority, and it leaves the full elevator travel available for manoeuvring rather than spending part of it on trim.
Jhfn3s0ACTr4BsYlfdmu: The bow wave is a detached shock standing ahead of the aeroplane, and it appears once the FREE STREAM reaches M1.0 - at that point pressure disturbances can no longer propagate ahead of the aircraft and pile up into a shock. Note the distinction from Mcrit, which is where the LOCAL flow somewhere on the airframe first reaches M1.0 and a shock forms ON the surface.
JmiwNxCij1WamViimnym: Moving the CG aft shortens the moment arm to the tailplane, so a given elevator deflection produces more pitching moment and less stick force is needed per g. Beyond the aft limit that stick force per g falls below the certified minimum, leaving the aeroplane dangerously easy to over-stress with almost no force cue that it is happening. Static longitudinal stability falls too, and spin recovery becomes worse, not better.
jNpllTVBt8CggWt60B6f: Spanwise flow toward the tips thickens the outboard boundary layer, so a swept wing stalls at the TIPS first. Because the tips are well aft of the CG on a swept planform, losing their lift moves the centre of pressure FORWARD, producing a nose-UP pitching moment that drives the angle of attack higher still - a self-worsening divergence. It also costs aileron authority. Fences, vortex generators, washout and stick pushers are the usual countermeasures.
JqwskIkhMt8rOhAPEJve: Lift and drag are defined relative to the RELATIVE AIRFLOW, not to the airframe or the horizon: drag acts parallel to it, opposing the motion, and lift perpendicular to it. This is why the lift vector rotates with the flight path - tilted forward in a climb, and tilted into the turn when banked, which is what provides the turning force.
JRo64S4JnMEIe01Bx7Iz: The area rule states that transonic wave drag depends chiefly on how the total cross-sectional area of the whole aircraft varies along its length, so that distribution must change as smoothly as possible. Waisting the fuselage where the wing joins - the classic 'coke bottle' shape - compensates for the wing's area and smooths the curve, cutting WAVE drag substantially. It has no effect on induced, form or skin friction drag.
JrQYR1XIcxHnhKHmJxjw: Stall speed rises with the square root of load factor: Vs(n) = Vs x sqrt(n) = 100 x sqrt(1.5) = 100 x 1.22 = 122 kt. Note that 1.5 g corresponds to about 48 degrees of bank in a level turn, and that the relationship is the reason a steep turn at low speed is so much more hazardous than the bank angle alone suggests.
JtNGf9RnfQn3yDlPl4mn: V2 must be at least 1.1 VMCA - a 10% margin - so that adequate directional control remains available with the critical engine inoperative during the second segment climb. V2 must simultaneously satisfy the stall margin requirement (1.2 VS or 1.13 VSR depending on the aeroplane), and the higher of the two floors governs. At high flap settings VMCA is often the binding one.
jwbs2tRFXCkEwkBXjDnL: A slotted flap does two things at once: hinging down increases the CAMBER of the section, and the slot that opens between the wing and the flap ducts high-energy air from the lower surface onto the flap's upper surface, re-energising the BOUNDARY LAYER so it resists separation. The combination gives a much larger CLmax increase than a plain flap of the same deflection. It does not raise the critical angle of attack - that is what slats do.
jwlG9gkHWSGIuldjVcMB: Angle of attack is the angle between the CHORD LINE of the aerofoil and the RELATIVE AIRFLOW (free stream direction). It is not measured against the fuselage - that fixed angle is the angle of INCIDENCE - nor against the horizon, which gives the pitch attitude. The distinction matters because an aeroplane can be at a high angle of attack in a nose-down attitude, which is how a high-speed stall happens.
jXffBMRvCULcZ7njDyDi: Induced drag coefficient is proportional to CL squared divided by aspect ratio, so a HIGH aspect ratio wing produces LESS induced drag: its tips are a smaller proportion of the span, so the tip vortices influence less of the wing and the downwash is reduced. The trade-offs are greater structural weight and bending loads, and greater sensitivity to gusts, since a higher aspect ratio gives a steeper lift curve slope.
jyA72zELVaTawESCPlg4: A Fowler flap travels rearward on tracks and then rotates down, so it increases BOTH the wing AREA and the CAMBER - which is precisely why it produces the largest CLmax increase of any trailing-edge device. Because both terms in the lift equation grow, the early stages give a large lift gain for little drag (ideal for take-off) while the final stages add mostly drag.
jYEbUqyJ3d4YPyejFcai: The absolute ceiling is the altitude at which the excess thrust or power has fallen to zero, so the rate of climb is theoretically zero and only one speed - where VX and VY have converged - can be flown in level flight. It takes infinite time to reach, so the practical figure quoted is the SERVICE ceiling, defined by a residual rate of climb of 100 ft/min.
jYkdDioPcMdQ1ojqqKix: Where the AFM gives no specific wet-runway data, the required landing distance must be increased by 15% over the dry figure. That factor is applied on top of the normal dispatch factoring - 60% of LDA for a turbojet or 70% for a turboprop - so the two compound: a jet's wet requirement is effectively 1.67 x 1.15 = 1.92 times the demonstrated distance.
JYyqhRcNOFLRPkU5R2Yj: The SERVICE ceiling is defined by a residual all-engines rate of climb of 100 ft/min - a practical figure, since the absolute ceiling (zero rate of climb) would take infinite time to reach and leaves no manoeuvre capability at all. Both fall as weight or temperature increase, since both reduce the excess thrust available.
K3Tmuy4mJ57W5lkmEbED: Lift means higher pressure beneath the wing than above it, and at the tip - where the two regions meet around the end of the wing - the air simply flows from high to low pressure: from BENEATH the wing, around the WING TIP, to the top. That escaping flow rolls up into the tip vortex, which induces downwash over the wing and is the source of induced drag.
k6bsWEYSfjdftbn3zflh: At a constant Mach number and altitude the thrust required is essentially fixed, so the fuel flow follows the engine's specific fuel consumption - and a turbojet's SFC rises with the square root of the ambient absolute temperature. Hourly fuel consumption therefore INCREASES with T. (Of the options offered, only a directly proportional relationship captures that increasing behaviour; the exact dependence is on the square root of T.)
Kbh22DZWphHiXhq4kULY: With the CG BEHIND the centre of pressure, the wing's lift acts ahead of the CG and produces a nose-UP moment about it. Balancing that requires a nose-down moment from the tail, and since the tailplane sits aft of the CG, that means an UPWARD tail load. This is the aft-CG case, and the reason an aft CG reduces trim drag: the tailplane helps carry the weight instead of pushing down against it.
Kcz3rWqextnaJxflx4is: Take-off performance must be computed from the ACTUAL conditions, not standard ones: airport elevation and runway slope are physical properties of the runway, pressure altitude and outside air temperature together determine the density that governs thrust and lift, and the wind components determine the groundspeed and hence the distances. Using standard temperature or standard pressure would invalidate the whole calculation.
KdXRj9NXASr4UpEzXS8R: Newton's second law gives force = mass x acceleration, so the SI unit of force is the kilogram-metre per second squared, named the newton. For comparison: the pascal is N/m2 (pressure), the joule is N m (work or energy) and the watt is J/s (power). Reading off the base units is the fastest way to identify which quantity is meant.
KEa51sCK8ufBBFPdFz8Z: Adverse yaw arises because the down-going aileron generates more induced drag than the up-going one removes, yawing the aeroplane away from the intended turn. Differential rigging fixes it at source: the UP-going aileron is made to travel further than the down-going one, so the extra parasite drag it creates balances the extra induced drag on the other wing. Frise ailerons and rudder-aileron interconnects achieve the same end differently.
khyNOZqoOY0l0DUBGVYS: Both methods work by reducing how much the flow has to accelerate over the wing. A THIN aerofoil has less curvature, so the local velocity peak is lower and the flow reaches M1.0 only at a higher free-stream Mach number. SWEEPBACK means only the component of airflow perpendicular to the quarter-chord line does the work, reducing the effective velocity by the cosine of the sweep angle. Camber and dihedral do the opposite or nothing at all.
kIVtshhuDEbWgcyAKcMY: Both statements are wrong. VMCL is the minimum control speed in the LANDING configuration, so it is a go-around and approach limit, not a take-off one - VMCG and VMCA govern the take-off case. And VMCL is not 'always' rudder-limited: certification also requires the aeroplane to roll from a 5 degree sideslip to 20 degrees of bank within 5 seconds, so ROLL capability can be the limiting factor instead.
kk2YmZMPKtvE3W7c4Dln: There is no single fixed relationship. The stabiliser setting needed for trim is scheduled against CG position and configuration, and the elevator then takes up whatever residual position the current speed demands - so speed, flap and slat position and CG all enter. This is why the take-off trim setting is computed from the load sheet rather than being a fixed number, and why a take-off configuration warning system checks it.
Kko1K0QoB7nDyqX8T5GK: Drag = CD x 1/2 rho V2 x S, in which density appears to the FIRST power. Halving the density therefore halves the drag - a factor of 2. It is SPEED that appears squared; confusing the two is what produces the square-root and fourth-power distractors.
kn48Etw7aBkqnky21CfN: The Mach angle is given by arcsin(1/M), so as Mach number rises the angle gets smaller and the shock wave sweeps further back. At M1.0 the wave is perpendicular to the flow (90 degrees); at M2 it is 30 degrees. This is why supersonic aircraft need highly swept or delta wings - the whole wing must stay behind the Mach cone.
kPAnNW4u9d0bDwi9nXVf: By Newton's third law, the upward force on the wing must be matched by an equal downward momentum imparted to the air - so lift is produced by accelerating a mass of air DOWNWARDS. The Bernoulli pressure-difference description and this momentum description are two views of the same phenomenon, not competing explanations. Camber and airspeed affect how much lift is produced, but they are not the mechanism.
kpOjPCZvBfC3oEiWfpUQ: Cruising well below optimum altitude costs fuel, so it is only worth doing when the wind more than pays for it. Substantially less headwind or more tailwind lower down can improve the GROUND specific range enough to outweigh the aerodynamic penalty. Flying lower into MORE headwind would compound both losses, and temperature alone does not justify a 4000 ft descent.
kQeGfYl24atAfNRrEu2s: The stabiliser setting is scheduled against CG, and a FORWARD CG calls for a nose-UP setting to assist rotation. Pairing a forward CG with the maximum nose-DOWN setting therefore works against the pilot twice over, so rotation demands abnormally high stick force and may be sluggish. Note the contrast with an AFT CG, where the nose-down end of the green band is the correctly scheduled setting and rotation is normal.
kshg83lyZPC573p2Aj5C: A propeller blade is a small aerofoil, and like any aerofoil its angle of attack is measured between its chord line and the airflow it actually meets - the LOCAL air speed vector, which is the resultant of the aeroplane's forward speed and the blade's rotational speed. That resultant changes along the blade, which is why blades are twisted from root to tip to keep the angle of attack roughly constant.
KUn78s3ZmjZzjVs5oLKm: Adverse yaw is the yaw AWAY from the intended turn caused by the down-going aileron producing more induced drag than the up-going one. Differential deflection cures it by making the up-going aileron travel further, so its extra parasite drag offsets the other wing's extra induced drag. Aileron reversal is a high-speed wing-twisting problem, cured by inboard ailerons and spoilers instead.
kvr7fxtijb4bF7oOpv9Y: Sweep is stabilising in yaw. In a sideslip the leading wing presents a smaller effective sweep angle to the airflow, so it generates more drag (and more lift) than the trailing wing; the drag difference produces a yawing moment that turns the nose back into the airflow. The lift difference simultaneously produces a strong DIHEDRAL effect, which is why swept-wing aircraft are prone to Dutch roll.
kWvB33LE7i1MoFdAuD0R: The balanced field length is the condition where the accelerate-stop distance exactly equals the accelerate-go distance - achieved by choosing the V1 at which the two curves cross. Because the stop case shortens and the go case lengthens as V1 is reduced (and vice versa), the crossing point is the MINIMUM field length that satisfies both, which is what makes it the optimum for an engine failure case.
KXR4mVjq4tnoffKBM7Ys: Minimum fuel for a given distance means the greatest distance per kilogram of fuel - maximum specific range, which is the maximum range procedure. Long range cruise deliberately gives up 1% of that in exchange for speed, and maximum endurance maximises TIME aloft rather than distance, so it is the wrong target entirely when the aim is to get somewhere on the least fuel.
LBNDgpe38tmnaroJQhoF: Density is mass per unit volume, so kg/m3 - ISA sea-level density is 1.225 kg/m3. Force follows from F = ma, so its unit is the newton (kg m/s2). The distractors mix mass and force units: a kilogram is a mass, not a force, and N/m3 would be a weight density rather than a mass density.
ldLjDX0x8v1ajynziQjA: On a wet runway the accelerate-stop distance grows substantially, which would impose a heavy weight penalty. To offset it, the regulations permit the take-off distance to be measured to a reduced SCREEN HEIGHT of 15 ft instead of 35 ft, provided the net take-off flight path still meets the obstacle clearance requirement. Note also that wet-runway data may credit reverse thrust, so it cannot simply be used as published with a reverser inoperative.
ldxgk2mFqKWeRuOBR84n: Long range cruise is defined as the HIGHER of the two speeds that deliver 99% of the maximum specific range - so it is always faster than the maximum range speed. Because the specific range curve is very flat near its peak, that 1% fuel penalty typically buys 3-5% more speed, which is almost always worth it once crew time and schedule are costed in.
Le6LKcsIagQXsJQ4mtCZ: Endurance is time aloft, so it is fuel on board divided by fuel flow. For a piston engine the fuel flow follows POWER required, which depends on the mass (how much lift is needed), the speed (where on the power curve it sits) and the altitude (which shifts the whole power-required curve). All four quantities therefore enter.
lhRTwukgnX9xOYSc8gBk: Shock stall is separation of the BOUNDARY LAYER behind the shock wave: the steep adverse pressure gradient across the shock is more than the layer can survive, so it detaches. Lift falls sharply, drag rises steeply and the unsteady separated flow produces Mach buffet. Note that it occurs at LOW angles of attack - it is a compressibility phenomenon, quite distinct from the high-alpha low-speed stall.
lJ0XwlmzGZ0wvb8dzpws: Spanwise flow thickens the boundary layer toward the tips of a swept wing, so the TIPS stall first. Since the tips sit well aft of the CG on a swept planform, losing their lift moves the centre of pressure FORWARD and produces a nose-up pitching moment that drives the angle of attack higher still. Boundary layer fences, vortex generators and washout are remedies for this, not causes of it.
Lk4eML8Xi3kAiiuiaPaW: Turbulence and gusts produce transient losses of indicated airspeed and transient increases in load factor, both of which erode the margin above the stall. Adding an increment to VREF - typically half the steady headwind plus the full gust factor, up to a defined maximum - restores that margin. The cost is a longer landing distance, which is why the increment is capped.
Lkr3YQ0OwFYQoMRbzfmU: The flow accelerates most where the aerofoil is thickest and the curvature greatest, which on a swept wing is the upper surface near the WING ROOT. That is therefore where the local flow first reaches M1.0 and the first shock wave forms - by definition, at the critical Mach number. As Mach increases further the shock strengthens and moves aft and outboard.
lKzA1UgsStyTIbzFMSGM: As Mach number rises toward Mcrit the centre of pressure moves aft and the aeroplane tucks nose-down, which means the pilot must push LESS - or even pull - as speed increases: the stick force gradient flattens or reverses, destroying apparent speed stability. A Mach trimmer senses Mach number and applies an automatic nose-up input to restore a positive gradient. It corrects the stick force stability, not the drag or the buffet.
LLf7WAkZcOWPWfnH5y4i: Climbing at a constant IAS, the temperature falls so the speed of sound falls, while the TAS for a given IAS rises steadily as density drops. Both effects push the Mach number up, so it climbs continuously through the climb and MMO is the limit that will be reached. This is why climb schedules are flown at constant IAS to a crossover altitude and then at constant Mach.
LO0xR8OMQiFM7aqfu7HS: Maximum gliding distance requires the shallowest glide angle, which occurs at (L/D)max - and total drag is at its minimum exactly where induced drag and parasite drag are EQUAL. That is the bottom of the U-shaped drag curve. Fly faster or slower than that speed and one component grows faster than the other shrinks, so the glide steepens either way.
lo76TlyZUvHFE7fFIf3z: Induced drag coefficient is proportional to CL squared divided by aspect ratio, so a HIGH aspect ratio wing produces LESS induced drag: its tips are a smaller proportion of the span, so the tip vortices influence less of the wing and the downwash is reduced. The trade-offs are more structural weight and bending load, and greater gust sensitivity, since a higher aspect ratio gives a steeper lift curve slope.
