lODgFY4j21748Y4qEQwj: The take-off flight path and its climb segments are certified for the failure of the CRITICAL engine - the one whose failure produces the most adverse effect on control and performance - on a multi-engine aeroplane. Certification does not require the aeroplane to cope with the loss of two engines, and specifying the critical one covers the worst case, which is what makes the demonstration meaningful.
lOTfsstbHjf4UtxzPoSf: The buffet onset boundary chart plots the LOW-SPEED and HIGH-SPEED (Mach) buffet boundaries against weight, altitude and load factor - so it shows the Mach numbers between which the aeroplane can be flown buffet-free, and how that gap narrows with height. It is the chart used to establish the maximum altitude for a required manoeuvre margin, typically 1.3g. MMO is a fixed limit and does not vary with weight.
lQ77rIcbJLCY32jqXKE6: VD, the design dive speed, forms the right-hand boundary of both the manoeuvre and the gust envelopes - it is the highest speed for which the structure is designed and demonstrated. VC (design cruising speed) lies to its left, and VMO is the operating limit set below VD with a margin. Beyond VD lies the risk of flutter and structural failure.
lQy1niRQIBd9DUFjTa4r: Air has viscosity, so the molecules in contact with the surface are brought to rest and each successive layer above is dragged along a little less. The result is a thin layer in which the velocity rises from zero at the skin to the free-stream value - the boundary layer. It exists at all speeds and on all surfaces, and it is the source of skin friction drag and the site of every separation phenomenon.
luTZB2ND4MIIQ2DXR5bx: Descending at a constant Mach number, the rising temperature increases the local speed of sound and hence the TAS, while the rapidly increasing density drives the IAS up steeply. VMO is an indicated-airspeed limit, so it is the one reached first. This is exactly why a descent profile is flown at constant Mach only down to a crossover altitude, then at constant IAS.
LvHAV1u3xHsaihfwjvyA: In a steady climb the excess of thrust over drag lifts the weight up the slope, so sin(gamma) = (T - D)/W, and for small angles the sine is close to the tangent - which is the gradient. Expressed as a percentage: gradient = ((T - D)/W) x 100. Note that LIFT does not appear: in a climb it merely balances the component of weight perpendicular to the flight path.
LVjU7WpGat8pHVVO9Rkg: A fixed-pitch propeller is optimised for one combination of airspeed and rpm and its efficiency falls away sharply either side of it. A constant-speed unit varies blade angle to hold the selected rpm, so the blades stay near their best angle of attack throughout climb, cruise and descent. Its PEAK efficiency is no higher than a fixed-pitch prop's - it simply maintains near-peak efficiency across a far wider range.
lXbH9HRNUTt0mSrlqLkp: Slats RAISE the stalling angle of attack, typically by 5-10 degrees, by re-energising the boundary layer through the slot. Trailing-edge flaps do the opposite: they add camber, which raises CLmax but LOWERS the stalling angle. The clean wing sits between the two, so the ascending order is flaps extended, then clean, then slats extended.
lz215ZyGjDV6lKZE7nhl: At VMD the total drag is at its minimum, so tan(glide angle) = CD/CL is at its minimum too - the shallowest glide, and the greatest gliding distance. Checking the others: CL/CD is at its MAXIMUM there, not minimum; induced and parasite drag are EQUAL at that point, not unequal; and a propeller aeroplane's maximum endurance is at minimum POWER, a slower speed than VMD.
Lzr5xCHzhlnWJ0nIPMFW: The balanced V1 is where the accelerate-stop and accelerate-go distances are equal, and that crossing point is the MINIMUM field length that satisfies both cases. So even when the take-off is limited by climb performance rather than by runway length, choosing the balanced V1 leaves the largest possible margin between the field length required and the runway available.
mB4FxpRVJ2fN7y08MeKP: The tyre speed limit caps the GROUNDSPEED at lift-off. High elevation means low density, so a given lift-off IAS corresponds to a much higher TAS; a tailwind then adds directly to the TAS to give the groundspeed. The two together produce the highest lift-off groundspeed for a given indicated airspeed, which is exactly when tyre speed becomes the limiting factor.
mf3oudEkiXGPGbXiP120: The neutral point is the CG position at which the aeroplane has zero longitudinal static stability. Positive stability therefore requires the CG to lie AHEAD of it, and the distance between them - the static margin - measures how stable the aeroplane is. Relative surface areas influence WHERE the neutral point sits, but it is the CG's position relative to that point that creates the stability.
MgcvSts9KcvqP6Ch7JIW: Drag = CD x 1/2 rho V2 x S: it depends on the shape (through CD), the frontal area, the air density and, above all, the SQUARE of the airstream velocity. The body's mass, weight and centre of gravity have no bearing on the aerodynamic force at all - they matter for the accelerations that force produces, not for its magnitude.
Mi3VkWKGD01mxRqOnTMx: Geometric pitch is the theoretical distance a blade element would advance in one revolution if it moved through the air like a screw through a solid nut - determined purely by the blade angle and the radius. The difference between that theoretical distance and the actual distance advanced is SLIP. Note the other definitions: blade angle is measured from the PLANE OF ROTATION, and blade angle of attack from the relative airflow.
mjTFq9htaAZBizqhnoWh: Dihedral INCREASES static lateral stability. In a sideslip the lower wing meets the relative airflow at a greater effective angle of attack than the upper one, so it generates more lift and rolls the aeroplane back toward wings level. It is not the only means to this end - sweepback, a high wing position and keel surface above the CG all produce the same dihedral effect, which is why swept-wing jets often need ANHEDRAL to avoid excessive lateral stability and Dutch roll.
Mk1aif6bdfvOcQlxI6oh: A low flap setting gives less drag and therefore a better sustained climb GRADIENT, at the cost of a longer ground run. So it suits a long runway (the extra distance is affordable) with DISTANT obstacles (the sustained gradient is what matters), and it is especially valuable when high elevation and high temperature have already eroded the climb performance. CLOSE-IN obstacles argue the other way - more flap, to get airborne sooner.
MK6AHoxouR6kCw2YIgNK: Endurance is time aloft, so maximum endurance means minimum fuel flow - and that is achieved in steady, unaccelerated LEVEL flight at the speed of least fuel consumption: minimum power for a propeller aeroplane, minimum drag for a jet. Climbing or accelerating both consume energy that could otherwise be spent staying airborne, and specific range is a distance measure, not a time one.
mK7ENZlFBoo26QgZ3SLW: Maximum lift means flying at the stall, and the critical Mach number is a compressibility limit - neither has anything to do with gliding endurance. The speed for minimum drag is the meaningful aerodynamic reference here: it gives the shallowest glide angle and the greatest distance. (Strictly, the greatest TIME aloft comes at the minimum SINK speed, at (CL^3/CD^2)max, which lies a little below the minimum drag speed.)
Mkg1ApnTzLYeVWaqVeu0: Induced drag coefficient is proportional to CL squared divided by aspect ratio, so a HIGH aspect ratio wing produces LESS induced drag - its tips are a smaller proportion of the span, so the tip vortices influence less of the wing and the downwash is reduced. The trade-offs are greater structural weight and bending loads, and MORE gust sensitivity, since a high aspect ratio gives a steeper lift curve slope.
MkmpJuZccC0HvS4dONKj: V2 must be at least 1.1 VMCA - a 10% margin over the minimum control speed in the air - so that directional control remains assured throughout the second segment climb with the critical engine inoperative. V2 must simultaneously meet the stall margin requirement (1.2 VS, or 1.13 VSR), and whichever floor is higher governs.
MKuXSsIu2rSVe1JZxJL5: A deep stall is reached by continuing past the normal stall to a very high angle of attack - often 30-40 degrees - at which the stalled wing's wake completely blankets a T-tail, so the elevator loses effectiveness and cannot lower the nose. Because it is stable in that condition it is unrecoverable by normal means, which is why affected designs carry stick pushers. A shock stall, by contrast, occurs at LOW angle of attack.
MLSmuTa4SDjStIUaqYE1: Maximum range corresponds to a particular aerodynamic condition - a fixed point on the drag polar - and that point is defined by a lift coefficient, which is therefore the same at every altitude. What changes with altitude is the true airspeed at which that CL is achieved: it increases as density falls, which is exactly why cruising higher gives more miles per kilogram until thrust or buffet limits intervene.
mluoIttVjwSiL39JqjQF: The net take-off flight path may include turns, but the bank angle is limited to 15 degrees up to a height of 400 ft. Above 400 ft up to 1000 ft the limit is 20 degrees, and above 1000 ft it is 25 degrees. Banking reduces the vertical component of lift and hence the climb gradient, so the restriction is tightest where the aeroplane is lowest and closest to obstacles.
mmHD0wsMTVbEBoS08iJp: A servo tab and a trim tab are the same physical surface used two ways: the pilot's control run drives it to fly the main surface, and a separate trim input biases its neutral position so the surface settles at a new position with zero stick force. Combining the two functions in one tab is standard, which is why many aircraft carry a single 'servo/trim tab' on the elevator.
mo4hgBkvy0hrWUfd5r5h: Higher atmospheric pressure means DENSER air, which improves everything: the wing generates the required lift at a lower TAS so the touchdown groundspeed and landing distance are reduced, and the engines produce more thrust so go-around performance is better. Both effects work in the aeroplane's favour. It is LOW pressure - and high elevation or temperature - that penalises landing performance.
MoLSO3cJWsOhoc1Y4UEG: Holding the angle of attack fixed means holding CL fixed, so a heavier aeroplane must fly FASTER to generate the extra lift. Drag also rises, since CD is fixed and both the weight being supported and the speed have increased - and power required is drag multiplied by speed, so it rises on both counts. More speed AND more power are needed; the power setting certainly cannot stay unchanged.
Mqa7OK1CH4FTklXmyJF9: Flutter is a self-exciting oscillation in which aerodynamic, inertial and elastic forces couple: bending and torsional distortions of the structure feed energy into each other at a resonant frequency, so the amplitude grows rapidly and can destroy the structure within seconds. It appears only above a critical airspeed, so the immediate action is to reduce IAS; it is designed out by structural stiffness and mass balancing of control surfaces.
mSHGwzoS97CeV6fLfiW2: A stick shaker vibrates the control column to give an unmistakable tactile and aural warning as the stalling angle is approached. A stall STRIP is a small triangular section fitted to the inboard leading edge to trigger separation at the wing ROOT first, so the resulting buffet reaches the tailplane and warns the pilot while the ailerons are still effective. Both are warning devices; an angle of attack indicator is an instrument rather than a warning.
mSxhnP2HfFTZ0Qq48VWR: Flap extension raises CLmax, so the stall speed falls - but it also adds a great deal of drag and REDUCES (L/D)max, so the glide angle steepens and the maximum glide distance shortens. Both halves of that statement are correct. Note the corollary: flaps also increase the minimum rate of descent, so they shorten both the distance and the time available in a glide.
MW0CXtGyt2wO7sCp1yAz: As fuel burns the aeroplane needs less lift, flies at less drag for the same speed, and burns less fuel per mile - so specific range INCREASES steadily through the cruise. The altitude at which that best specific range occurs also rises, because a lighter aeroplane can achieve its optimum lift coefficient in thinner air. This continuous rise in optimum altitude is why step climbs are flown.
mwj4uhYMIMhgGATOBpif: A spring tab is a servo tab whose linkage includes a spring, so it only comes into play when the hinge moment is large. At LOW speeds the aerodynamic loads are light, the spring barely deflects and the tab moves with the surface as if rigidly attached. At HIGH speeds the loads are heavy, the spring compresses and the tab deflects, acting as a servo tab to keep the stick forces manageable - exactly where the help is needed.
MYBFaPya6Ga7wr54unPs: In a steady glide tan(glide angle) = CD/CL, so the descent angle is fixed entirely by the lift-to-drag ratio - and that ratio is determined by the angle of attack together with the configuration (flaps, gear, spoilers) that defines the drag polar. Mass and altitude change the SPEED at which a given angle of attack is flown, but not the glide angle achieved.
MZ5oXyjDXi1bkZqfNusQ: Above a certain Mach number the aft shift of the centre of pressure makes a swept-wing aeroplane tuck nose-down, so the stick force gradient flattens or reverses - apparent speed stability is lost. The Mach trimmer senses Mach number and applies an automatic nose-up input to restore a positive gradient. Straight-wing aeroplanes generally do not operate high enough into the transonic region to need one.
mZFZUFqbswAlD7CXOnup: Lift and drag are simply the components - perpendicular and parallel to the relative airflow - of the single resultant force produced by integrating the PRESSURE DISTRIBUTION over the whole surface (plus skin friction for drag). They are always normal to each other by definition, at every angle of attack, and neither varies linearly with alpha once the stall is approached.
n2cxEJixCFoZ8QWgti9V: In steady level flight lift must equal weight, so at a constant IAS the dynamic pressure is fixed and the lift COEFFICIENT cannot change - the aeroplane simply flies at a lower angle of attack with the flaps out. What flap extension does raise is CLmax (which is why the stall speed falls) and the drag. Confusing CL with CLmax is the trap here.
n6GRPqDmoMnIW54sLw7u: Leading-edge ice reduces CLmax and, critically, lowers the angle of attack at which the wing stalls. The highest angle of attack of the entire take-off occurs at the END of rotation, as the aeroplane unsticks at minimum speed - so that is where the reduced stalling angle bites first. During the ground run and the subsequent climb the angle of attack is lower and the margin correspondingly greater.
n6MZ9CfqkDoBcm7m0IDT: At holding speed the aeroplane is at (L/D)max, so the thrust required equals W/(L/D)max - directly proportional to weight. With equal specific fuel consumption, the fuel flow scales with weight in the same way: 4300 x (115,000 / 130,000) = 3804 kg/h. This proportionality is why holding fuel figures must always be quoted against a weight.
n8a0G898QXEx5Hjjivxa: Anhedral - wings angled downward from the root - reduces static lateral stability, because in a sideslip it lessens or reverses the effective angle of attack advantage the lower wing would otherwise gain. It is deliberately used on high-wing and swept-wing aircraft, whose configuration already produces a strong dihedral effect, to trim lateral stability back and avoid excessive Dutch roll tendency.
nBa5rPjRHRgQpJit60LY: In a spin the ailerons must be held NEUTRAL: at the very high angles of attack of autorotation an aileron input aggravates the rotation rather than opposing it, because the down-going aileron on the rising wing simply deepens that wing's stall. The correct sequence is throttle closed, ailerons neutral, full opposite rudder, control column progressively forward, then centralise the rudder as rotation stops.
NcukoNE5ofFzvmy4YWZi: The neutral point is by definition the CG position at which static longitudinal stability is exactly zero. Ahead of it the aeroplane is stable; behind it, unstable. The distance between the CG and the neutral point is the static margin, and certification requires a minimum value of it - which is precisely what sets the aft CG limit.
ncuv3cEJt1R3F2ZTXvuE: With the speedbrakes already deployed, both spoiler panels are part-raised. A roll demand is then superimposed by moving them differentially about that raised position: the panels on the DOWN-GOING wing rise further (killing more lift there) while those on the UP-GOING wing retract downward toward the faired position (restoring lift). The net differential is what produces the rolling moment.
nd5E0bxaW5F7YGKUyVGU: A straight wing stalls from the ROOT outward, and losing the inboard lift - which lies ahead of the wing's overall centre of lift - moves the centre of pressure aft, producing a natural nose-DOWN pitching moment that begins the recovery. This benign behaviour is exactly what certification seeks. Note that pre-stall buffet comes from the WING's separated wake striking the tailplane, not from the tail stalling.
nH79jbla8cnsodXN4cBf: Maximum level speed is reached at the high-speed intersection of the thrust available and drag curves - the point where the maximum thrust the engines can produce is exactly consumed by the total drag, leaving no excess to accelerate further. Beyond that speed the drag would exceed the available thrust. Minimum drag corresponds to a quite different, much slower condition.
nHMxbNySSUKB3C27vGQ4: Optimum altitude is by definition the pressure altitude at which specific range - nautical miles per kilogram of fuel - is at its MAXIMUM for the current weight. Because a lighter aeroplane achieves its optimum lift coefficient in thinner air, that altitude RISES steadily as fuel burns off, which is exactly why step climbs are flown through a long cruise.
NiKHgt0lLM10tCnlaFbL: Contaminated runway performance data is derived largely by CALCULATION, using models of displacement drag, spray impingement and degraded braking friction, with only limited flight test validation - the conditions are too variable and too hazardous to demonstrate exhaustively. That is why contaminated data carries more uncertainty than dry or wet data, and why reduced thrust is prohibited on contaminated runways.
NJfTcraHpx9CFesrox56: In the transonic region the dominant physics is compressibility: shock wave formation, the aft movement of the centre of pressure, shock-induced separation and buffet all depend on how close the LOCAL flow is to the speed of sound. Since Mach number is the ratio of TAS to the local speed of sound, it is the parameter that captures all of this - which is why high-level cruise is flown to a Mach number rather than an airspeed.
nJiGsjNr8zD8fjUznxkV: The line drawn midway between the upper and lower surfaces from leading edge to trailing edge is the MEAN CAMBER LINE. Its shape defines the aerofoil's camber: on a symmetrical section it coincides exactly with the straight chord line, and the further it bows away from the chord, the more cambered the section. The CHORD line, by contrast, is the straight line joining the leading and trailing edges.
Nk0cRJ3zgoUfpZpmyPHK: The second segment begins the moment the landing gear is FULLY RETRACTED and runs to the acceleration altitude (at least 400 ft). It is flown at V2 with take-off flap and take-off thrust, and it is the most demanding segment for climb gradient - 2.4% for a twin - which is why the climb-limited take-off mass is usually set here.
NNP1RTy0M0muOERosBOH: In a level turn the lift must both support the weight and provide the turning force, so the load factor n = 1/cos(bank) is always GREATER than 1. Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor, so it is correspondingly HIGHER than in straight and level flight - by 19% at 45 degrees of bank and 41% at 60 degrees.
nOIccNFkDYVYYHrp0q2h: VMCG is defined using PRIMARY AERODYNAMIC CONTROL only - essentially the rudder. Nosewheel steering and differential braking are deliberately excluded, because on a wet or contaminated runway their effectiveness cannot be relied upon, and the demonstration must hold good in the worst case. This is why VMCG is comparatively high and why it forms the lower bound on V1.
NPMIrS6cPOmEnDJiyK33: As the aeroplane accelerates, the airflow meets the blades at a flatter helix angle, which would reduce their angle of attack and let the rpm rise. The governor detects the rpm change and COARSENS the blade angle to restore the selected rpm - so blade angle increases with speed. That is the essence of constant-speed operation: rpm is held while blade angle varies.
nPRSulFMoPiuUBV6RpT2: Lift means higher pressure beneath the wing than above it, and at the wing TIP - where the two regions meet around the end of the wing - air simply flows from high to low pressure: from BENEATH the wing, around the tip, to the upper surface. That escaping flow rolls up into the tip vortex, which induces downwash across the wing and is the origin of induced drag.
NqeKzLzzpRE9vpXhjZHH: As angle of attack increases, the oncoming flow meets the aerofoil from further below, so the stagnation point migrates DOWN and aft along the lower surface. Simultaneously the suction peak on the upper surface sharpens and moves FORWARD toward the leading edge - which is why the centre of pressure of a cambered section moves forward with increasing alpha.
nrprz6esQyxEVGJ2VwfJ: A constant-speed unit senses rpm and adjusts blade angle to hold the selected value. Medium turbulence produces only small, transient variations in the airflow through the disc and hence small rpm excursions, so the governor responds with correspondingly small blade angle changes. Gentle, continuous pitch adjustment is precisely what the system is designed to deliver.
ntn4lOa2x10EDlOTRDwU: Climbing at a constant IAS, the falling temperature reduces the local speed of sound while the falling density raises the TAS for that IAS - both effects drive the Mach number up continuously. MMO is therefore the limit that will be reached. This is why climb schedules are flown at constant IAS only up to a crossover altitude, then at constant Mach.
NUC75cDAaLwjKEuhUV1a: Underslung engines put the thrust line BELOW the centre of gravity, so a thrust increase produces a nose-UP couple about the CG. To keep the net pitching moment at zero the tailplane must generate a nose-down moment, which requires DOWN elevator. This is why a go-around from a low-speed configuration demands prompt forward pressure, and why the effect is most pronounced on large-diameter engines slung well below the wing.
nUvBRGXzJVIBaksNcD8k: Moving the CG aft shortens the arm between the CG and the tailplane, so the restoring moment for a given disturbance shrinks - static longitudinal stability DECREASES. The same shortened arm means a given elevator deflection now produces more pitching moment, so LESS deflection (and less stick force) is needed for a given manoeuvre. Both quantities fall together, which is the trade between stability and manoeuvrability.
NWIQg23Na7JJFEYFBV4G: The accelerate-stop case is built on an engine failure recognised at V1, followed by an allowance of 2 seconds of pilot reaction time at V1 speed before the first retarding action takes effect, and the aeroplane must then stop within the ACCELERATE-STOP DISTANCE AVAILABLE (runway plus stopway). That 2-second allowance is precisely why V1 is a decision speed rather than the failure speed VEF, which occurs earlier.
Nwn6C7AYVcJyoOPQYEwo: A wing stalls at a fixed ANGLE OF ATTACK, not at a fixed speed - so as long as alpha remains below the critical angle the wing cannot stall, whatever the airspeed, attitude, weight or load factor. This is why an aeroplane can be stalled at high speed in a steep turn, or in a nose-down attitude during a recovery, and why stall protection systems sense angle of attack rather than airspeed.
NX3JtqZthCoKOu6Vz3Vn: V2 must give an adequate stall margin with an engine failed, and for a jet without provisions to significantly reduce the one-engine-inoperative stall speed the floor is 1.2 VS (modern rules express this as 1.13 VSR). V2 must simultaneously exceed 1.1 VMCA, and whichever floor is higher governs - at high flap settings that is often VMCA.
O17e01tnrd7OvCXhj5wI: Gyroscopic precession appears only when the plane of the spinning disc is TILTED, which happens when the aeroplane pitches or yaws - rolling turns the aeroplane about the propeller's own axis and produces no precession at all. The applied force then takes effect 90 degrees onward in the direction of rotation, which is why raising the tail on take-off produces a yaw.
O77HX5GSIUBiHKgzp51A: In a right turn the outside of the turn is to the LEFT, so a ball displaced left has swung to the outside - a SKID, meaning the rate of turn is too high for the bank angle. Two coordinated fixes exist: reduce the rate of turn with less rudder, or match the bank to the rate by rolling in MORE right bank. Of the options offered, more right bank is the coordinating input.
o7fPs0FQg9YtkL59hVt9: Pulling out of a dive raises the load factor, and stall speed increases with the SQUARE ROOT of n - so the wing can stall at a speed far above its 1g value. This is the accelerated stall, and it is why a high-speed recovery must be flown smoothly. The other options all reduce the stall speed: retracting spoilers restores lift, and less weight needs less lift.
ObJeWXqOLk5aVPwIc2LI: The angle of INCIDENCE is the fixed rigging angle built into the airframe between the wing chord line and the fuselage longitudinal axis - it does not change in flight. Angle of ATTACK, by contrast, is measured between the chord line and the RELATIVE AIRFLOW and varies continuously. Confusing the two is a common trap, since only one of them is a variable.
OChNlELpPSWug7uLHci2: In a climb the propeller disc is inclined to the airflow, so the DOWN-going blade meets the air at a greater angle of attack and higher relative velocity than the up-going blade, and therefore produces more thrust. With a right-turning propeller the down-going blade is on the RIGHT, so the extra thrust is on the right side of the disc and the aeroplane yaws LEFT. This P-factor adds to torque and slipstream effects in the climb.
OcRAmaQQkhRriDgeyUsU: An elliptical planform produces an elliptical spanwise lift distribution, which gives uniform downwash across the entire span - the theoretical minimum induced drag for a given lift and span. Rectangular and tapered wings depart from that ideal and pay a small penalty, expressed as a span efficiency factor below 1. In practice taper and washout are used to approximate the ellipse at far lower manufacturing cost.
OcZZjtoOLDmRJ1tOOSV5: Work through it in steps. Doubling the speed at constant lift requires CL to fall to a quarter, since lift depends on CL x V2. Induced drag COEFFICIENT is proportional to CL squared, so it falls to (1/4)2 = 1/16. Induced DRAG then equals that coefficient multiplied by the dynamic pressure, which has quadrupled: 1/16 x 4 = 1/4. So the coefficient falls by 1/16 and the force by 1/4.
OdvVsDNCMfs5Cmp8WoOY: In a level turn the vertical component of lift must equal the weight, so L cos(bank) = W, giving n = 1/cos(bank). Nothing else appears - not speed, not radius, not weight. This is why a 60 degree bank always means 2 g whatever the aeroplane or the airspeed, and why bank angle alone determines how close a level turn takes you to the structural limit.
oIjbxINbmgGoX5lhie7C: A high aspect ratio wing has a smaller proportion of its span influenced by the tip vortices, so downwash and INDUCED DRAG are reduced - the primary benefit. It also stalls at a LOWER angle of attack: a low aspect ratio wing is strongly influenced by tip effects that keep some flow attached to much higher angles, which is why delta-winged aircraft can be held at very high alpha.
OjgscaRcuTQLRZmxDvhN: A symmetrical aerofoil has identical upper and lower surfaces, so at zero angle of attack the pressure distributions are mirror images and the net lift - and hence CL - is exactly zero. This is why symmetrical sections are used for tailplanes and fins. A cambered section, by contrast, still produces positive lift at zero alpha, and reaches zero CL only at a small NEGATIVE angle of attack.
OmBTSnZkz8wMqFioWhBe: Outboard ailerons give a long moment arm and hence powerful roll control, which is wanted at low speed with the flaps out. At high speed that same long arm applied to a flexible outer wing risks aileron reversal and imposes large bending loads, so the outboard surfaces are locked out once the flaps and slats are retracted or the speed exceeds a threshold, leaving roll control to the inboard ailerons and the spoilers.
OmTyXhavIDVIlW5IWQNU: A downhill slope helps the acceleration but HINDERS the deceleration, because gravity now works against the brakes - so the accelerate-stop distance lengthens. To keep the stop case within the distance available, V1 must be REDUCED. Note that the take-off SPEEDS themselves - VR, VLOF, V2 - are aerodynamic and unaffected by slope; it is only the decision speed that shifts.
onEQxokCYT30bPk1jqGr: Stick force per g needs both bounds. Too LOW and the aeroplane can be over-stressed inadvertently, since the pilot gets almost no force cue as the load factor builds - the danger of an excessively aft CG. Too HIGH and it becomes physically tiring and slow to manoeuvre, the penalty of a very forward CG. Certification therefore specifies a minimum and a maximum, and the CG envelope is set to keep the aeroplane between them.
OoFSvpcYeF6LIiB7iEFQ: Underslung engines put the thrust line BELOW the centre of gravity, so increasing thrust produces a nose-UP couple about the CG. To hold the net pitching moment at zero the tailplane must generate an opposing nose-down moment, which requires DOWN elevator. This coupling is why a go-around from a low-speed, high-drag configuration demands prompt forward pressure.
opBuAU3lKfaezWFnitV2: CS-25.113 requires the certified figure to be the GREATER of the one-engine-inoperative distance and 115% of the all-engines-operating distance. Here that is the greater of 1950 m and 1.15 x 1747 = 2009 m, so 2009 m governs. The 15% factor exists because the all-engines take-off is the one flown routinely, so it needs its own safety margin rather than relying on the engine-out case to cover it.
OtaSnpxA5DGeUSZlCAUk: Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for the deviation from standard temperature, and it is the figure that actually governs performance - thrust, lift, take-off distance and climb gradient all depend on air DENSITY. On a hot day at a high-elevation aerodrome the density altitude can be several thousand feet above the physical elevation. It plays no part in altimetry or terrain clearance.
OTPcps0KNhp9X5DAq35Q: A swept wing's natural failing is that it stalls at the TIPS first, producing a nose-up pitching moment and a loss of aileron authority. Slats give the largest increase in stalling ANGLE of any device, so they are fitted where that margin is most needed - the tips. Leading-edge (Krueger) flaps, which add camber rather than raising the stalling angle as much, go at the roots, where an early stall is actually desirable.
OuurNoMcdyhzPLw2oxe1: Turbulence produces gust-induced load factor excursions, and any increase in load factor raises the stall speed by the square root of n - so it MAY increase during turbulence. A coordinated level turn always requires n greater than 1, so banking ALWAYS raises the stall speed there. Note the traps in the other options: MORE FLAP raises CLmax and therefore LOWERS the stall speed, and an AFT CG reduces the tail download and also lowers it.
oXCsHYZmF1ohIhHcVXXl: The low-tow position places the glider BELOW the towplane's wake. Releasing from there, the glider's natural tendency is to climb as the tow load comes off, which takes it straight up through the towrope's path and into the towplane's wake turbulence. The correct procedure is to release from the high-tow position, or to descend and turn away before releasing from low tow.
p0QNEqMVkZWjuugYQ84W: Flap deflection sets up two opposing pitching moments. The extra lift is generated behind the original centre of pressure, which is nose-down, but the flap also greatly increases the DOWNWASH reaching the tailplane, reducing its effective angle of attack and hence its download - which is nose-up. Which effect wins depends on the geometry: on a low-mounted tailplane sitting in the increased downwash the nose-up contribution dominates.
P3f4ySRmQQLt8fvpJ3Rd: VS0 is the stalling speed, or minimum steady flight speed at which the aeroplane remains controllable, in the LANDING configuration - full flap and gear down. VS1 is the equivalent in a specified configuration, typically clean. VS0 is the reference from which VREF is derived, at 1.3 VS0.
P5nPo70I570wt1Gvhg3u: Two climb requirements can limit the landing mass. The APPROACH climb is the one engine inoperative case in the approach configuration with the gear UP, requiring 2.1% for a twin - and because it is flown on one engine it is usually the limiting one. The LANDING climb is the all-engines case in the full landing configuration with the gear DOWN, requiring 3.2%. Mixing the two - all engines but gear up - is not a defined requirement.
PaRoGtpNNIgWHlWmwPMw: VA is the speed at which the aeroplane stalls at exactly the limit manoeuvring load factor, and since stall speed rises with the square root of load factor, VA = VS x sqrt(n). For a large transport aeroplane the positive limit load factor is 2.5, giving VA = VS x sqrt(2.5), about 1.58 VS. Below VA a single full elevator deflection stalls the wing before it overstresses the structure.
PCK7GMrXvSV9OZrmlOTX: The balanced field length is the condition in which the accelerate-stop distance exactly equals the accelerate-go (take-off) distance, achieved by selecting the V1 at which the two curves cross. Because reducing V1 shortens the stop case while lengthening the go case, that crossing point is the MINIMUM field length satisfying both - which is what makes it the optimum V1 for an engine failure.
PCUvN1EztLbwkPVKn9F0: Downstream of transition the layer is turbulent, which means continuous mixing brings fast free-stream air down toward the surface. The velocity profile therefore becomes much fuller - a higher mean speed close to the skin - and the steeper velocity gradient at the wall produces MORE skin friction drag. The layer also gets thicker. The compensation is that all that extra energy makes it far more resistant to separation.
PdauclI6g33cQXBmZY70: The glide angle relative to the AIR is fixed by L/D and is unaffected by mass or wind - a heavier aeroplane simply flies the same angle faster. What extends the ground distance is a TAILWIND, which carries the aeroplane along while it descends and so flattens the path traced over the ground. A headwind does the reverse.
PDTyq5GvaLBX1urMgzhZ: Controllability is the aeroplane's capacity to respond to the pilot's control inputs - how readily it can be made to follow a desired flight path and attitude. Manoeuvrability is the related but distinct quality of how easily and quickly it can be manoeuvred and how much load it can sustain. The two trade against stability: a very stable aeroplane resists being moved off its trimmed condition, which is exactly what reduces controllability.
PEbp3gUeKZMc8XrVaoto: Trailing-edge flaps work by increasing camber, which shifts the whole CL-alpha curve up and to the LEFT - so CLmax rises but it is reached at a SMALLER angle of attack. This is why the nose attitude is lower on a flapped approach, and why flap does not help the stall MARGIN in angle-of-attack terms. Slats do the opposite, raising the stalling angle by 5-10 degrees.
PG3LrSD4t0Wav1bWrEkB: The critical Mach number is the FREE STREAM Mach number at which the flow somewhere on the airframe - normally the upper surface of the wing, near the point of greatest curvature - first reaches M1.0 locally. It is the threshold, not the consequence: shock waves, shock stall and Mach buffet all appear at Mach numbers ABOVE Mcrit, not at it.
PGV4izw9KaBFFbys159P: In level flight lift equals weight, so minimising CD/CL is the same as minimising DRAG - which is the lowest point of the drag curve, VMD, and the point of maximum L/D. The tangent from the ORIGIN is a different construction: it minimises D/V rather than D, and it identifies the higher speed for a jet's maximum specific range.
pHDk604yl1zZfqJ1wvkT: At a given angle of attack the lift coefficient is the same for both aeroplanes, so the heavier one must fly FASTER to generate the extra lift - and since the glide angle is unchanged, its rate of descent is proportionally greater too. The whole polar therefore stretches outward along a line through the origin: same angles, higher speeds. The glide DISTANCE achieved is identical; only the speeds differ.
PIb7gZzCxG8tNcjFU724: VMCG is set by the balance between the asymmetric yawing moment from the live engine and the rudder's ability to oppose it. Higher elevation and higher temperature both reduce air density, which reduces the ENGINE THRUST and therefore the yawing moment that has to be countered - so a lower speed suffices and VMCG decreases. (A flat-rated engine holds full thrust to a certain altitude, so VMCG stays constant until that point.)
pkRhyDaDSJQcm1mMK6zi: A 5 degree change in angle of attack raises CL by 5 x 0.09 = 0.45, so the new lift coefficient is 0.4 + 0.45 = 0.85. Because the speed has not changed in that instant, the lift is directly proportional to CL, so the load factor is simply the ratio of the new coefficient to the old: 0.85 / 0.4 = 2.13. Note how a modest gust produces over 2 g - which is why turbulence penetration speed matters.
poYx7Uu7IlFs2zkMBaZ4: CS-25.113(b) defines the take-off RUN as the distance from brake release to a point equidistant between the point at which VLOF is reached and the point at which the aeroplane is 35 ft above the take-off surface - so half the airborne segment is counted. It is distinct from the take-off DISTANCE, which is measured all the way to the 35 ft screen, and from the accelerate-stop distance.
Poz5RKPkPMA8yJ1Qpx8p: The take-off sequence runs VMCG (the lowest speed at which the aeroplane can be kept straight after a failure, and hence the floor on V1), then V1 (the decision speed), then VR (rotation), then V2 (the take-off safety speed achieved by 35 ft). VMU and VLOF fall between VR and V2. Each speed bounds the next, which is why the ordering is fixed.
PpG74U3Ma0blaThiJSbN: Interference drag arises where the airflows around two adjoining components - wing and fuselage, nacelle and pylon, fin and tailplane - meet and interact, producing separation and turbulence that neither component would generate alone. It is a component of parasite drag and is minimised by fairings and fillets at the junctions. It is quite distinct from induced drag, which comes from the tip vortices.
prfSh7taLdau9m895mXj: A horn balance places part of the control surface area FORWARD of the hinge line, so the airflow acting on it produces a moment that assists the pilot's input and reduces the hinge moment to be overcome. It is a form of aerodynamic balance, aimed at reducing stick forces. MASS balance is a different device entirely - a weight ahead of the hinge fitted to prevent flutter.
PRPBUp6O9cDQnj20IISr: The blade angle is measured from the plane of rotation, and the airflow actually arrives along the helix angle - the resultant of forward speed and rotational speed. The blade's angle of attack is the difference between the two, so blade angle minus angle of attack equals the HELIX angle. Slip, by contrast, is the difference between geometric and effective pitch.
PRXGbo2wjQjgTtVh51Zi: Both maximum range and maximum endurance correspond to fixed points on the drag polar, so each is flown at a fixed lift coefficient and therefore a fixed INDICATED airspeed for a given weight. Since TAS = IAS divided by the square root of the density ratio, and density falls with height, the TRUE airspeed for both conditions INCREASES with altitude - which is a large part of why cruising high is efficient.
Q1ten2gdZtF9MXVb6ogW: Both statements hold. The tanks add wetted area and frontal area, so PARASITE drag rises. But sitting at the tips they act as endplates, obstructing the flow that would otherwise spill around the tip from the high-pressure lower surface to the low-pressure upper surface - so the tip vortices weaken and INDUCED drag falls. This is the same principle that winglets exploit.
q8Wg6gaS1XclH0ophIv0: Angle of attack is measured between the aerofoil's CHORD LINE and the RELATIVE UNDISTURBED AIRFLOW. It is referenced to the airflow, not to the airframe or the horizon - which is why an aeroplane can be at a high angle of attack in a nose-down attitude, and why the fixed angle between chord and fuselage is a separate quantity, the angle of incidence.
QBWGiQqqvznglQsZoEkC: The second segment is a ONE-ENGINE-INOPERATIVE case, so with three engines only two remain: thrust = 2 x 50,000 = 100,000 N. Then sin(gamma) = (T - D)/W gives 0.027 = (100,000 - 72,569)/W, so W = 27,431 / 0.027 = 1,015,963 N. Dividing by g = 10 gives a mass of 101,596 kg. The trap is using all three engines' thrust.
qCMHg6UiXEO9DUu37Ha8: Static stability describes the INITIAL tendency after a disturbance, and dynamic stability describes what happens over time. If the aeroplane does not even start back toward its original condition, there is nothing for the motion to converge upon - so a statically unstable aeroplane can NEVER be dynamically stable. Static stability is a necessary condition for dynamic stability, though not a sufficient one.
qdwMJySLODwXhnKCH4JW: Stall speed is proportional to the square root of the weight: a heavier aeroplane needs more lift, and since it stalls at the same CLmax the only way to get it is more speed. Doubling the weight raises the stall speed by about 41%. Wing SPAN does not enter directly - what matters is wing loading, weight divided by area.
qGwuuSrDy926YQ87XYZN: Optimum altitude is where the aeroplane achieves its best specific range for its current weight. A lighter aeroplane needs less lift, so it can reach its optimum lift coefficient in THINNER air - the optimum altitude therefore RISES as fuel burns off. This continuous rise is why step climbs are flown through a long cruise, and why the optimum is always quoted against a weight.
QjUn98J4ljXApOpacbeD: A slat moves forward and down, opening a slot that ducts high-energy air from beneath the wing onto the upper surface. Two things follow: the boundary layer is re-energised so it resists separation, and the suction peak transfers from the fixed wing's leading edge onto the SLAT itself, so the main wing's own adverse pressure gradient is much gentler. Together these postpone the stall by 5-10 degrees of angle of attack.
QKm4mwrkMtOtAXobJYY6: Climbing at constant IAS on maximum climb thrust, the thrust available falls steadily with density while the drag at a given IAS does not - so the excess thrust, and with it the climb ANGLE, reduces continuously. Pitch attitude is the climb angle plus the angle of attack, and at constant IAS the angle of attack is essentially unchanged, so the pitch attitude falls with the climb angle.
QnYGtYEzCNm8sTBBI4uR: Holding the greatest possible altitude on one engine means minimising the thrust required, and thrust required is least where DRAG is least - at the angle of attack giving the greatest lift-to-drag ratio. Any other speed needs more thrust than the remaining engine can supply for level flight, so the aeroplane will drift down further. Long-range cruise speed is faster than this and would cost height.
QOydrgf5Ech5DNjkjJEn: A 2 degree change in angle of attack raises CL by 2 x 0.079 = 0.158, so the new lift coefficient is 0.35 + 0.158 = 0.508. Since the speed has not changed in that instant, lift is directly proportional to CL, so the load factor is the ratio of the new coefficient to the old: 0.508 / 0.35 = 1.45.
qPbNqp2pjQA9l3wwS5cU: Dutch roll is a coupled ROLL-YAW oscillation. A sideslip generates both a rolling moment (through dihedral effect) and a yawing moment (through the fin), and the two feed each other: the aeroplane rolls, yaws, rolls back and yaws back in a wallowing motion. Pitch is not involved at all. It is characteristic of swept-wing aircraft, whose strong dihedral effect outweighs their directional stability - hence the yaw damper.
qPLQiPkAgNXe4rNwY58G: In the transonic region the dominant physics is compressibility: shock wave formation, the aft movement of the centre of pressure, shock-induced separation and buffet all depend on how close the LOCAL flow is to the speed of sound. Mach number is the ratio of TAS to the local speed of sound, so it captures all of this - which is why high-level cruise is flown to a Mach number rather than an airspeed.
QQgaOAAbSghblQlgIDxN: In ground effect the reduced downwash means more lift and much less induced drag, so the aeroplane floats: it is reluctant to stop flying and decelerates slowly in the flare. That extends the airborne portion of the landing and INCREASES the landing distance. The same effect can produce a premature lift-off on take-off, with the aeroplane sinking back as it climbs out of ground effect.
qqJGmixk1yCUK3cWod6n: VX, the best angle of climb speed, occurs where EXCESS THRUST is greatest; VY, the best rate of climb speed, occurs where EXCESS POWER is greatest - and excess power peaks at a higher speed than excess thrust. So VX is always below VY. The two converge with altitude and meet at the absolute ceiling, where the rate of climb reaches zero.
QrWUdtY6GaHDH87sFR28: Static stability guarantees only the INITIAL tendency to return; what happens afterwards is a separate question. A statically stable aeroplane may converge smoothly (dynamically stable), oscillate at constant amplitude (dynamically neutral), or oscillate with growing amplitude (dynamically unstable). Static stability is a necessary but not sufficient condition for dynamic stability.
qSpTeynVaBzwtyj4XLe9: Below the crossover, climbing at constant IAS means the TAS is steadily INCREASING, so part of the excess power is spent accelerating rather than climbing. Above it, climbing at constant Mach in the troposphere means the TAS is DECREASING, so kinetic energy is released and contributes to the climb instead. Swapping one for the other therefore improves the rate of climb - the TAS is momentarily equal at the crossover, but the trend either side is opposite.
qV9zaeEEBurFyRyb9OTn: The climb limit comes from the second segment gradient, so anything that improves the climb gradient raises the climb-limited mass. A LOWER flap setting cuts drag substantially and improves the gradient, and a HIGHER V2 moves the aeroplane closer to the best climb speed, improving it further. The cost is a longer ground run, which is why this trade only works when runway length is not the limiting factor.
QxDEMbuJp45mxO35cAbD: A ventral fin is keel area added BELOW the fuselage and behind the CG. Behind the CG it adds directional stability, so the effect on that axis is POSITIVE. Below the CG, however, the sideforce it generates in a sideslip acts beneath the roll axis and therefore rolls the aeroplane INTO the slip - a NEGATIVE contribution to lateral stability. It is exactly this combination that makes it useful for taming Dutch roll. Pitch is unaffected.
QYVvbsmqEor429iTEVgj: The Mach trim system senses Mach number and, as it rises toward Mcrit, automatically repositions the trimmable stabiliser nose-up to counter the tuck-under produced by the aft movement of the centre of pressure. It restores a positive stick force gradient so the aeroplane retains apparent speed stability. It does not hold the Mach number constant - that is the autothrottle's job.
r2H3rNoIQoCozV6RnASj: The aft shift of the centre of pressure lengthens the nose-down moment arm about the CG, producing Mach tuck. Countering it requires a nose-UP pitching input, which on a transport aeroplane is applied automatically by the Mach trim system repositioning the stabiliser. Increasing thrust or speed would only make matters worse, since the tuck deepens as Mach number rises.
r9gVXJhEuGA1xATWq4Ns: An elliptical spanwise lift distribution produces uniform downwash across the whole span, which is the theoretical MINIMUM induced drag for a given lift and span. All the other options increase it: high angles of attack mean high CL and induced drag varies as CL squared; flap extension raises CL further; and induced drag is inversely proportional to aspect ratio, so a low aspect ratio makes it worse.
rDJVAMBCb3U8WrFEd5qG: The induced drag coefficient is proportional to CL SQUARED divided by ASPECT RATIO (with a span efficiency factor and pi as the constants). Two consequences follow directly: induced drag climbs very steeply as speed falls and CL rises, and a long slender wing suffers far less of it than a short stubby one.
RDxmoFKZUY7p5PHD44U5: Climbing at constant IAS, the falling density raises the TAS for that IAS while the falling temperature lowers the local speed of sound - both effects drive the MACH NUMBER up. Checking the others: at constant IAS the TAS increases, at constant TAS the Mach number also increases, and at constant Mach the IAS decreases. This is why a climb schedule runs at constant IAS to a crossover altitude and then at constant Mach.
rDysduF8zWU50hrd8Z4w: Mach number is TAS divided by the local speed of sound, and the speed of sound depends only on temperature. Climbing through the troposphere the temperature falls steadily, so the speed of sound falls with it, and holding the TAS constant means the Mach number must INCREASE. This is why a climb at constant TAS or IAS steadily erodes the Mach margin and eventually meets MMO.
rGBg9rhcLZ3okQsNMJp0: An auto-slat system extends the slats automatically once the angle of attack exceeds a preset threshold, restoring the stall margin at a moment when the crew may be fully occupied - typically during a windshear escape or an aggressive manoeuvre at a take-off flap setting. It is an angle-of-attack driven protection, not part of the roll control system and not tied to the ground/flight logic.
rgP9FksjODK48yMDNnl6: A blade element's angle of attack is the difference between its fixed blade angle and the HELIX angle of the airflow it meets - and that helix angle depends on the ratio of the element's rotational speed to the aeroplane's true airspeed. Rotational speed rises with radius while the TAS is the same everywhere along the blade, so the helix angle is steep at the root and shallow at the tip. The blade is twisted to compensate, keeping the angle of attack roughly constant along the span.
RIGcRcHBHx80Xo5LoVZp: Slack towline is removed by adding a little drag without changing the glider's position relative to the towplane. Yawing the nose to one side with rudder while holding the wings level with aileron produces exactly that - a controlled increase in drag that takes the slack up gradually. Pitching up or turning would change the geometry and risk a sudden snatch load when the rope comes taut.
rIqrbRNtyt9Vh74nWa28: Descending at a CONSTANT Mach number, the Mach limit obviously cannot be exceeded - the Mach number is not changing. What does change is the IAS: the rising temperature increases the local speed of sound and hence the TAS, and the rapidly increasing density then drives the indicated airspeed up steeply. VMO is an indicated-airspeed limit, so it is the one reached first, and the aural overspeed warning is the cue.
Rjqc1n5PwD6EbKcVem32: Drift down is the procedure for exactly this case: an engine failure at a cruise level above the one-engine-inoperative maximum altitude, where the aeroplane can no longer hold height. It descends at the speed for the best gradient on maximum continuous thrust until it reaches the level-off altitude, and the net flight path during that descent must clear the terrain.
Rk3NreGyiFpQzUMcc4gL: For a jet, thrust available is roughly constant with speed, so the maximum EXCESS thrust - and hence the best climb angle VX - occurs at VMD, which is also the maximum endurance speed. Maximum range lies higher, at about 1.32 x VMD, and long range cruise is faster still. So Vs, then VX, then maximum range speed is the correct ascending order.
RkZmg8WzRAAyYJJcL5iq: A swept wing generates a spanwise flow toward the tips, which thickens the outboard boundary layer and makes the tips stall first - producing a pitch-up and a loss of aileron authority. A boundary layer fence is a chordwise plate that physically blocks that spanwise drift. It is therefore a LOW-SPEED fix, addressing stall behaviour rather than compressibility, and it does not change Mcrit.
RLe5Bwd1BZXpic9kG0wZ: Descending at a constant Mach number, the density rises rapidly, so the dynamic pressure increases and the lift coefficient needed to support the weight FALLS. A lower CL means the aeroplane is further from the angle of attack at which low-speed buffet occurs, so that margin INCREASES. The high-speed buffet margin improves too, which is why descending is the standard escape from coffin corner.
rm26silwFbI7zOuoAsjG: A reduced V1 means the failure is recognised at a lower speed, so the aeroplane spends longer accelerating to VR and reaches 35 ft further down the runway. The whole one-engine-inoperative flight path is therefore displaced along track, which erodes the OBSTACLE CLEARANCE. The climb gradient itself is a function of thrust, drag and weight, none of which V1 affects, so climb performance is unchanged.
RM4S86psV6LUuH0dhTvz: The climb is flown at an indicated airspeed, and wind has no effect on the aeroplane's performance relative to the AIR - so the rate of climb, the time to height and the fuel burnt are all unchanged. What a tailwind changes is the GROUND distance covered during the climb, which increases. Wind affects the ground track, never the air-mass performance.
RM9pNTtKa6xmIZ6kx2OU: VREF is defined as 1.3 times the stalling speed in the landing configuration (1.23 VSR0 under modern rules), so the margin is 30%. That margin gives protection against gusts, turbulence and handling errors in the flare. Increments are then added for wind and gusts, typically half the steady headwind plus the full gust factor, up to a capped maximum.
rMlKi4lNLvROiVtrXYjE: VA is proportional to the square root of the weight, since it is the speed at which the aeroplane stalls at the limit load factor. A 19% weight reduction leaves 81% of the weight, and the square root of 0.81 is exactly 0.9 - so VA falls by 10%. This is why a lighter aeroplane must slow down MORE in turbulence, a counterintuitive but important point.
RNsUdEUc2rwvBOsNMk8W: V1 is the take-off DECISION speed - the maximum speed at which the first stopping action must be taken to reject, and the minimum speed at which the take-off may be continued after a failure. It is deliberately distinct from VEF, the speed at which the engine actually fails, which occurs one reaction time earlier.
rnYhFaq0tNdQBTlXCHaw: A buffet onset boundary chart is entered with weight, altitude and load factor to read off the low-speed and high-speed buffet Mach numbers. The key step here is the LOAD FACTOR: a 50 degree bank gives n = 1/cos 50 = 1.56, which raises the lift coefficient required and therefore pushes the LOW-SPEED boundary up to a higher Mach number, narrowing the buffet-free range. The high-speed boundary is far less affected by g.
rPiRmLeFD0vYf8Oq0drH: A shock wave is an abrupt, irreversible COMPRESSION. The flow decelerates violently from supersonic to subsonic, and much of its ordered kinetic energy is converted into random thermal energy - so static pressure, DENSITY and TEMPERATURE all INCREASE across it. Only TOTAL pressure falls, and that loss is what constitutes wave drag.
RPYJzzAHHLxKC8FpHkGe: The induced drag coefficient is proportional to CL SQUARED divided by ASPECT RATIO (with a span efficiency factor and pi as the constants). Two consequences follow: induced drag rises very steeply as speed falls and CL climbs, and a long slender wing suffers far less of it than a short stubby one - which is why aspect ratio is the primary design lever for efficiency.
rqp8xqomLo60uQuVu34X: The shock first appears near the point of maximum thickness, just downstream of the suction peak, and as Mach number increases further it STRENGTHENS and migrates toward the TRAILING edge. Eventually a second shock forms on the lower surface and travels aft too, until at fully supersonic speeds both stand at the trailing edge and a bow wave forms ahead of the leading edge.
rSsitfGftLMEYL8yDmRM: Obstacle clearance is about height gained per unit of DISTANCE, which is the climb gradient - and the greatest gradient is achieved at VX, the best angle of climb speed, where excess THRUST is greatest. VY gives the best height per unit of TIME, which gets you high quickly but covers more ground doing it, so it is the wrong choice when an obstacle is close ahead.
RStQvodvqTKmspotjqi2: A forward CG requires a larger tailplane DOWNLOAD, so the wing must generate the weight plus that download. More lift means a higher stalling speed, and it also means more induced drag - so for a given power setting the cruising speed FALLS. This is why an aft CG (within limits) gives the best cruise performance and the lowest stall speed, and a forward CG the most stability.
rt23PnHgUWQwiXnQNQzC: A laminar boundary layer's smooth parallel flow produces a gentle velocity gradient at the wall and therefore LOW skin friction drag - typically less than half that of a turbulent layer. The trade-off is that it carries very little energy near the surface, so it separates far EARLIER under an adverse pressure gradient. That is exactly why vortex generators deliberately trip the flow turbulent where separation matters more than friction.
rtuKnGSAHhnJgVf1WaEI: The certified thrust ratings are maximum take-off, maximum continuous and go-around - each defined with a time limit and demonstrated during engine certification. Maximum CRUISE thrust is an operational setting published by the manufacturer for normal cruise, not a certified rating. Maximum continuous is the highest thrust permitted for unlimited duration and is the figure used in one-engine-inoperative performance.
Rw1O08YrTzJM9qcYPrTE: Spanwise flow toward the tips thickens the outboard boundary layer on a swept-back wing, so the TIPS stall first. Because the tips sit well aft of the CG on a swept planform, losing their lift moves the centre of pressure FORWARD, producing a nose-up pitching moment that drives the angle of attack higher still - a self-worsening divergence. Fences, vortex generators and washout are the remedies.
RxZuh0xqSiNy068AYwEX: Deploying trailing-edge flap adds lift at the REAR of the section, so the centre of pressure moves AFT. Note what does not change: in steady level flight at constant IAS the lift must still equal the weight and the dynamic pressure is fixed, so the lift COEFFICIENT is unchanged - only CLmax and the drag increase. And the stall speed FALLS, since CLmax has risen.
rykoEDvCYDwDzo9cIPFu: VMCA is defined by the ability to maintain CONTROL - specifically straight flight with not more than 5 degrees of bank - after the critical engine suddenly fails. There is deliberately no requirement to hold altitude or achieve any rate of climb: at VMCA the aeroplane may well be descending. That is why V2 is set at least 10% above VMCA, so that the climb requirement is met with a control margin in hand.
rzcezcuuc5AYpmS5Z9pd: V2 is the take-off safety speed - the speed to be attained by the 35 ft screen height and maintained through the second segment climb with the critical engine inoperative. It must be at least 1.2 VS (1.13 VSR) and at least 1.1 VMCA. VLOF is the lift-off speed, V1 the decision speed and VEF the engine failure speed, all of which occur earlier.
S0o5eI935UubeKlEnE7i: At a positive angle of attack the flow must travel further and faster over the more curved UPPER surface, so that is where the highest velocities - and therefore, by Bernoulli, the lowest static pressures - occur. The resulting suction over the upper surface accounts for most of the lift, typically around two thirds of it. At the stagnation point the velocity is zero, the exact opposite.
s1lG71miShKJ3fQUfEUr: A fixed-pitch propeller has one blade angle, so it can only be optimised for a single flight condition - and one designed for cruise achieves its best blade angle of attack, and hence its best efficiency, in stabilised cruising flight. Away from that point efficiency falls off: at low forward speed with the same rpm the helix angle flattens and the blade angle of attack rises, so during the ground run it is HIGHER, not lower.
s31aJcVAVFxigJgG8twZ: Tip vortices induce a downward velocity component over the wing, tilting the local relative airflow downward. The angle between the free-stream direction and that tilted local flow is the INDUCED angle of attack, and it tilts the lift vector rearward, producing the rearward component we call induced drag. It is the direct consequence of the tip vortices, which is why anything that weakens them - high aspect ratio, winglets, tip tanks - reduces induced drag.
S4MrGc3czHy1GetuvlSQ: Induced drag coefficient is proportional to CL SQUARED, so it climbs steeply as lift coefficient rises - which is why induced drag dominates at low speed and high angle of attack. It also varies inversely with aspect ratio, so a HIGHER aspect ratio reduces it, and it grows with stronger tip vortices rather than weaker ones.
s4n7sf7arNqgJ2lIvHmL: The ETOPS diversion time is defined as the flying time to a suitable aerodrome in STILL AIR at the approved ONE-ENGINE-INOPERATIVE cruise speed. Both conditions matter: still air makes the figure a fixed planning distance independent of the day's winds, and the one-engine-inoperative speed reflects the case the rule exists to cover. Actual weather is then assessed separately when selecting the alternates.
SCD5DVvP7ZyUz9VJaMxp: Static stability describes the INITIAL tendency after a disturbance; dynamic stability describes what happens over time. If the aeroplane does not even begin to return toward its original condition, there is nothing for the subsequent motion to converge upon - so a statically unstable aeroplane can NEVER be dynamically stable. Static stability is a necessary, though not sufficient, condition for dynamic stability.
sCpKwk5UwFBDMdx0L9LM: The optimum altitude rises steadily as fuel burns, so economics always argue for climbing. What stops you is the buffet boundary: at high altitude the manoeuvre margin before buffet onset shrinks, and a step climb cannot be taken to a level where the required incremental g - conventionally 1.3g - is no longer available. Buffet, not fuel economics, is the practical ceiling on a step climb.
sDcVf7LsGY9BYRC9SwRw: The critical Mach number is defined as the FREE STREAM Mach number at which the flow somewhere on the airframe first reaches M1.0 LOCALLY - normally on the upper surface of the wing, near the point of greatest curvature. It is the threshold, not the consequence: shock waves, buffet and shock stall all appear at Mach numbers ABOVE Mcrit.
SeKA2BD1DbYw3hBQC3yv: VMCA is defined with the CRITICAL ENGINE INOPERATIVE: below it, the rudder can no longer generate enough yawing moment to balance the asymmetric thrust, so straight flight cannot be maintained. Note the qualifier - with all engines running the aeroplane is perfectly controllable well below VMCA, so a blanket statement that it is 'uncontrollable' is wrong. VMCA applies to any multi-engine aeroplane, not just four-engine types.
SfcYSnBRwoT8gTNMl56L: Density is mass per unit volume, so kg/m3 - ISA sea-level density is 1.225 kg/m3. Force follows from F = ma and is measured in newtons. The distractors confuse mass with force: a kilogram is a mass, not a force, and N/m3 would be a weight density rather than a mass density.
siQqvzOGWJdokl924UB6: Converging streamlines mean the flow is being squeezed through a smaller area, so by continuity it must ACCELERATE. Bernoulli's theorem then requires the static pressure to FALL to pay for the increased dynamic pressure. This is precisely the mechanism that produces suction over the upper surface of a wing, where the streamlines crowd together over the curved section.
sJh5yszJE6QTkTozgw86: Thrust equals drag only when there is no unbalanced force along the flight path - that is, in steady LEVEL flight at constant speed. In a climb the thrust must also overcome the rearward component of weight, so T = D + W sin(gamma); in a descent that component helps, so T is less than D; and in accelerated flight thrust must exceed drag to provide the acceleration.
sLxZZHKcL0Dj22g9pceS: The optimum altitude rises continuously through the cruise as fuel burns off, but ATC assigns discrete flight levels rather than permitting a continuous cruise climb. The aeroplane therefore drifts BELOW optimum as the optimum rises above it, then step climbs - sometimes ending up slightly ABOVE optimum immediately afterwards. Both excursions are a consequence of ATC constraints, not of economics.
SM3kxGNEfGo0T1bxVlXX: Glide distance through the AIR is set entirely by the lift-to-drag ratio, which is a function of angle of attack and configuration. Converting that to distance over the GROUND then requires the wind. Mass does not enter at all - a heavier aeroplane flies the same glide angle, just faster - and CLmax governs the stall, not the glide.
so5dAmn0AeIoCEKLJNYC: Work in metres. Over 5000 m at a 5% gradient the aeroplane gains 0.05 x 5000 = 250 m. It started from the 50 ft screen height, which is 15 m, so its total height above the runway at the obstacle is 265 m. The obstacle is 160 m high, so the clearance is 265 - 160 = 105 m. Remember to include the screen height - omitting it is the usual error.
sopEG4tp6lz5jQodbkaA: For a jet, thrust available is roughly constant with speed, so all three of these conditions coincide at VMD, the minimum drag speed: holding (maximum endurance, since fuel flow follows thrust), maximum climb ANGLE (where excess thrust is greatest), and minimum glide angle (where L/D is greatest). Maximum RANGE is the odd one out - it lies higher, at about 1.32 x VMD.
soPqk3cLK3Ufw35O9OtF: Downstream of transition the layer is turbulent, so continuous mixing brings fast free-stream air down toward the surface. The velocity profile becomes much fuller - a higher mean speed near the skin - and the steeper velocity gradient at the wall produces MORE skin friction drag. The layer also thickens. The compensation is that all that extra energy makes it far more resistant to separation.
sQ1DMyzVGIfYdRjyIHX9: An aft CG needs a smaller tailplane download, so the wing carries less total lift, generates less induced drag, and the aeroplane needs less thrust for a given speed - specific range improves and maximum range increases. The cost is reduced longitudinal stability and lighter stick forces, which is exactly why an aft limit exists. Stalling speed also falls slightly.
ST9Es7f51hz3paKIZUV6: Range over the GROUND depends on ground miles per kilogram, so in a headwind the optimum shifts to a HIGHER airspeed - the aeroplane spends less time exposed to the wind. The speed for maximum climb ANGLE, however, is an air-mass quantity determined by where excess thrust peaks, and wind cannot change that: it stays constant, even though the gradient achieved over the ground improves.
stPAPWRW6jJ6oc0YtW73: A yaw damper senses yaw rate with a rate gyro and applies rudder to oppose it, which breaks the roll-yaw coupling that produces DUTCH ROLL. It is essential on swept-wing aircraft, whose strong dihedral effect outweighs their directional stability. Buffeting and tuck under are compressibility phenomena, and spiral dive is a slow divergence corrected by the pilot or autopilot, not by a yaw damper.
STPGh7B7ya7kIUmAgvqa: VMCG must be a figure the crew can rely on in the WORST case, and on a wet or contaminated runway the nosewheel has little grip - steering and differential braking may be useless. Determining VMCG with primary aerodynamic control (essentially rudder) alone therefore makes the number valid on any surface. This conservatism is why VMCG is comparatively high and why it sets the lower bound on V1.
sVDLZWjeeuPoE0d0bVPI: Spanwise flow thickens the boundary layer toward the tips of a swept wing, so the TIPS stall first. Because the tips lie well aft of the CG on a swept planform, losing their lift moves the centre of pressure FORWARD, producing a nose-up pitching moment that drives the angle of attack higher still. Note it is the centre of PRESSURE that moves, not the centre of gravity.
SXB2bz7ZaJrlkF7wdKLO: Drag = CD x 1/2 rho V2 x S, so at constant angle of attack (fixed CD) and constant TAS, the drag is directly proportional to DENSITY. Raising the pressure while holding the temperature constant raises the density, so the drag increases. The same reasoning explains why the drag at a given IAS is independent of altitude: IAS is itself a measure of 1/2 rho V2.
sYTdsagu5TcuY8yF9pNy: In a steady descent the weight resolves into a component perpendicular to the flight path, which the lift balances, and a component along it, which helps drive the aeroplane forward. Lift therefore equals W cos(gamma), which is always LESS than the weight. The same is true in a climb - lift is only exactly equal to weight in level flight.
t5FnCeLDBkEXxQlFKwvq: VMCA must lie above the stalling speed (there is no point in a control speed below which the wing has already stopped flying), and V2 must be at least 1.1 VMCA to guarantee a control margin during the second segment climb. So the ordering is VS < VMCA < V2min. VMCA normally lies below VR as well, so any sequence placing it above VR or VLOF is wrong.
T8lklocRbZeDBqf8Iiu6: Compressibility effects - shock formation, wave drag, the aft shift of the centre of pressure, buffet - all depend on how close the LOCAL flow is to the speed of sound, and the MACH NUMBER (TAS divided by the local speed of sound) is precisely that measure. IAS, EAS and TAS on their own say nothing about it, because the speed of sound varies with temperature and therefore with altitude.
tbDZabxX8Gy7ect55HdR: The third segment is the level ACCELERATION segment: it begins at the acceleration altitude (at least 400 ft) when the aeroplane levels off and starts accelerating from V2 toward the flap retraction speed, and it ends when the flaps are up and the final climb speed is reached. Second segment ends where third begins; fourth (final) segment then follows in the clean configuration.
tBjBDN9clUxLkFMhItRp: At n = 2 the lift must double, and with the speed unchanged that means the lift COEFFICIENT doubles. Induced drag varies as CL SQUARED, so it quadruples - a factor of 4. Note what does not: lift itself only doubles, and TOTAL drag rises by less than 4 because the parasite component, which depends on speed alone, is unchanged.
TFNwTa8rKjZmgR78gI4l: A rate-one turn is 3 degrees per second, and rate of turn = g tan(bank)/V - so with the rate fixed, the bank angle required depends entirely on TAS. The rule of thumb follows: bank angle is roughly TAS in knots divided by 10, plus 7. Weight does not appear in the turn equations at all, and load factor is a consequence of bank rather than an independent input.
tGup8767m8CjPkx4Vozd: Moving the CG forward lengthens the moment arm to the tailplane, so a pitch disturbance generates a larger restoring moment - static longitudinal stability INCREASES and the static margin grows. The trade is that manoeuvrability decreases: more elevator deflection and more stick force are needed for a given g, and the larger tail download increases both trim drag and stalling speed.
tlCrzd1HUT7Ommj8bc2G: As angle of attack increases, the stagnation point migrates DOWN and aft along the lower surface of the leading edge. A flapper-switch or vane-type stall warner is positioned so that when the stagnation point passes below it, the local flow through its slot reverses and operates the switch. The device therefore senses stagnation point movement, which is a direct proxy for angle of attack.
tlD5vGpGeMnIOnu6xghv: A yaw damper senses yaw rate with a rate gyro and applies opposing rudder, breaking the roll-yaw coupling that produces DUTCH ROLL. Swept-wing jets need it because their strong dihedral effect outweighs their directional stability. Flutter is a structural phenomenon cured by stiffness and mass balance; buffeting is aerodynamic separation; and spiral dive is a slow divergence handled by the pilot or autopilot.
tLmMkbj1kBl2FsHiZrpL: About two thirds of the lift comes from the reduced pressure - the SUCTION - over the upper surface, where the flow is accelerated by the greater curvature, and only about one third from the increased pressure beneath. This is why contamination or damage to the upper surface is so much more damaging to lift than the same disturbance underneath, and why the wing stalls when the upper surface flow separates.
tMO7Pt039gBWZZEyMhaq: The buffet margin widens as altitude decreases, because the aeroplane needs a lower lift coefficient to support its weight in denser air, moving it away from the low-speed boundary. Descending at the same Mach number therefore increases the incremental g available before buffet onset. Flying at a larger angle of attack or extending flap would do the opposite, and flap has much lower structural limits in any case.
tMqpFJEB0wKtlqHKoIch: A higher OAT means less dense air, which reduces thrust while the drag at a given IAS is unchanged - so the excess thrust available for the second segment climb falls and the climb-limited mass must be reduced to restore the required gradient. Note the other traps: the climb limit is assessed at V2, not the best rate of climb speed, and wind does not affect an air-mass climb gradient at all.
TmveNoAggKDNHhP2SdpD: In level flight lift equals weight, and at a fixed lift coefficient the drag - and therefore the thrust required - is directly proportional to weight: D = W/(L/D). With specific fuel consumption unchanged, the hourly fuel flow follows the thrust, so a 5% increase in mass produces approximately a 5% increase in fuel flow. The relationship is essentially linear over small changes.
tpoJK5t2ZOG8Ot9GQ7x8: Beyond Mcrit a shock wave forms on the upper surface, and the separated flow behind it shakes the airframe - Mach buffet. The shock also moves the centre of pressure AFT and reduces the downwash reaching the tailplane, and both effects generate a nose-DOWN pitching moment: Mach tuck. The insidious part is that the nose-down pitch raises the Mach number further, so the tendency reinforces itself.
TQ40rg4LrDMbVHcUVrSX: Angle of attack is the angle between the wing's CHORD LINE and the RELATIVE AIRFLOW. It is referenced to the airflow, not to the airframe or the horizon - the fixed angle between chord and fuselage is the angle of INCIDENCE, and the angle between flight path and horizon is the climb or descent angle. Only angle of attack varies continuously in flight and determines whether the wing stalls.
Tr4lnh4RpxQqr4eGlVxu: The shock wave system is attached to the aeroplane and travels with it, so the point where it intersects the ground - the sonic boom carpet - sweeps across the surface at the aeroplane's GROUNDSPEED. Anyone on that track hears the boom once as the cone passes over them; the boom is continuous along the flight path, not a one-off event at the moment M1.0 is exceeded.
TsLpIy8voqXJYO8UrSMc: Spiral instability arises when directional stability is strong relative to lateral stability. In a disturbance the fin swings the nose into the sideslip faster than the dihedral effect can raise the lower wing, so the bank persists, the turn tightens and the nose drops - a slowly steepening descending turn. The opposite imbalance, strong lateral effect with weak directional stability, gives Dutch roll instead.
tsr2MlkuReXeBOhYuKa6: Being TODA-limited simply means the runway and clearway available are the binding constraint, so the actual take-off mass has been reduced to exactly the field-length limited mass. It says nothing about V1 being balanced - the balanced condition is a separate choice of V1 that equalises the accelerate-stop and accelerate-go distances, and a take-off can be field-length limited with an unbalanced V1.
TvQegLvn7gXVWUOoqcGR: The Fowler flap is the most effective because it does BOTH things at once: it translates rearward on tracks, increasing wing AREA, and then rotates down, increasing CAMBER - so both terms in the lift equation grow. Single-slotted flaps add camber plus boundary layer control, split flaps add drag more than lift, and plain flaps add camber alone.
TxJleClLAAbUJgu7oB8q: V2 is the take-off SAFETY speed - the speed to be attained by the 35 ft screen height and maintained through the second segment climb with the critical engine inoperative. It must be at least 1.2 VS (1.13 VSR) and at least 1.1 VMCA. The decision speed is V1, and the minimum control speed in the air is VMCA.
u0pVDTuPmbZHfnusXzbU: Maximum glide TIME means minimum rate of descent, and rate of descent scales with the square root of the weight - a lighter aeroplane flies the same angles at lower speeds, so it sinks more slowly. Low mass therefore maximises time aloft. Note that mass does not affect the glide DISTANCE, and wind affects distance over the ground but not the time aloft.
U2ZB2kaKGxptu92TbqxU: Slats give a large increase in CLmax - and therefore a large reduction in stall speed - for comparatively little drag, because they work by raising the STALLING ANGLE rather than by adding camber. Flaps give lift at a much higher drag cost. So the sensible retraction order is to shed the draggy device first and keep the efficient stall margin until the aeroplane is faster.
U47oqfi6znkR33EviYHR: In a steady descent the weight resolves into a component along the flight path that helps drive the aeroplane forward, so it acts with the thrust against the drag: T + W sin(gamma) = D. This is why a descent can be flown with reduced or idle thrust - the weight component is supplying part of the propulsive force. In a climb the same component opposes motion, giving T = D + W sin(gamma).
u6x3qkGbDyi8uh8PaI2F: A super (deep) stall requires the stalled wing's turbulent wake to blanket the horizontal tail, and a T-TAIL sits exactly in that wake at high angles of attack - the elevator loses effectiveness precisely when it is needed to lower the nose. Combined with a swept wing's tendency to pitch up at the stall, the condition can be stable and unrecoverable, which is why such designs carry stick pushers.
ub016FyC4BLGea0u2uKJ: Minimum sink rate is flown at (CL^3/CD^2)max and best glide ANGLE at (CL/CD)max, and the minimum-sink condition always occurs at the LOWER speed - typically around 76% of the best-glide speed. Fly slower to stay airborne longest; fly at best glide to travel furthest. The ordering never reverses between aeroplane types.
uc12aG0NynSjenwq6IJV: Raising the tail tilts the propeller disc, and a tilted spinning disc precesses: the applied force takes effect 90 degrees onward in the direction of rotation, producing a YAW. For a clockwise-turning propeller (seen from the cockpit) that yaw is to the left.
