Slipstream, torque and asymmetric blade effect are all present too, but they do not depend on raising the tail - precession is the ADDITIONAL effect that appears at that moment.
Ucm2rwIzJZIQ6f07P5Wk: The service ceiling is where the rate of climb has fallen to 100 ft/min, and rate of climb depends on excess POWER divided by weight. A lighter aeroplane needs less lift, produces less induced drag and therefore has more excess power available - so it can maintain 100 ft/min to a GREATER altitude. Reducing mass always raises both the service and the absolute ceiling.
ucXL7qPtRhJl05n3gnLb: The shock wave sits upstream of the aileron, and behind it the flow is separated and low in energy, so the aileron is operating in a wake of much reduced pressure and dynamic pressure. On top of that, pressure changes caused by deflecting the aileron cannot propagate FORWARD through the shock, so the surface can only influence the small region behind it instead of altering the pressure distribution over the whole wing. Both effects cut its authority.
UeznZkiNa9oA54dE1mp7: Both statements are correct. In ground effect the surface suppresses the tip vortices, so downwash is reduced, the effective angle of attack is greater and CL is higher while induced drag is much lower. LEAVING ground effect removes those benefits: at the same geometric angle of attack the lift coefficient falls and the induced drag coefficient rises - which is why an aeroplane that got airborne prematurely in ground effect may sink back as it climbs out of it.
UgBluCkHHHb10WkuNa0H: A gust changes the angle of attack, and the lift change that follows is proportional to the wing's LIFT CURVE SLOPE. Sweeping the wing reduces that slope, because only the flow component perpendicular to the quarter-chord line does the aerodynamic work - so the same gust produces a smaller lift change and a lower load factor. This gust alleviation is a useful secondary benefit of sweep.
ugLvsA2cjBrsYuu7Nq5E: A vertical gust abruptly changes the angle of attack and therefore the lift, producing a load factor above (or below) 1 - which is why turbulence penetration speeds exist. Note that increasing MASS actually REDUCES the gust load factor, since the increment is inversely proportional to wing loading: a heavier aeroplane has more inertia to resist the gust. CG position and density are not primary factors.
UGMcG1K5cMvdreaQtVJ5: Both statements are correct. An expansion wave is an isentropic ACCELERATION of supersonic flow around a convex corner, and static pressure, DENSITY and temperature all DECREASE through it while velocity and Mach number increase. So the values ahead of the wave are higher than those behind it in each case - the exact opposite of a shock wave, across which all three rise abruptly.
UhkDqqrWTzm0W2rwexvo: In a steady descent the weight resolves into a component perpendicular to the flight path, balanced by lift, and a component along it. Lift therefore equals W cos(gamma), which is always LESS than the weight - equivalently, weight is greater than lift. At a 1000 ft/min descent at 160 kt the angle is only about 3.5 degrees, so the difference is small, but the relationship holds in any descent.
uJ57qensuXz9wCAGl1vE: Take-off and landing performance calculations must use not more than 50% of a reported headwind and not less than 150% of a reported tailwind. The asymmetry is deliberately conservative: it guards against the headwind dying away or the tailwind being stronger than reported, either of which would lengthen the distances actually required.
Uj7YThKTjwPwPhjJ1mEQ: A fixed-pitch propeller has one blade angle, so it can only be optimised for a single flight condition - and one designed for cruise achieves its best blade angle of attack, and hence its best efficiency, in stabilised cruising flight. Away from that point efficiency falls off: at low forward speed with the same rpm the helix angle flattens and the blade angle of attack RISES, so it is higher during the ground run, not lower.
Ung19E8mcWDOZTmkTxAW: In a servo tab system the pilot's controls drive only the tab, and the main surface is free to float on its hinge. On the ground with little or no airflow there is nothing to position it, so the surface hangs wherever gravity and any local wind leave it - and a tailwind can blow it hard against its stops. This is why such aircraft have gust locks and why control checks must be done with care.
UnsELlZDVyLu3G5dQb1L: The 35 ft is a genuine vertical clearance: the minimum distance between the LOWEST part of the aeroplane and every obstacle within the obstacle accountability area, measured against the NET flight path (the gross gradient reduced by a mandatory margin). It is not a height at which any configuration or thrust change occurs - those are defined separately by the segment structure.
UnTAUnvpnjKFA5a68WIe: Optimum altitude - where specific range is greatest - rises continuously as fuel burns off, because a lighter aeroplane reaches its optimum lift coefficient in thinner air. Since ATC assigns discrete flight levels rather than allowing a continuous cruise climb, the aeroplane climbs in steps to stay as close to that rising optimum as possible. It is a fuel-economy technique, and it applies squarely to jets.
UnuuvihqnUi2FVrch7gR: Weight = 50,000 kg x 10 = 500,000 N, and total thrust = 2 x 60,000 = 120,000 N. In a climb the lift is close to the weight, so drag = W/(L/D) = 500,000/12 = 41,667 N. Then gradient = (T - D)/W = (120,000 - 41,667)/500,000 = 0.157, i.e. 15.7%. Note the two traps: use BOTH engines' thrust, and derive drag from the L/D ratio rather than guessing it.
UoAg5XoX6Xy851O7klGh: Contamination adds displacement drag as the wheels plough through the slush or wet snow, plus spray impingement drag on the airframe, both of which slow the acceleration and LENGTHEN the take-off distance. It also degrades braking should the take-off be rejected. This is why contaminated-runway take-off performance is separately certified and why reduced thrust is prohibited.
UoMEjTK05tYE5yDh7WZd: In a level turn the lift must support the weight and provide the turning force, so L = W / cos(bank). At 45 degrees, cos 45 = 0.707, giving L = 50,000 / 0.707 = about 70,700 N - a load factor of 1.41. Useful reference points: 30 degrees gives n = 1.15, 45 degrees n = 1.41 and 60 degrees n = 2.0.
UqabDOgTk5Xbv8VdFdEx: More flap means a higher CLmax, so the approach and touchdown speeds are lower and less energy has to be dissipated - the landing distance shortens. But more flap also means far more drag, so if a go-around becomes necessary the climb gradient available is significantly worse. That is precisely the trade a full-flap landing makes: runway length gained, go-around performance given up.
uSDCLv4HEmoehYz8BzFF: Best glide speed is by definition the speed at which (L/D)max is achieved, so it already gives the maximum distance available - any departure from it, faster OR slower, reduces the glide distance. Raising the pitch attitude slows the aeroplane below best glide, moving it onto the back of the drag curve where induced drag climbs steeply, so the glide angle steepens and the distance shortens.
UtB79UZP3zEzAo1Wf6iR: Moving the entire stabiliser provides far greater trim authority than a small tab on the elevator - essential on a large transport, which must be trimmed across an enormous range of speed, weight, CG and configuration. It also leaves the full elevator travel available for manoeuvring rather than spending part of it on trim. The costs are complexity and weight, and it does not change the aeroplane's stability.
uWzqL4CRWU18lLNp3k0c: In steady level flight the lift must equal the weight, and at a constant IAS the dynamic pressure is fixed - so the lift COEFFICIENT is determined and cannot change. Extending flap simply means the same CL is achieved at a lower angle of attack. What does change is CLmax (which is why the stall speed falls) and the drag.
uYznJ3sATbGWpU6e9QYP: Newton's third law: the engine turns the propeller to the right, so the propeller applies an equal and opposite reaction to the airframe, rolling it to the LEFT. The effect is greatest at high power and low airspeed - take-off - where it combines with slipstream effect and asymmetric blade effect to produce the familiar left-yawing and left-rolling tendency countered by right rudder.
uz0baWXRjkEEnTA0nYJJ: Aquaplaning is prevented by breaking through the water film and getting the tyres onto the surface. A firm, positive touchdown at the correct point does that - a soft, floated landing lets the aeroplane skim on the water at high speed with no braking available. Reverse thrust works regardless of runway friction and should be selected promptly, and brakes should be applied early so anti-skid can find whatever friction exists.
v3aKa0vJ1MmHjUNanz7t: Flap adds a great deal of drag for its lift, so (L/D)max falls and the best glide angle steepens - the aeroplane covers less distance for the height available. Note the other traps: flap LOWERS the angle of attack for maximum lift rather than raising it (that is what slats do), it makes the zero-lift angle MORE negative, and it certainly increases drag rather than lowering it.
V4QTHiIeNGFZVo8isC4c: For a turbojet the landing distance required must not exceed 60% of the landing distance available on a dry runway: 0.60 x 2400 = 1440 m. A turboprop would be allowed 70%, and a further 15% is applied to the required distance if the runway is expected to be wet.
v7QTWxyzEHhbArvAxOTi: The stick shaker must fire early enough to give the pilot a usable warning, but late enough not to be a nuisance - so it is set just above the stall, typically around 5-10% above VS depending on the aeroplane. The precise multiple is type-specific, so the safe general statement is simply that it triggers at a speed GREATER than VS. Note that 1.3 VS is VREF, the approach speed, far above the shaker.
vbvJFOXvXyIcZHhHfuwG: Total drag is the sum of induced drag, which varies as 1/V2 and dominates at low speed, and parasite drag, which varies as V2 and dominates at high speed. Adding the two gives the classic U-shaped curve: drag FALLS as speed rises from the stall, reaches a minimum at VMD where the two components are equal, then RISES again toward VNE.
vcNggN08D5rb7atr2w4b: The stall recovery is: unstall the wing first by moving the stick centrally forward to reduce the angle of attack, keeping the AILERONS NEUTRAL because aileron input at high alpha can provoke a wing drop or spin; apply FULL POWER to minimise height loss; and level the wings with RUDDER, which remains effective when the ailerons are not. Leaving the power at idle or waiting passively both cost far more height than necessary.
Vd54lSk4cSVSIjRjfewt: An aeroplane in flight is supported by the air rather than pivoted anywhere, so any unbalanced moment rotates it about its CENTRE OF GRAVITY - the point through which its mass is effectively concentrated. This is why every moment in stability and control analysis is taken about the CG, and why moving the CG changes the moment arms of the lift, the tail load and the thrust line.
VDm22QPRUZ42x4GB0m1I: An expansion wave is an isentropic ACCELERATION of supersonic flow around a convex corner. Static pressure, density and TEMPERATURE all decrease through it, so statement 1 is correct - the temperature ahead is higher than behind. But the VELOCITY increases, so statement 2 is wrong: the speed ahead of the wave is LOWER than behind it, not higher.
VF6QJzmr9jfJ8VJDGyOa: A turbulent boundary layer continuously mixes fast free-stream air down toward the surface, so the velocity climbs very steeply in the first fraction of a millimetre before levelling off. A laminar layer changes velocity gradually through its whole depth. That steeper wall gradient is exactly why the turbulent layer produces more skin friction - and also why it carries more energy and separates later.
Vf9BwcvppMfRh5IEpJxN: Drag depends on the dynamic pressure and the drag coefficient, and IAS is itself a direct measure of dynamic pressure. Holding IAS and mass constant therefore holds the lift coefficient - and hence the drag coefficient - essentially constant too, so the DRAG is almost unchanged throughout the climb. What does change dramatically is the THRUST available, which falls with density.
VfODVPhg7PtUf3XJeKc3: Trimming for a LOWER speed means trimming nose-UP, which requires the elevator to sit further up. A trim tab always acts in the OPPOSITE sense to the surface it drives: deflecting the tab DOWN generates an upload at the tab that levers the elevator UP. So the visible change is a down-deflected tab with the elevator further up.
VHAbzYdKe23bzSoAqJ90: Propeller efficiency is the ratio of useful power out to power in - the thrust power actually delivered to the airflow (power available) divided by the shaft or brake power supplied by the engine. Typical peak values are around 85%, the losses going to profile drag on the blades, the energy left in the slipstream, and tip and compressibility effects.
VhnW1nE1kNidPhDT9SvD: A forward CG lengthens the moment arm between the CG and the tailplane, so the tailplane's own moment about the CG is larger - but the wing's restoring moment is larger still, and the aeroplane is correspondingly more stable and more reluctant to change attitude. Producing a given load factor therefore requires MORE elevator deflection and more stick force, which is exactly why stick force per g rises as the CG moves forward.
VJjBymDKlP6oATTzQDdC: The climb-limited take-off mass is derived from the climb GRADIENT achieved relative to the AIR, which is a function of thrust, drag and weight - none of which the wind affects. So a tailwind leaves the climb-limited mass unchanged. What a tailwind does hurt is the field-length limited mass and the obstacle-limited mass, since both depend on distance over the ground.
VO6FPuLph1bcKjM3dU9l: The buffet onset boundary chart plots the LOW-SPEED and HIGH-SPEED (Mach) buffet boundaries against weight, altitude and load factor - so it shows the Mach range within which the aeroplane can be flown buffet-free, and how that range narrows with height. It is the chart used to establish the maximum altitude for a required manoeuvre margin, typically 1.3g. MMO is a fixed limit that does not vary with mass.
vRDPtNUcTB0lBaL2i2St: The critical Mach number is the highest free-stream Mach number at which the flow remains subsonic EVERYWHERE on the airframe - the moment any point (normally the upper surface of the wing) reaches M1.0 locally, Mcrit has been reached. Above it shock waves form, with wave drag, buffet and the transonic trim change following. It is an aerodynamic threshold, not a certified operating limit like MMO.
VSMOcbMjDy1V9OwAOvcu: Stall speed rises with the SQUARE ROOT of the load factor. At 45 degrees of bank n = 1/cos 45 = 1.41, and the square root of 1.41 is 1.19 - an increase of about 19%. Note the trap: 41% is the increase in LIFT (the load factor itself), not in stall speed. At 60 degrees n = 2 and the stall speed rises by 41%.
vSZ31XXkWlzAa21FjxoM: A trim tab acts in the opposite sense to the surface it drives, so an UP-deflected tab levers the elevator DOWN, which pitches the nose down and trims the aeroplane for a higher speed. The cockpit indicator shows the trimmed condition of the AEROPLANE, not the position of the tab - so it reads nose-down.
vtEkPV5XsYJnDgC4AdrS: Below V1 the accelerate-stop distance available is still sufficient, so a failure recognised there requires the take-off to be REJECTED. Above V1 it must be continued, because the stop is no longer assured. That is the entire purpose of defining V1 - to settle the decision in advance rather than at the moment of the failure. Clearway and stopway affect the distances available, not the rule itself.
VZuZQuOhs0dmv8XB9zOO: Clearway adds to the take-off distance available but NOT to the accelerate-stop distance available, so it improves only the go case. To exploit it you unbalance the field length by REDUCING V1: a lower V1 shortens the stop distance (which must still fit the unchanged ASDA) while lengthening the go distance (which now has the extra clearway to run into). The net result is a higher field-length limited mass at a lower V1.
w17FSBytisDto3yPkVXu: Trailing-edge flap increases the camber of the section, which shifts the whole CL-alpha curve UP and to the LEFT: CLmax rises, but it is reached at a SMALLER angle of attack. This is why the nose attitude is lower on a flapped approach, and why flap does not improve the stall margin in angle-of-attack terms. Slats do the opposite, raising the stalling angle by 5-10 degrees.
W8HLOTKocQRsB7oxetjV: The rejected take-off drill begins by closing the thrust levers - removing the force that is accelerating the aeroplane must come first, and it also arms the automatic ground spoilers and autobrake logic on many types. Braking, spoilers and reverse then follow in quick succession. The certified accelerate-stop distance assumes this sequence, which is why deviating from it invalidates the calculation.
WBOD1I3MHIjis7ulKLZ0: Sweeping a wing reduces the effective airflow over the aerofoil section by the cosine of the sweep angle, which lowers the CLmax achievable and therefore RAISES the stall speed. So reducing the sweep angle lowers the stall speed. T-tails, anhedral and dihedral affect stability and stall behaviour but not the stalling speed itself, which is governed by CLmax and wing loading.
wBxXCTZIY6dN8NUvGF4F: An aeroplane in flight is supported by the air rather than pivoted about any fixed point, so any unbalanced moment rotates it about its CENTRE OF GRAVITY. This is why all stability and control moments are taken about the CG, and why shifting the CG alters the moment arms of the wing lift, the tail load and the thrust line all at once.
Wd0HqaIk6aYKKWwH8e6y: VREF, the landing reference speed to be maintained down to 50 ft on short final, is 1.3 times the stalling speed in the landing configuration: 1.3 x 100 = 130 kt. That 30% margin protects against gusts, turbulence and handling errors in the flare. Wind and gust increments are then added on top, up to a capped maximum.
wfVtEKk7fSOjWTqf7p65: TAS = IAS divided by the square root of the density RATIO, so the two are equal only when the density equals the ISA sea-level value. BELOW sea level the air is denser than that, the ratio exceeds 1, and the TAS is therefore LOWER than the IAS. Note also that TAS IS the aeroplane's speed relative to the undisturbed airstream - it is neither higher nor lower than it.
wHeL7WLSDitKwtwVMdqo: Climbing into a headwind that strengthens with height means the aeroplane is continuously flying into faster-moving air, so its inertia converts that into extra indicated airspeed - an increasing-performance shear. Holding IAS constant releases that surplus energy into the climb, improving the rate. The headwind simultaneously reduces the groundspeed, so the climb angle over the ground improves as well.
WijUahEmtiKU6JnSx6ru: Vortex generators are small vanes that trip the boundary layer turbulent, mixing high-energy free-stream air down toward the skin. That extra energy lets the layer survive the steep adverse pressure gradient behind a shock wave, so shock-induced separation - and the Mach buffet and control degradation that follow - is much reduced. They do not change Mcrit or the strength of the shock itself; they manage its consequences.
wiUTc5qdUy4dn62D2sse: Induced drag is proportional to lift squared divided by speed squared, so at a fixed weight it varies as 1/V2 - it falls away rapidly as speed increases. It is the dominant drag component at low speed, which is why the drag curve rises so steeply behind VMD, and it increases with WEIGHT rather than decreasing with it.
WIx1Ub33MNxloOhXcyDr: The aerodynamic centre is defined as the point about which the pitching moment coefficient stays CONSTANT as the angle of attack changes - for a subsonic aerofoil it lies at about 25% chord, moving to about 50% in supersonic flow. Working moments about this fixed point is what makes stability analysis tractable, since the centre of pressure itself moves with angle of attack.
wJEQCn2AY9SPUQ5bJjzr: The buffet margin widens as altitude decreases, because the aeroplane needs a lower lift coefficient to support its weight in denser air, moving it away from the low-speed boundary. Descending at the same Mach number therefore increases the incremental g available before buffet onset. Flying at a LARGER angle of attack does the opposite - it takes the aeroplane straight toward the low-speed buffet boundary.
WmEdHxM0j8HQ1Xp7jogD: An expansion wave is an isentropic acceleration of supersonic flow around a convex corner: velocity and MACH NUMBER increase while static pressure, density and temperature all decrease. It is the exact opposite of a shock wave, across which the flow decelerates and those three properties rise abruptly - and unlike a shock, an expansion involves no loss of total pressure.
wnhLuYN6ji8fqOJDxdRm: The standard approach speed rule is 1.5 times the stall speed - a 50% margin - plus half the estimated wind speed. The base margin covers gusts and handling errors in the flare; the wind additive covers the airspeed loss as the aeroplane descends through a wind gradient into slower-moving air near the surface. Both parts matter: omitting the wind allowance is what produces an undershoot in a steep gradient.
wo6xGm7ucNRp2MKLJ7Y4: For a jet, thrust available is roughly constant with speed, so the maximum EXCESS thrust - and therefore the steepest climb angle - occurs where the drag is least: at the speed giving the highest CL/CD ratio, VMD. Note that the highest CL/CD SQUARED ratio is the minimum-power condition, which governs a propeller aeroplane's endurance, not a jet's climb angle.
WtTIIx7fczMAOqJo4xvx: The best glide angle occurs at a fixed angle of attack, and therefore a fixed lift coefficient, whatever the mass - so (L/D)max and the glide ANGLE are unchanged by weight. What changes is the SPEED at which that angle of attack is flown: a heavier aeroplane needs more lift at the same CL, so it must fly faster. Same distance covered, just more quickly and with a higher rate of descent.
wUJ9T0uPJ5Hx9AryJezk: The shock wave sits upstream of the aileron, and behind it the flow is separated and low in energy, so the aileron operates in a wake of much reduced pressure and dynamic pressure and generates far less force. Compounding this, pressure changes from deflecting the aileron cannot propagate FORWARD through the shock, so the surface can influence only the small region behind it rather than the whole wing.
WUWguQbxiTRxx1ucwgBd: VA is defined as the speed at which the aeroplane stalls at exactly the manoeuvring LIMIT load factor - 2.5 for a large transport, 3.8 for a light aeroplane in the normal category. Below VA a single full elevator deflection therefore stalls the wing before it can overstress the structure. The ULTIMATE load factor (1.5 times the limit) is a structural design figure and plays no part in defining VA.
WxmJubg4aHmBwNEU68kg: V1 is bounded below by VMCG - below that speed the rudder cannot keep the aeroplane straight after a failure, so a decision to continue would be meaningless - and bounded above by VR, since the decision must be made before rotation begins. Within that window V1 is chosen to satisfy the accelerate-stop and accelerate-go distances available.
wYol1Yk5JopGKcl36H0S: The short period mode is a rapid, heavily damped PITCH oscillation - rotation about the lateral axis - with a period of only a few seconds, in which the angle of attack changes but the speed barely does. It must be well damped, because a poorly damped short period is what makes an aeroplane feel twitchy and can lead to pilot-induced oscillation. The phugoid is the long-period pitch mode.
wYvSsq90qsNlPV8O9nXp: The flow accelerates most where the aerofoil is thickest and the curvature greatest, which on a swept wing is the upper surface near the WING ROOT. That is therefore where the local flow first reaches M1.0 and the first shock wave forms - by definition, at the critical Mach number. As Mach increases further the shock strengthens and moves aft and outboard.
wZIEmO7dMq1KnkiLN4gj: A balanced V1 is by definition the V1 at which the accelerate-stop distance exactly equals the one-engine-inoperative take-off distance. Because reducing V1 shortens the stop case while lengthening the go case, that crossing point gives the MINIMUM field length satisfying both. Note that with a clearway available the balanced V1 is no longer optimal - a lower, unbalanced V1 gives a higher mass.
wzPGalQBbn4xtiOoV1kh: At a constant angle of attack and mass, the lift coefficient is fixed and the lift must still equal the weight - so the dynamic pressure, and therefore the CAS, is unchanged. With CD fixed and dynamic pressure fixed, the DRAG is unchanged too. What increases is the TRUE airspeed, because the same dynamic pressure requires a higher V as density falls.
x0UEg88hM9oH4NPcXz5N: Any body producing lift also produces drag - the two are simply the components, perpendicular and parallel to the airflow, of a single resultant force. A flat plate at a small angle of attack deflects the airflow downward and so generates lift, and it necessarily generates induced drag along with skin friction and form drag. A lifting surface with no drag is not physically possible.
X3ArXG12UFXUbEW64G1B: Stopway lengthens the accelerate-stop distance available and clearway lengthens the take-off distance available - each improving one side of the V1 trade but not the other. V1 is therefore the speed that shifts to exploit whichever is present. VR, V2, VMCG and VMCA are all aerodynamic or control speeds determined by the aeroplane, not by the runway environment.
xbyC6RozYKikyPX8i4BD: A clearway is an obstacle-free area beyond the runway over which the aeroplane may make its initial climb to 35 ft, so it counts toward the TAKE-OFF DISTANCE AVAILABLE - up to a maximum of half the take-off run available. It cannot be used for stopping, so it adds nothing to the accelerate-stop distance available; that is what a STOPWAY does.
xcCD5yj7VuxRTOeEP5w8: Both statements have the direction wrong. Gyroscopic precession makes an applied force take effect 90 degrees onward in the direction of rotation, so for a propeller turning clockwise as seen from the cockpit, pitching up precesses into a yaw to the RIGHT (not left), and yawing right precesses into a pitch DOWN (not up). The familiar tailwheel case follows the same rule: raising the tail yaws the aeroplane left.
xDrJLG6jUuXWX9VwPd0C: Leading-edge devices work on the mechanism that actually limits CLmax - boundary layer separation - by ducting or guiding high-energy air over the upper surface. They therefore RAISE the critical (stalling) angle of attack, typically by 5-10 degrees, and raise CLmax with it. Trailing-edge flaps do the opposite to the stalling angle, lowering it while adding camber, and all high-lift devices increase drag.
xEo7HFJ85m9TXpTUJ84t: Mass flow is density multiplied by area multiplied by velocity. Raising the temperature at constant pressure makes the air LESS DENSE, and with the area and velocity unchanged the mass flow must therefore DECREASE. This is the same density effect that reduces engine thrust and degrades take-off performance on a hot day.
XFf0tlN9szMlde30JnpO: The V2 floor depends on how much the aeroplane can reduce its one-engine-inoperative stall speed. Turboprops with MORE than three engines - and jets with provisions for significantly reducing the power-on stall speed - are allowed the lower figure of 1.15 VS. Two- and three-engined turboprops must use 1.2 VS. V2 must also be at least 1.1 VMCA.
XGQJhf6JnqfbzOAX4H1H: The phugoid is the long-period pitch mode, a slow exchange of speed for height in which the angle of attack barely changes - period typically 40-60 seconds. Its damping is normally very WEAK, so it can take many cycles to die away, but because it is so slow the pilot corrects it without conscious effort. The short period mode, by contrast, is a few seconds long and must be heavily damped.
xl9cpFBSKy77Ob3MNf3P: A swept wing stalls at the tips first, which moves the centre of pressure forward and produces a NOSE-UP pitching moment. If the wing's turbulent wake then blankets the horizontal tail - the classic T-tail geometry - the elevator loses effectiveness at exactly the moment it is needed to lower the nose. That combination is the deep or super stall, and it is why such designs carry stick pushers.
xpBiSTQnsLtkIWn6Xpli: The induced drag coefficient is proportional to CL SQUARED (divided by aspect ratio, with a span efficiency factor and pi as constants). The square law is why induced drag climbs so steeply at low speed and high angle of attack, and why it quadruples in a 2g turn where the lift coefficient doubles.
xQK5YpqqzUExJpadxGkr: In a holding pattern the aeroplane flies at (L/D)max, so the thrust required equals W/(L/D)max - directly proportional to weight. With specific fuel consumption assumed constant, the fuel flow scales with weight in the same way: 3100 x (105,000 / 95,000) = 3426 kg/h. Sense-check the direction: the heavier aeroplane must burn MORE, not less.
XqNibvHvLg80LNUIBZ6d: A nose-heavy (forward CG) aeroplane needs a larger nose-up balancing moment, which means a greater tailplane DOWNLOAD - and to generate a download the stabiliser must sit at a negative incidence, with its LEADING EDGE LOWER. A tail-heavy aeroplane needs less download, so its stabiliser leading edge sits higher. This is exactly why the take-off trim setting is scheduled against the CG from the load sheet.
xtyomuXPsuNFifhtYyOh: The climb-limited take-off mass derives from the climb GRADIENT relative to the AIR, which depends on thrust, drag and weight - none of which the wind can change. A headwind therefore has no effect on it. What a headwind does improve is the field-length limited mass and the obstacle-limited mass, since both depend on distance measured over the ground.
XUyvhmuVwygrEvtHYBFY: Induced drag originates at the WING TIP, where air spills from the high-pressure lower surface around the tip to the low-pressure upper surface and rolls up into the tip vortex. That vortex induces downwash over the whole wing, tilting the lift vector rearward. Every device aimed at induced drag - winglets, tip tanks, high aspect ratio, elliptical loading - works on what happens at the tip.
xWdQjOcCIj6KyZHigf1E: A stick pusher applies a firm automatic nose-down input once the angle of attack reaches a value beyond which the aeroplane's natural stall behaviour would be unacceptable - a deep stall or a violent wing drop. It is a last-resort protection fitted where the stall characteristics fail certification, and it acts AFTER the stick shaker, which is a warning rather than an intervention.
XWgKDtYUNUS39lBUNB2I: Stall speed rises with the SQUARE ROOT of the load factor: Vs(n) = Vs x sqrt(n) = 100 x sqrt(2) = 141 kt. A load factor of 2 corresponds to a 60 degree bank in a level turn, so the familiar result follows - a 60 degree turn raises the stall speed by 41%.
xX9zQs3dWvzOyEbmMKHL: Static pressure is the pressure of the air molecules themselves, arising from their random thermal motion, so it acts equally in ALL directions - it has no preferred orientation. That is precisely why a static port can be a flush hole in the fuselage side, aligned parallel to the flow, and still sense it correctly. DYNAMIC pressure, by contrast, is directional, acting only along the flow.
XYb4WP4V1fGI6xT41xMq: Vortex generators re-energise the boundary layer so it can survive the steep adverse pressure gradient behind a shock wave, which delays shock-induced separation and cuts the associated transonic drag rise. They do NOT alter the critical Mach number - the shock still forms at the same free-stream Mach - they simply manage its consequences.
xYgm5Lcy1KhTFvLG5GgO: V1 cannot exceed VR, because the decision to continue or reject must be made before rotation begins - there is no meaningful 'stop' decision once the aeroplane is being rotated. At the other end V1 must be at least VMCG. Tyre speed and brake energy (VMBE) impose further ceilings on V1 when they are limiting.
y3Vetgq1j9BS3NK2Qvik: Specific range for a jet improves with altitude, and for two reasons: the same indicated airspeed corresponds to a higher TRUE airspeed in thinner air, so more miles are covered per hour, and jet engines become more efficient in the colder air aloft. This is why jets cruise as high as weight and buffet margin permit, and why optimum altitude rises as fuel burns.
YaJLyARdaDM3vlMvPkSN: An uphill slope means gravity opposes the acceleration all the way to V1, and although it then HELPS the braking, the extra distance used in accelerating outweighs the saving in stopping - so the accelerate-stop distance increases overall. All the other options shorten it: a headwind, a lower mass and colder (denser) air all improve both acceleration and deceleration.
yCTajK2jMVSdIf5SKRkW: The aerodynamic ceiling - coffin corner - is where the rising low-speed buffet boundary meets the falling high-speed buffet boundary, leaving a single speed at which the aeroplane can be flown and no manoeuvre margin at all. Practical maximum altitude is set well below it, at the height where a specified margin (conventionally 1.3g) still remains.
YIrbwIhmEgVahUiNHcoQ: Two effects stack up. A fully forward CG demands the largest nose-up moment from the tail, and full flap increases the downwash at the tailplane while producing a nose-down pitching moment of its own. Both call for maximum tailplane download, which means maximum UP elevator - which is precisely why the forward CG limit is set by elevator authority in the landing flare.
yNbPo26nrab5PHmxAB7I: Wing loading is weight divided by wing area, and stall speed is proportional to the square root of wing loading divided by CLmax. Increasing the wing loading - by adding weight or reducing area - therefore raises the stall speed. It does not change CLmax, which is a property of the aerofoil and configuration, and it worsens rather than improves the glide angle.
yngAqrEEsaFYor61o3H8: The buffet margin widens as altitude decreases, because the aeroplane needs a lower lift coefficient to support its weight in denser air, taking it further from the low-speed boundary. Descending at the same Mach number therefore increases the incremental g available before buffet onset. Increasing angle of attack or extending flap would do the opposite - and flap has far lower structural limits in any case.
yNxiBN0Hh54Ev6gQqzoU: For a jet at constant rpm, two effects roughly cancel as speed increases: momentum drag rises (the engine has to accelerate air that is already moving fast), but ram compression raises the mass flow through the engine. The net result is that thrust is very nearly INDEPENDENT of airspeed - the assumption used throughout jet performance work. Thrust does fall markedly with altitude, however, as density decreases.
Yp44MukQPhK6qrfvygHh: The second segment runs from gear-up to the acceleration altitude, so its defining conditions are: gear UP (1), flaps still in the TAKE-OFF position (4), one engine inoperative with the remainder at take-off thrust (6), and the speed held at V2 (9). It is the most demanding segment for gradient - 2.4% for a twin - which is why the climb-limited take-off mass is usually set here. Statement 10 describes where the segment begins, not the gradient condition.
yQYaQBlUNMnfIQ59o2i3: Moving the CG aft shortens the moment arm to the tailplane, so a given elevator deflection produces more pitching moment and less stick force is needed per g. Beyond the aft limit that stick force per g drops below the certified minimum, leaving the aeroplane dangerously easy to over-stress with almost no force cue. Static longitudinal stability falls too, and spin recovery becomes worse, not better.
yrZu7MGF8y6bP5cwu0uM: Below the tropopause, climbing at a constant Mach number, the temperature falls so the local speed of sound falls - and with the Mach number fixed, the TAS falls with it. The density falls faster still, so the IAS decreases as well, and more rapidly. This decaying IAS is why the lift coefficient and angle of attack must rise through the climb, narrowing the buffet margin.
YTVTEI501PcPVh6G7B2U: Adding blades increases the total blade area, so the propeller can absorb more shaft power without having to grow in diameter - which matters because tip speed limits diameter. The trade-offs are a small loss of efficiency (each blade works in the wake of the one ahead) and extra weight and cost, though noise generally REDUCES because the same power is spread over more, less heavily loaded blades.
YwinMyn2AQZdznwIOhoJ: Lift coefficient is a function of the aerofoil shape and the ANGLE OF ATTACK, so at a given configuration the only way to raise it is to raise alpha. Flap extension does the same job by changing the shape, shifting the whole CL-alpha curve upward. Speed is not a means of increasing CL - in level flight, flying FASTER actually reduces the CL required, since the lift must stay equal to the weight.
YX4kYWohkdZi1tcr6FBK: In incompressible terms the stalling IAS is constant at all altitudes, since IAS is a direct measure of dynamic pressure. But at high altitude the true airspeed for a given IAS is much higher, so compressibility effects appear: local shock waves reduce the achievable CLmax and the stalling IAS therefore INCREASES. This rising low-speed boundary, meeting the falling high-speed one, creates coffin corner.
YXMvHUXfokC39VAk9ag5: The brake energy limit is about how much kinetic energy the brakes must absorb in a rejected take-off. An UPHILL slope means gravity helps the deceleration, so the brakes absorb less energy for the same speed - and a higher mass therefore becomes acceptable. Note the trade: the same uphill slope lengthens the take-off distance, so if the take-off were field-length limited instead, the effect would be the opposite.
YZn2qtmM1PihX0js6i9k: Apply each correction in turn to the 800 m baseline. Elevation 2000 ft: +2 x 20 = +40. Temperature: ISA at 2000 ft is 11 C, so 21 C is a +10 C deviation, giving +10 x 5 = +50. Up-slope 2%: +2 x 15 = +30. Tailwind 5 kt: +5 x 10 = +50. Total = 800 + 40 + 50 + 30 + 50 = 970 m. The step most often missed is computing the ISA deviation at FIELD elevation rather than against 15 C.
Z4oMSpEMfXgpUYwvCQ7L: Tuck under is caused by the shock wave moving the centre of pressure aft and reducing the downwash at the tailplane - and no shock wave can exist until the local flow reaches M1.0, which by definition is the critical Mach number. So the phenomenon appears only ABOVE Mcrit. Below it the flow is entirely subsonic and there is no mechanism to produce it.
z9aGWMmq3gPmfQiwAj5N: The approach climb requirement is a go-around case with ONE ENGINE INOPERATIVE, assessed in the approach configuration (gear up, approach flap) at go-around thrust. It sets a minimum gradient - 2.1% for a twin, 2.4% for three engines, 2.7% for four - and it frequently limits the landing mass. The all-engines, full-flap, gear-down case is the separate LANDING climb requirement.
ZAL36pISeIPgFrf2UZjn: In transonic flight shocks appear wherever the local flow first goes supersonic, so they can form at several places on the airframe independently - typically the wing upper surface first, then the lower surface, then the tailplane, fin, canopy and nacelles as Mach increases. Note the other errors: a normal shock is perpendicular to the local FLOW rather than to the surface, and pressure and temperature RISE across it.
ZAQmC41HBQ6WSoUxi20D: A small upward (negative) flap deflection reduces the wing's camber, which lowers the lift coefficient at a given angle of attack but also reduces the drag - useful in high-speed cruise, where less lift is needed anyway. Some aircraft use exactly this, deflecting the flaps or ailerons slightly up in cruise to optimise the wing's section for the lower cruise CL.
ZddpSK798yFZfcwcFL8k: The centre of pressure is by definition the point at which the resultant aerodynamic force - and hence the lift - can be considered to act. On a cambered aerofoil it moves forward as angle of attack increases, which is why the fixed AERODYNAMIC CENTRE at about 25% chord is preferred as the reference point for stability calculations.
ZDklnWGiG9LboxEUu0YF: At cruise Mach number the outboard ailerons are locked out, because their long moment arm applied to a flexible outer wing risks aileron reversal and imposes heavy bending loads. Roll control is provided by the INBOARD ailerons, assisted by the spoilers. The outboard surfaces are re-activated at low speed with the flaps and slats extended, where their extra authority is needed.
ZDNBeVL7S72TjN3W8msz: Lift must still equal weight, so at a lower speed the dynamic pressure is smaller and the lift COEFFICIENT must be higher - achieved by increasing the angle of attack. That is the one thing that is certain here. What happens to thrust depends on which side of VMD the aeroplane is on: above it, slowing down reduces drag; below it, in the region of reversed command, slowing down INCREASES the drag and requires more thrust.
ZECMwD3ArlM7EswLJG3L: Angle of attack is defined as the angle between the RELATIVE AIRFLOW and the aerofoil's CHORD LINE. It is referenced to the airflow, not the airframe or the horizon - the fixed angle between chord and fuselage is the angle of INCIDENCE, and the angle between flight path and horizon is the climb or glide path angle. Only the angle of attack determines whether the wing stalls.
zfCB8DktEfiStWdARhkL: The polar plots CL against CD for the whole aeroplane. Two things are read directly from it: the maximum lift COEFFICIENT, at the top of the curve, and the maximum CL/CD ratio, found where a tangent drawn from the ORIGIN touches the curve - that tangent point being the best lift-to-drag ratio and hence the best glide angle. Absolute forces cannot be read from a coefficient plot.
zfulgMmT5Rur03N123kZ: Static longitudinal stability is read from the SLOPE of the pitching moment coefficient plotted against angle of attack: a negative slope means a restoring nose-down moment, which is stability, and the steeper that negative slope, the greater the static margin. A curve whose negative slope becomes progressively shallower at higher angles of attack therefore represents DECREASING positive stability - the aeroplane is still stable, but less so as alpha increases.
zGmL0i9erj8Aq7YNMF1r: Holding thrust constant while increasing airspeed means the engine must accelerate air that is already arriving faster, so the momentum drag rises and more fuel is needed to sustain the same net thrust. The increase is modest, which is why jet specific fuel consumption is often treated as roughly constant, but the trend is upward with speed - not downward and not flat.
zhamD2RZZv2HXWWHobUI: Descending at a constant Mach number, the density increases rapidly, so the dynamic pressure - and hence the IAS - climbs steadily. With the same weight to support and more dynamic pressure available, the lift coefficient required falls. Note that the TAS actually INCREASES in the descent (the warmer air raises the speed of sound), so the falling CL cannot be attributed to a speed loss.
ZJjXBdRRM5mhwmY2F0RC: Two effects stack up. A fully forward CG demands the largest nose-up moment from the tailplane, and full flap both increases the downwash at the tail and produces a nose-down pitching moment of its own. Both call for maximum tailplane download, which means maximum UP elevator - which is exactly why the forward CG limit is set by elevator authority in the landing flare.
ZPPLFkrIoHqcYKMWyMQy: Dihedral is what creates the dihedral effect: in a sideslip the lower wing meets the airflow at a greater effective angle of attack and generates more lift, rolling the aeroplane back toward level. Increasing the dihedral strengthens that rolling moment, so holding a given sideslip angle requires MORE opposing aileron and therefore a greater lateral control force. This is why excessive dihedral makes an aeroplane tiring to fly in a crosswind sideslip.
zq62N344zs7WI6o76mMd: TAS = Mach number multiplied by the local speed of sound, and the speed of sound depends only on temperature. Descending from FL350 the temperature RISES, so the speed of sound rises and, with the Mach number held constant, the TAS increases with it. Pressure and density play no part in the speed of sound - only temperature does.
ZQgxGPJ3ne0KU263zSUG: The Mach trimmer exists to restore a positive stick force gradient above the Mach number at which tuck under would otherwise flatten or reverse it. Without it the aeroplane loses apparent speed stability at high Mach, so the only safe response is to restrict the MAXIMUM MACH NUMBER to a value below where the problem appears. Weight and CG do not address the underlying compressibility effect.
ZQLcmwSXw1CZzn9y1aHs: With a trimmable horizontal stabiliser, 'in trim' means the stabiliser has been driven to the position at which the elevator is faired with it and no control force is required - so the elevator deflection is zero. That is the whole point of trimming with the stabiliser rather than the elevator: it returns the full elevator travel to manoeuvring use rather than spending part of it holding an out-of-trim load.
zsAsZi4AUQpwhgxIn2Fb: Differential deflection makes the UP-going aileron travel further than the down-going one, so that the extra parasite drag from the raised surface balances the extra induced drag from the lowered one. Equalising the drag of the two ailerons is exactly what cancels adverse yaw. It is not needed to obtain roll rate, and it does not affect CLmax or total lift.
ZUvY3MQ8MRriQKwe802q: Long range cruise deliberately accepts a specific range 1% below the maximum in exchange for the HIGHER of the two speeds that deliver it. Because the specific range curve is very flat near its peak, that 1% fuel penalty typically buys 3-5% more speed - which is almost always worth it once crew time, maintenance and schedule are costed in. Operating near buffet onset is a hazard, not a reason.
ZWnzQzGY997phWdaYUUd: The area rule states that transonic wave drag depends chiefly on how the total cross-sectional area of the whole aircraft varies along its length, so that distribution must change as smoothly as possible. Waisting the fuselage where the wing joins - the 'coke bottle' shape - compensates for the wing's area and smooths the curve, cutting WAVE drag substantially. Form, skin friction and induced drag are unaffected.
ZWW8sXbh0DVUp3msv9OX: In transonic flight shocks form wherever the local flow first goes supersonic, so they appear at several places independently as Mach increases - typically the wing upper surface first, then the lower surface, then the tailplane, fin, canopy and nacelles. Note the other errors: a normal shock is perpendicular to the local FLOW rather than to the surface, and pressure and temperature RISE across it, they do not drop.
Zy9D8ZZFXvfxaL3ktvD6: Weight = 150,000 x 10 = 1,500,000 N, and total thrust = 4 x 75,000 = 300,000 N. In a climb the lift is close to the weight, so drag = W/(L/D) = 1,500,000/14 = 107,143 N. Gradient = (T - D)/W = (300,000 - 107,143)/1,500,000 = 0.1286, i.e. 12.86%. The two traps are forgetting to use ALL FOUR engines' thrust and forgetting to derive the drag from the L/D ratio.
zYDNZOTGIlKsngnITbV8: A downhill slope means gravity assists the acceleration throughout the take-off run, so the aeroplane reaches its speeds in a shorter distance and a HIGHER take-off mass fits within the runway available. The trade-off is that the same slope hinders braking, lengthening the stop case - which is why V1 must be reduced on a downhill runway and why the benefit is smaller than the acceleration alone suggests.
ZYp85S1U6xxW9oSh9ejr: Two factors compound. First the turboprop dispatch rule: the landing distance required must not exceed 70% of the LDA, so 0.70 x 2200 = 1540 m is the maximum permitted WET landing distance. Then the wet correction: a wet runway requires 15% more distance than a dry one, so the dry-runway figure must not exceed 1540 / 1.15 = 1339 m. Applying only one of the two factors is the usual error.
